Title: US bans MEXC crypto exchange over sanctions evasion, cybercrime links
Context: Founded in 2018, the Seychelles-based MEXC is one of the world's largest crypto exchanges, giving more than 40 million users from more than 170 countries access to 3,000...
Full Text:
The US Department of the Treasury has cut off the MEXC Global crypto exchange from the US financial system over sanctions evasion and links with cybercrime gangs.

Founded in 2018, the Seychelles-based MEXC is one of the world's largest crypto exchanges, giving more than 40 million users from more than 170 countries access to 3,000 cryptocurrencies and tokenized assets.

According to a Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) order, MEXC has allowed illicit transactions of at least $16 billion linked to cybercrime operations and Iranian, North Korean, and Russian sanctions evasion between May 2021 and May 2026.

The Treasury Department said that, as recently as June 2026, MEXC was still processing transactions with sanctioned Russian entities Garantex and Grinex, and it also facilitated or processed at least $226 million in transactions benefiting or connected to the Russia-based, OFAC-sanctioned A7 sanctions evasion network.

"MEXC Global has not only facilitated Russian illicit finance but has also served as a hub for other types of illicit financial activity, including Iranian and DPRK sanctions evasion, ransomware and scam payments, and Russian and other darknet market activity," the Treasury Department said.

"Between May 2021 and May 2026, MEXC Global had sent or received approximately $1 billion in direct transactions with more than 40 identified Iranian CVC exchangers, some of which are subject to U.S. and international sanctions."

FinCEN has blamed this on deficiencies in the crypto exchange's anti-money laundering (AML) and customer identification and verification policies.

The ban exposes US financial institutions and individuals to secondary sanctions or enforcement actions for transfers of funds to or from the MEXC Global crypto exchange.

In response to FinCEN's ban order, MEXC said that its legal and compliance teams have launched a review of its sanctions and AML controls.

"MEXC is aware of the order issued by the U.S. Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) on November 6, 2026, and is reviewing it closely in coordination with our legal and compliance teams. MEXC is operating normally, and user assets remain secure," MEXC said.

"We take the concerns raised seriously and intend to engage constructively with FinCEN, as well as other relevant regulators and competent authorities worldwide. We have also begun an independent review of our AML and sanctions controls."

According to XLab, a shell script named "cwpsrv_update.sh" is used to download "cwpsrv" from a remote server ("136.0.141[.]71") and replace the legitimate file on the system. "The downloaded cwpsrv is a passive backdoor that can be triggered by specific headers in HTTP/HTTPS traffic to remotely execute commands specified by the attacker," XLab said. "Its backdoor logic is triggered only when it receives a specially crafted request from the attacker. At the same time, it suppresses logging for that request, leaving no trace of the interaction in the access logs. This combination of directly replacing the legitimate cwpsrv binary, passive triggering, and log suppression makes CWPdoor exceptionally stealthy."

Debian and Ubuntu APT Flaw Allows Code Execution as Root — A vulnerability in the APT package manager (CVE-2026-109518, CVSS score: 7.7) can be exploited to install a package under certain conditions and achieve code execution with elevated privileges. The issue affects Ubuntu and Debian operating systems. "Under specific conditions, when APT is configured to use HTTP package sources with retry settings enabled, a third-party with a network position between the host and the package mirror can cause APT to install a package that did not pass verification," Amazon said in an advisory. "Maintainer scripts within that package then run with elevated privileges."

CERT-In Flags AI-Driven Attacks Targeting Financial Organizations — The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has disclosed that an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted threat actor it tracks as Crafty Falcon is targeting organizations in the Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance (BFSI) sectors in the country. Calling it a "significant escalation" in attacks, the threat actor is said to be re-targeting entities that were originally targeted last month after incomplete remediation, adding that the intrusions "have been timed to coincide with holidays, weekends and other low-monitoring windows to delay detection and response."

Zyxel Fixes 0-Day exploited to Hack About 1,000 Network Switches — Zyxel has fixed a zero-day vulnerability in its GS1900 series network switches that threat actors exploited to compromise nearly 1,000 devices worldwide and steal configuration files and credentials. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-107441 (CVSS score: 8.8), is an out-of-bounds write flaw that could "allow a LAN-based, unauthenticated attacker to exploit the flaw and potentially execute OS commands via a crafted HTTP request." The activity has been attributed to a Chinese-speaking threat actor tracked as Kapibala (aka Red Heron). The attacker has been found to weaponize the flaw to deploy the JITTERLY backdoor and SIXZUT, a ring 3 rootkit.

cPGuard Update Mechanism Hijacked to Deliver Backdoor — Unknown threat actors compromised the update infrastructure for the cPGuard web security suite to distribute a backdoor and a data-stealing script. "On 2 November 2026 at 02:06 UTC, an unidentified attacker used compromised credentials to gain unauthorized access to OPSSHIELD's update distribution infrastructure (CDN)," OPSSHIELD said. "The attacker used this access to distribute a malicious script through the cPGuard update channel." The attacker is said to have gotten in through its billing application at manage.opsshield[.]com and logged in to a customer account they had registered.

mSecure Urges Customers to Change their Passwords — Password manager mSecure has warned customers to change their passwords, reset two-factor authentication, and potentially remove their passkeys after detecting suspicious activity, but it has not explained what happened or whether anyone's secrets were exposed. "mSeven Software ('mSeven') recently learned of suspicious activity associated with the mSecure password management application," the company said. "In response, mSeven quickly launched an investigation, took steps to mitigate the issue, and engaged external cybersecurity experts to assist." However, the company has yet to answer what the suspicious activity involved, when it occurred, or whether attackers accessed customer information. The lack of specifics has understandably riled up customers, with one user on Reddit stating "their silence on this is mind-bending." In December 2025, Germany's cyber agency BSI found that mSecure's maker could, in theory, access the data users store in it.

"The attack began with a SharePoint-themed PDF distributed from an apparently legitimate sender and progressed through redirects and browser checks before presenting Microsoft authentication inside an attacker-controlled remote browser," ZeroBEC said. "Its client reconstructs the remote DOM, forwards keyboard and clipboard interactions over WebSocket, survives connection interruptions and supports live operator control," it added.

The findings build upon a previous out-of-bounds read in CPython that could result in a sandbox escape. The issue has been fixed and backported to 3.13, 3.14, and 3.15 branches.

"These external dependencies authorize third-party senders, route incoming mail, provide DNS delegation, and receive security telemetry," SH Consulting said. Title: PyPI makes release attestations easier to find with new security tab
Context: She stressed that such a release isn’t necessarily malicious, since the missing attestation only means its origin can’t be cryptographically verified
Full Text:
The Python Package Index (PyPI) has added a security tab to its project pages, giving developers a place to check where individual release files came from.

How PyPI shows where release files came from

The Security tab shows whether release files have digital attestations, which provide verifiable information about how a file was published or built. A release has full provenance when every file has at least one attestation. A PyPI Publish attestation identifies the Trusted Publisher that uploaded the file, while a SLSA Build Provenance attestation links the file to its source commit, build platform and build instructions. Users can review the attestation details in the tab or open the linked transparency log.

A release has no provenance when none of its files has an attestation. Nicole Harris, PyPI design contributor, said this is common for older releases and projects that have yet to configure Trusted Publishing. She stressed that such a release isn’t necessarily malicious, since the missing attestation only means its origin can’t be cryptographically verified.

In those cases, developers can look at maintainer history, release patterns and repository activity when assessing a package.

Where PyPI shows warnings and release details

PyPI warns users when only some files in a release have attestations or when files in the same release come from different repositories or build systems. Warnings appear when a release comes from a different repository or workflow than a previous version, or when a project that previously provided attestations stops doing so.

A change in workflow often has a legitimate explanation, such as an organization renaming itself or moving its repository, though it may signal a compromised pipeline or an account takeover.

An example provenance warning on PyPI, showing a release with incomplete provenance (Source: PyPI)

The redesigned project page displays provenance warnings at the top, alongside notices for yanked releases, archived projects and pre-releases. If a project or release is quarantined, the page displays only the quarantine banner. For releases where every file is attested or a warning applies, the sidebar shows that status and links to the Security tab.

The Release Files tab lets users search and filter downloads and see the provenance status of each file. For releases that predate PyPI’s July 2026 policy change, the tab flags files uploaded more than 14 days after the initial release. Since that change, PyPI has refused any late uploads.

The Release History tab shows the file count, provenance status and any applicable release status for each version, so users can compare releases from the same page.

Title: 13.3 million people’s medical data exposed; companies pay $300,000
Context: The result: the companies only discovered the attack when the attackers contacted them on May 2, 2023, and demanded payment
Full Text:
The New York attorney general (AG) has reached a settlement over a medical data breach that affected 13.3 million people after basic security failures.

Perry Johnson & Associates (PJ&A) and four related companies have agreed to pay $300,000 and implement extensive security reforms following a breach that exposed personal and medical information belonging to more than 13.3 million people. They face another $9.7 million in penalties if they fail to meet the settlement’s terms.

New York AG Letitia James announced the agreement on November 6, alongside the attorneys general of Connecticut, Michigan, and New Jersey. Approximately 4.2 million of the people affected were New York residents.

The investigation describes a series of failures: remote access without multifactor authentication, nearly identical passwords circulated by email, sensitive files without file-level encryption, and security software that detected malicious activity but did not alert security staff.

The result: the companies only discovered the attack when the attackers contacted them on May 2, 2023, and demanded payment.

How many people were affected?

The stolen database files contained records associated with more than 13.3 million people, including approximately 4.2 million New Yorkers.

Earlier reporting put the number of affected patients at approximately 8.95 million. The settlement documents now give the larger figure of more than 13.3 million. The total could be higher, since the AG found that attackers also accessed files in shared network storage containing personal and health information, but the companies did not review those files to identify additional affected people.

The information included:

Names, dates of birth, and home addresses.

Social Security numbers.

Medical record and hospital account numbers.

Insurance information.

Admission diagnoses and dates of treatment.

Clinical information from medical transcriptions, including test results, medications, treatment facilities, and healthcare providers.

See if your personal data has been exposed.

SCAN NOW

Notifications were also slow. PJ&A began contacting clients about the stolen database files in July 2023, and its clients notified affected individuals between October 31, 2023, and February 8, 2024. The New York AG found that the companies violated state requirements to disclose a breach as quickly as possible and without unreasonable delay.

The settlement

Although the announcement describes a settlement worth up to $10 million, the companies must pay $300,000 in penalties to the states. The remaining $9.7 million is suspended and could become payable. New York will receive $100,000 from the initial payment. These are payments to the states, not an announced compensation payout to patients.

The exposed information could be valuable to criminals. Our research found stolen identity packages selling for as little as 95 cents apiece on the dark web.

The settlement also requires extensive security changes for the relevant active companies, including:

MFA for individual user accounts, including administrator accounts, and remote network access.

Stronger password management and access restricted to what employees need for their jobs.

Encryption of personal and protected health information.

Monitoring that automatically alerts security personnel to suspicious activity.

Annual risk assessments and penetration testing.

Network segmentation and measures to detect and prevent unauthorized data transfers.

Written incident response procedures and clearer rules for retaining and securely disposing of sensitive information.

Given the carelessness, number of exposed records and people, do you think the companies got off cheap? Let us know in the comments.

How to stay safe

A breach does not automatically mean someone has misused your information, but you can take these precautions while you wait for more details:

Verify unexpected messages independently. Don’t let a message about the breach rush you into clicking a link, sharing sensitive information, or making a payment. Go to your healthcare provider or insurer’s official website yourself or use contact details you already trust.

Review medical bills and insurance statements. Look for appointments, tests, prescriptions, or services you did not receive. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) identifies unfamiliar medical bills and unexpected items on an Explanation of Benefits statement, which explains how your insurer processed a claim, as warning signs of medical identity theft. Report discrepancies to your healthcare provider and your insurer.

Review your credit reports. Look for unfamiliar accounts or debts and dispute errors. Free reports are available through AnnualCreditReport.com.

Act if you find signs of identity theft. Visit IdentityTheft.gov for a recovery plan. If someone has received care in your name, ask the providers involved for copies of your medical records and request corrections in writing.

Medical identity theft is not just a financial problem; it can also affect your care. Someone using your identity to obtain treatment or submit insurance claims could introduce incorrect information into your health records. Checking medical statements and reporting anything unfamiliar can help you catch that misuse.

Let’s face it, an incognito window can only do so much. Breaches, dark web trading, credit fraud. Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection monitors for all of it, alerts you fast, and comes with identity theft insurance.

Title: Japanese homeware giant pulls online store after cloud breach puts 7.7M records at risk
Context: Japanese electronics giant Iris Ohyama has taken down its online store after discovering that attackers may have accessed the personal information of 7
Full Text: Japanese electronics giant Iris Ohyama has taken down its online store after discovering that attackers may have accessed the personal information of 7.7 million customers, leaving shoppers unable to place orders. The retailer, which sells everything from home appliances and furniture to pet supplies, first disclosed the incident on October 29, a day after discovering a suspicious file on a third-party cloud service used by its Iris Plaza ecommerce operation. Iris Plaza immediately suspended its website and associated systems and began investigating, subsequently confirming unauthorized access. Iris Ohyama has since revealed that the potentially compromised cloud environment contained personal information belonging to approximately 5.8 million registered customers, including former members, and another 1.9 million people who had purchased products without creating an account or participated in promotional campaigns. The potentially exposed information includes names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, gender, and passwords, although the company says the exact information at risk varies between customers. Some of that data, including passwords, was encrypted, but Iris Ohyama hasn't explained what protection was used. It has advised customers who reused their Iris Plaza passwords elsewhere to change them, presumably before someone else gets the opportunity. There is some good news for anyone who has handed over their credit card details, as the retailer says it didn't store payment information in the affected cloud service and that it hasn't been compromised. It remains unclear whether the attackers actually made off with any personal information. In its FAQ, Iris Plaza says it is still investigating the possibility of a data leak and has yet to establish the full extent of the intrusion. Meanwhile, Iris Plaza's website is still down, and the company isn't saying when it'll be back. Orders are also taking longer to ship, while customers trying to cancel a purchase have been told they may have to turn the delivery driver away if their parcel arrives before the cancellation is processed. Fortunately for anyone desperate to buy a new rice cooker, Iris Plaza's stores on Rakuten, Yahoo! Shopping, and auPAY Market are still operating. The company says it has found no evidence that those stores were affected. Iris Ohyama has reported the incident to Japanese authorities and says it will contact potentially affected customers individually. It has also warned shoppers to watch out for phishing emails, fraudulent calls, and fake websites impersonating the retailer. The company has yet to identify the cloud provider involved, explain how the attackers got in, or establish whether any of those 7.7 million records actually left its systems. ®

Title: Hackers Exploiting ‘SSHole’ Authentication Bypass in OpenSSH
Context: Threat actors have started exploiting SSHole, a recently patched high-severity authentication bypass vulnerability in OpenSSH
Full Text:
Threat actors have started exploiting SSHole, a recently patched high-severity authentication bypass vulnerability in OpenSSH.

Tracked as CVE-2026-123158, the flaw is “related to misinterpretation of whether a string is intended to be a password hash” and could let attackers access certain accounts by supplying any password between 257 and 1024 characters.

Successful exploitation could allow attackers to access accounts such as root, which should never accept a password.

On certain Linux distributions that use the musl libc implementation with the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) disabled, such as Alpine, Buildroot, OpenWrt, Yocto, and others, these accounts do accept a password.

This happens because the OpenSSH server (sshd) checks the supplied password by hashing it against a stored password hash associated with the username.

When an account has no password hash, as with root on Alpine (where the field is ‘*’), sshd borrows the salt from another account’s hash to process the login attempt. For passwords longer than 256 bytes, musl’s crypt() function fails and, instead of returning NULL, returns ‘*’. Because that matches the ‘*’ stored for the target account, sshd treats the password as correct.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

In Alpine, affected accounts include root, any key-only user created with adduser without a password, the Alpine user in the official tiny-cloud images, and any user coming from a directory service through musl-nscd.

Last week, OpenSSH rushed patches for the bug, and Alpine urged users to apply them and restart sshd as soon as possible.

Over the weekend, both WatchTowr and Previdian warned that hackers had started exploiting SSHole in the wild. According to WatchTowr, only botnets and crypto miners have picked it up so far.

“Previdian sensors have observed 20 exploitation attempts, 13 unique attacker IPs, and 9 countries targeting CVE-2026-123158. First observed Nov 06, 2026; last observed Nov 08, 2026,” Previdian said.

Exploitation attempts have also been reported by GreyNoise and Defused.

Users are advised to update to OpenSSH version 10.6p2 as soon as possible. As a mitigation, they can disable password authentication (on by default in OpenSSH) or disable SSH. They should also check logs for unusual requests to identify exploitation attempts.

Title: CISA and the FBI Warn Of Attacks against Industrial Refrigeration Controllers
Context: Attackers may exploit flaws in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to change settings remotely and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles
Full Text:
US agencies warn attackers are going after industrial refrigeration controllers. The fixes are basic, and most start with getting them off the internet.

CISA, the FBI, HHS, USDA and the Department of Transportation published a joint advisory on attacks against industrial refrigeration controllers and cold chain monitoring systems. The activity is global. Healthcare, chemical, food and transport companies use these systems to watch temperatures, keep logs, run defrost cycles and save energy, including in refrigerated trucks.

“The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities.” reads the advisory published by CISA. “The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.”

The targets are electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers used in grocery stores and cold-storage sites. Attackers may exploit flaws in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to change settings remotely and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles. In plain terms, someone could cook your freezer from the other side of the world.

The agencies identify three ways in: bypassing authentication, injecting arbitrary code, and exploiting weak configurations. Once inside, an attacker can change temperatures, which can shorten equipment life, create a fire hazard and destroy stock. Spoiled products that reach consumers can also create a safety risk.

“The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.” continues the adviosry.

An attacker can also hide the damage. Operators lose sight of current temperatures, and that’s a bad moment to learn a cold room has been warm for hours.

CISA’s Chris Butera adds that every organization that depends on these systems should assume it’s a target. The advice follows the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals from CISA and NIST, a minimum set of practices for any organization.

Start with exposure. Keep controller panels off the internet, and if you need remote access, put an up-to-date firewall or similar gateway in front of it. Then separate industrial equipment from the office network with its own virtual network.

Next, fix the basics. Change default passwords, use strong ones, and add phishing-resistant multifactor authentication where you can. Update firmware, and retire or replace devices the maker no longer supports.

Allow only trusted devices and IP addresses to change system settings. Keep tested backups in a separate location, disconnected from the network. Enable logging and regularly check the logs. If devices do not record activity, monitor the network traffic between them.

U.S. organizations should report suspicious activity to CISA’s 24/7 operations center or the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center. Healthcare organizations can also contact HHS.

Reports should include the date, time and location of the incident, a description of the activity, the number of people affected, the equipment involved, and a contact person within the organization.

One control gets forgotten more than the rest. A controller shouldn’t be able to push a freezer past what’s safe, whoever is giving the orders.

“The authoring organizations strongly urge industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring system owners and operators to secure remote access to their OT systems.” concludes the report. “To strengthen system security, owners and operators should review the following resources and implement recommended mitigations:

United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre and Partners: Secure Connectivity Principles for OT“

CISA: Primary Mitigations to Reduce Cyber Threats to Operational Technology

CISA: Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security

CISA: Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance

Three men allegedly used deepfakes of company CEOs and law firm attorneys to trick employees into wiring more than $129 million to accounts the group controlled, the Justice Department said.

The indictment names the three as Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42. Soall used the alias “Rocky Balboa,” and Hazan went by “Superman Cash,” “Impossible Mission” and “Fat Boy,” among others.

The scheme ran from 2024 to 2026 and usually opened with someone posing as the victim company’s chief executive, using AI to mimic the executive’s voice or image on calls.

“While pretending to be the CEO, they would direct the employee to get in touch with lawyers at large international law firms who they said were also working on the sham financial transaction,” the Justice Department wrote.

“They would then also impersonate those lawyers to further make the employee believe that the financial transaction was real. A member of the conspiracy, impersonating one of those lawyers, would ultimately direct the employee to wire a large sum of money in furtherance of that sham financial transaction to a particular bank account, which was in fact controlled by members of the conspiracy,” they added.

Soall mostly played the part of UK attorneys. He kept a handwritten script titled “Lawyer Call” to help him sound like the genuine article, and it included lines meant to keep victims from discussing the calls with their colleagues.

From hospitals to pet food

The victims named in the indictment range from healthcare to finance. Two US hospital systems, one in Missouri and one in California, lost close to $7.8 million between them, and a Rhode Island bank wired out $2.7 million. The largest single loss listed, $11.6 million, hit a UK financial technology company, while a Florida pet food company lost $5.2 million.

The stolen funds went to accounts in the US, Spain, Portugal, Greece, the United Arab Emirates, Singapore, Austria, Slovakia and China. Once a payment landed, the group converted it into cryptocurrency to hide where the money came from and who controlled it, then split it among the conspirators.

Hazan and Sheetrit allegedly handled the laundering. Hazan boasted of laundering money since 1994 and of moving over $400 million in the past three years alone, and he claimed that among professional money launderers he was “number one all over the world.”

Hazan is not a new face to prosecutors, since he was already convicted of conspiracy to commit bank fraud in the Southern District of New York in 2008.

Each of the three men is charged with seven counts, including conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, aggravated identity theft and money laundering. Five of the counts carry a maximum of 20 years in prison, and the two identity theft charges carry two years each.

Deepfakes on company calls

41% of CISOs reported at least one social engineering incident involving a deepfake during an employee audio call in the past 12 months, according to Gartner, and 36% said the same about video calls.

One of the best-known cases of executive impersonation came out of Hong Kong in 2024, when a finance employee at a multinational firm’s branch joined a video call that appeared to include the company’s CFO and several colleagues, then transferred over $25 million to accounts controlled by the scammers.

“The alleged scheme orchestrated by Soall, Hazan, and Sheetrit demonstrates how the use of advanced technology can be exploited to commit large scale fraud,” said FBI Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle, Jr.

US Attorney Jamie McDonald noted the public “should recognize that there are some who seek to use this emerging technology to pursue criminal goals,” and he urged individuals and businesses to think about protecting themselves from this type of crime.

Title: Default 'admin:admin' Server Password Helps Researchers Hack Two Automakers, Unlock and Start Cars
Context: They tested the full attack only on their own and consenting owners' cars in the United States, in February 2026, and both systems were fixed about two hours after they reported...
Full Text:
The login systems behind two car brands' mobile apps could be taken over completely, two security researchers found, allowing them to access any customer's account and, for an owner with a connected car, unlock the doors and start the engine.

Both apps signed customers in through ForgeRock, an identity platform now part of Ping Identity, and on those servers the researchers reached an administrator console that still used its default password.

They tested the full attack only on their own and consenting owners' cars in the United States, in February 2026, and both systems were fixed about two hours after they reported the problem.

Shubham Shah and Sam Curry published their work late last week. They had started with the apps: both brands signed customers in through the same platform, which runs in two parts: one for login and one, called OpenIDM, that holds customer records.

OpenIDM comes with a built-in administrator console powered by the Apache Felix tool. ForgeRock's own hardening guide tells operators to remove this console or protect it before going live because it stores its own password separately from the rest of the system. On these servers, it was still there and still used the documented default: the word admin for both the username and the password.

The console was blocked from the open internet, but the edge that guards the site and the Java software behind it read the same web address differently. By adding encoded slashes and extra characters, the researchers made the edge treat the request as a harmless static file while the server treated it as the path to the console, and the default password did the rest. The full method is in their technical analysis.

Inside the console, the researchers used a built-in scheduler to run small scripts that execute their own code on the identity server. That gave them a command prompt on the machine that holds the customer records for both brands' logins.

The records sat behind the same block as the console, but the researchers' code reached them from inside the server. They changed a target account's email address and password, signed in as that customer through the normal app, and received the same access tokens the real app uses.

Those tokens were the keys to the car. Using the account's own vehicle commands, the researchers unlocked the doors and started the engine of a test car, with the owner standing next to it, then stopped the engine and locked it again.

The researchers were careful about what they had shown. They reported being able to open a session for any customer account on the affected servers, but they ran the vehicle commands only on cars they owned or were allowed to use. They said they "tested the complete chain only with US accounts and vehicles."

Shubham Shah published a second attack on the Australian systems behind the same brands. There, the way in was different: admin credentials for the identity server had been left in the app's code, intended for a test setup. He set out the full Australia chain in a separate post.

With both attacks together, the researchers said, they could send unlock and engine-start commands to the brands' cars in Australia, the United States, and Canada. That second post does not give a date for when the Australian systems were fixed.

The attack left little for an owner to notice. Changing the email and password did not log the owner out of their app, and the researchers could direct the account's alerts to their own phone, keeping them off the owner's phone.

The researchers put the real email address back after the test. Neither write-up says whether anyone else found or used the path before it was closed.

What Identity Teams Should Check

The brands' mistake was in how they ran ForgeRock, not a new bug in the product, so there is no CVE, the public ID that tracks a flaw, and no vendor advisory to follow. The console and its default password have been documented for years, and the maker's production hardening guide already tells operators to remove the console or change its password before going live.

For teams running the same identity software, now sold as PingIDM, two checks matter:

Look for the Apache Felix console at /system/console, and remove it or change its default password.

Do not count on edge or WAF path rules to hide an admin page. A path the edge and the server read differently can slip past the rules, as it did here.

The two researchers have a long record of this kind of work, usually breaking into the web systems behind the apps rather than the cars themselves. They have shown remote access to vehicles from Honda, Kia, and Subaru, among others.

A Subaru flaw they reported exposed owners' accounts and their cars through that carmaker's connected-car service, and a broader 16-brand study in 2023 found the same kind of web weakness across much of the industry.

Title: Web3Auth Flaw Exploited to Steal Keplr Crypto, Provider Empties Other Wallets for Safety
Context: Josh Lee, a Keplr co-founder, gave an early estimate in his initial findings: about 20% of Google and Apple login accounts were affected, and only a fraction of those appeared...
Full Text:
Some people who set up a Keplr crypto wallet with their Google or Apple account have had money stolen by an attacker.

Keplr uses a company called Web3Auth to run that Google and Apple sign-in. The attacker used a security flaw at that company to reach the wallets, both companies said late last week.

Web3Auth then used the attacker's own route to empty other at-risk wallets before the attacker got to them, it said. It moved that money, with help from the wallet maker, into recovery wallets for safekeeping. So an empty balance may mean the money was rescued, not stolen.

Wallets made with a recovery phrase (a backup list of 12 or 24 words) or a hardware wallet are not affected, the wallet maker said. It has paused Google and Apple sign-in while it investigates.

What Affected Users Should Do

The wallet maker has given this user guidance for accounts created with Google or Apple login:

Do not send new funds to the account.

Do not re-import the account or recreate it anywhere.

Move any funds that are not staked or locked to an account that uses a recovery phrase or a hardware wallet.

Trust updates only from the official accounts of the wallet maker and the login provider, and ignore direct messages or links that offer "recovery."

Staked and locked assets are taking longer to secure. The wallet maker is also working with the login provider on a way for users to check whether their account was affected.

In the meantime, the login provider has published a recovery address list, which it says lets people tell its own transfers apart from possibly malicious ones.

It has also warned users not to assume that an unfamiliar destination address is linked to the attacker.

What Went Wrong

In an incident update, Web3Auth said a security issue in its own infrastructure affected certain wallets it provides inside the Keplr app.

Keplr went further, saying the flaw led to a "private key breach" for some users who signed in with Google or Apple. A private key is the secret code that approves payments from a wallet, so whoever holds it can move the money.

Neither company has said how the flaw worked, when the attacker first used it, or whether that route is now closed.

Where the Money Went

No dollar figure for the theft has come from either company. Josh Lee, a Keplr co-founder, gave an early estimate in his initial findings: about 20% of Google and Apple login accounts were affected, and only a fraction of those appeared to have been exploited.

GoPlus, a Web3 security company, said in a security alert that at least about $1 million had been stolen. It did not explain how it reached that figure.

The rescued money went into what the login provider calls secure recovery wallets, on 11 blockchains in the Cosmos family and eight Ethereum-style chains.

Bitquery, a blockchain data firm, counted at least $6.01 million moving from more than 44,000 wallets into the recovery wallets by late last week. The firm first reported the transfers as theft. It has since issued a corrected analysis that treats them as the rescue, though it says it cannot check who controls the recovery wallets.

The first of these transfers came 21 minutes before the login provider's first public notice, the firm's data shows. Most of the wallets, 86%, were emptied after the wallet maker warned users.

The moved funds are safe, the login provider said in its recovery thread, and it is working with the wallet maker to return them to users. It has not said how or when.

Beyond Keplr

The login provider said the issue affects its services used by some other companies, but Keplr is the only one it has named. It paused its embedded wallet service, which other apps use to build wallets for their users. Its status page still shows its login service as down today.

Consensys, the company behind the MetaMask wallet, bought the login provider in June 2025. Its acquisition announcement said the deal would let MetaMask users create and recover wallets with social logins. The provider said its initial investigation found "no evidence that MetaMask users are impacted."

Title: Exploited SonicWall SSL-VPN flaw lets attackers bypass SAML-enforced MFA (CVE-2026-19868)
Context: SonicWall has fixed an exploited SonicOS SSL-VPN vulnerability (CVE-2026-19868) that may allow attackers with valid credentials to bypass SAML-enforced multi-factor authentication
Full Text:
SonicWall has fixed an exploited SonicOS SSL-VPN vulnerability (CVE-2026-19868) that may allow attackers with valid credentials to bypass SAML-enforced multi-factor authentication.

With no workarounds listed, the company has urged admins to patch quickly.

About CVE-2026-19868

CVE-2026-19868 is an authentication enforcement flaw in the SonicOS SSL-VPN service, and is exploitable only if SAML is enabled for SSL-VPN logins.

According to SonicWall, a user with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method may be able to bypass SAML authentication controls and, with them, any MFA enforced through SAML.

In practice, that means a VPN login that should have gone through the organization’s identity provider (e.g., Okta or Microsoft Entra ID) and its MFA check can succeed with a password alone.

This is not an unauthenticated bypass: attackers need working credentials first. But stolen VPN credentials are hardly in short supply, and SAML-enforced MFA is exactly the control many organizations rely on to make them useless for attackers.

The same SonicOS releases fix six other vulnerabilities, none of which have been flagged as exploited.

The vulnerabilities affect Gen7 and Gen8 physical and virtual firewall appliances running firmware versions 7.3.3-7015 and older and 8.2.2-8015 and older. Fixes have been shipped in versions 7.3.4-7013 and higher, and v8.2.3-8015.

Gen6 firewalls are not listed as affected, but they have reached the end-of-support stage, and SonicWall advises customers running those or older hardware to upgrade to a Gen8 firewall.

No attack details and no IoCs

“SonicWall PSIRT has investigated a report indicating potential exploitation of [CVE-2026-19868],” the company said, but has not shared any details about the attacks.

SonicWall SSL-VPN devices have been a favorite target of ransomware-linked attackers for a while now: in 2025, Akira affiliates compromised SonicWall firewalls even though OTP-based MFA was enabled, and earlier this year ReliaQuest observed attackers exploiting CVE-2024-12802, another SonicWall SSL-VPN MFA bypass, in multiple environments.

CVE-2026-19868 was discovered and reported by Ryan Harris of IT services provider Electronic Office.

CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog based on evidence of active exploitation. US civilian federal agencies are required to address it by November 20, 2026.

It’s currently unknown how many organizations have been hit and what the attackers did once they got in. Neither SonicWall nor CISA has published indicators of compromise (IoCs), and no security company has yet published an analysis of the attacks.

With that in mind, organizations that use SAML for SSL-VPN logins should:

Review recent SSL-VPN logins and look for any that succeeded without a matching sign-in (and MFA check) in the identity provider’s logs.

Reset the credentials of any account that logged in that way, and check what was accessed via those sessions.

Title: Crédit Mutuel Arkéa Targeted in Reported $133m Heist
Context: Crédit Mutuel Arkéa issued a statement on November 4 confirming that it had been a victim “of an attack that enabled fraudulent transactions to be carried out
Full Text:
A leading French banking group has moved to reassure customers that their funds are safe after reports emerged of a $133m heist.

Crédit Mutuel Arkéa issued a statement on November 4 confirming that it had been a victim “of an attack that enabled fraudulent transactions to be carried out.”

The hackers reached the bank’s network via the platform of a service provider, it added in an FAQ on the incident.

“The attackers used Crédit Mutuel Arkéa's own account to make transactions to other banking institutions, which then potentially allowed them to convert this money into cryptocurrency via specialized platforms,” it said.

“They did not, therefore, use customer accounts belonging to its federations or subsidiaries. We have communicated that this incident has no financial consequences for our customers. As soon as this attack was identified, our teams immediately activated the necessary security measures to contain the incident and prevent any further fraudulent activity against us.”

Read more on big-money heists: Brazilian Fintech Giant Sinqia Reveals $130m Heist Attempt

Suspicious Withdrawals Traced Across Multiple Exchanges

The incident first came to light on November 2 when blockchain investigator, “ZachXBT,” claimed in a Telegram post that an unnamed “EU entity” had lost $106m from “multiple centralized exchange accounts.”

ZachXBT ruled out the involvement of notorious North Korean hackers the Lazarus Group.

“Over the past 24 hours the illicit actor has been aggressively swapping USDC for ETH, transferring to instant exchanges (WellWallet, Kyrrex, etc), converting to XMR via Wagyu, and bridging across multiple chains,” they explained.

The investigator posted an updated the day after claiming to have spotted an additional $27m of fraudulent centralized exchange account (CEX) withdrawals.

“My working theory is a large financial institution in Western Europe was exploited and it’s currently being covered up,” they said. “No proper incident disclosure has resulted in $30m+ being laundered away which could have been frozen by EU law enforcement.”

However, Crédit Mutuel Arkéa noted in its FAQ that it was “still too early” to say for sure how much was taken.

“Our teams are continuing their work to precisely assess the financial consequences of this attack: some of the funds involved have been frozen, and other actions are underway to recover them,” it said.

“We can already confirm that the amounts involved are in no way likely to jeopardize the financial health and stability of Crédit Mutuel Arkéa.”

The bank urged customers to be on the lookout for potential phishing attempts in the aftermath of the incident and resulting publicity.

The news comes just days after North Korean hackers stole an estimated $6.3bn from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, in what has been described as the biggest theft of its kind ever seen.

Title: $133 million stolen from French bank via exploited service provider
Context: The bank disclosed the incident in a press statement released on November 4, saying it had been hit by “an attack that allowed fraudulent transactions to be carried out
Full Text:
Attackers siphoned an estimated $133 million from Crédit Mutuel Arkéa by using the bank’s own account to wire money to other banks, from where it was possibly converted into cryptocurrency.

The French cooperative banking group, which has €211.5 billion in total assets and more than 5.8 million customers, confirmed the attack days after blockchain investigator ZachXBT began tracking over $100 million in suspected stolen funds moving out of centralized exchange accounts.

The bank disclosed the incident in a press statement released on November 4, saying it had been hit by “an attack that allowed fraudulent transactions to be carried out.” Once the attack was detected, the group informed the relevant authorities and supervisors and temporarily suspended some transactions to stop further fraudulent transfers.

“This incident has no consequences for their assets and has only caused a delay in the execution of certain transfers,” it told customers.

A theft traced on-chain

ZachXBT first flagged the incident in a “community alert” on his Telegram channel, saying an unnamed EU entity was suspected of losing over $106 million from multiple centralized exchange accounts on November 1. The funds were withdrawn as USDC and USDT stablecoins, and the thief then swapped them for ether, moved them through instant exchanges and converted part of them to Monero, he wrote.

He could not identify the attacker, but said he was confident “it is NOT Lazarus Group based on multiple laundering indicators.”

On November 3, he reported another $27 million in exchange withdrawals by the same threat actor, bringing the total to $133 million.

“My working theory is a large financial institution in Western Europe was exploited and it’s currently being covered up,” the investigator wrote. “No proper incident disclosure has resulted in $30M+ being laundered away which could have been frozen by EU law enforcement.”

The next day he named Crédit Mutuel Arkéa as the alleged victim, describing it as a French bank with $235 billion in assets. “The attack on the bank occurred for multiple days. I suspect the amount stolen is larger when accounting for OTC activity,” he added.

The Fortuneo claim

French journalist Grégory Raymond, who first linked the attack to Fortuneo, the group’s online bank, posted on X that the fraudsters were able to initiate transfers from Fortuneo while setting the beneficiary name themselves.

According to his sources, networks using falsified identities had opened accounts at crypto exchanges, and each transfer was sent in the exact name of the account holder so it would pass checks that match the sender with the account owner.

One of his sources described these networks as “perfectly well-oiled structures,” and Raymond believes the total losses may be higher than the $133 million visible on the blockchain. Arkéa rejects this, saying that contrary to some claims in the press, no “entry” was made through Fortuneo.

The bank’s version of events

The bank later published a Q&A addressing the main questions it had received about the attack. In it, Arkéa explained that the attackers did not go through the accounts of customers at its federations or subsidiaries, and reached the bank directly through the platform of one of its service providers, which it did not name.

The group denied that human error on its side caused the breach, and described it as a sophisticated attack from outside that has since been contained. Its teams are working with judicial and police authorities to determine where the attack came from and the methods used, the bank added.

Asked whether €118 million ($133 million) had been stolen, the bank declined to confirm the number and said it could “simply validate the order of magnitude.”

Part of the funds has been blocked and other recovery efforts are under way, according to Arkéa, which added that it is too early to give a final amount. It maintains that the sums involved do not threaten its financial health.

Phishing warning

The bank warned that phishing attempts may follow the attack and asked customers never to share login IDs, passwords, card numbers or verification codes received by SMS.

Asked whether this meant customer data had been compromised, the group said phishing campaigns often increase after attacks of this kind and that the warning was a preventive step.

“If in doubt, contact your bank adviser directly to confirm the message you received,” Arkéa advised.

Title: LNbits Urges All Operators to Shut Down Their Bitcoin Lightning Wallet Servers Amid Attacks
Context: The attack ran from 09:22 to 14:00 UTC yesterday, starting more than three hours before the project's first warning at 12:33 UTC
Full Text:
Everyone running LNbits, a free, open-source Bitcoin Lightning wallet system, should shut down their servers now because of a wave of attacks, the project said yesterday.

It has several security fixes to release and asked operators to be careful until they are out. One operator said new accounts used an exploit to withdraw 2,285,545 satoshis, about 0.023 bitcoin, from his server before he could stop it.

The shutdown notice came about 80 minutes after a first, narrower warning. That warning asked operators to disable Paywall, an add-on that makes people pay to view content, while the project looked into a possible bug.

As of 09:00 UTC today, the project had not released a fixed version. On X, it had not canceled the notice, offered another option, or told operators how to check whether their servers were hit before they were shut down.

Ben Arc, an LNbits developer, said in a patch estimate yesterday that patches "should be merged and available within 24-48hrs." Counted from his post, that means between about 14:00 UTC today and 14:00 UTC tomorrow.

The project also switched off all the LNbits instances it runs for users on its cloud service, my.lnbits.com, later yesterday. It said in a hosted-service notice that all services would be back within 24 hours, or by about 17:20 UTC today.

Kevin Ravensberg, the operator who reported the loss, said in a loss report on X that his server was exploited before the shutdown notice. The attack ran from 09:22 to 14:00 UTC yesterday, starting more than three hours before the project's first warning at 12:33 UTC.

He has promised to repay users of BitTipBot, a Telegram bot. They cannot reach their funds until the project fixes the flaws.

Later yesterday, Ravensberg said in a follow-up post that Arc and a team of security testers had confirmed "which exact extension exploit was used" on his server. Neither he nor the project had named that extension in posts on X as of 09:00 UTC today. The project also had not said whether it is Paywall, the add-on named in its first warning.

The shutdown notice covers LNbits servers and does not mention Lightning nodes or other wallet software. It did not say how many servers were attacked or how much was taken.

Title: DHS Has Used This Controversial Investigative Tool 185,000 Times Since Trump Took Office
Context: To put HSI’s estimate into perspective, a previous WIRED analysis found that in the more than six and a half years from the start of 2016 to mid-August 2022, ICE agents only...
Full Text:
Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative wing of Immigration and Customs Enforcement that normally takes on transnational crime, estimates it has sent out at least 185,000 administrative subpoenas since the start of the Trump administration, according to a recent court filing. The figure shows how HSI has increasingly relied on this warrantless authority to conduct investigations.

To put HSI’s estimate into perspective, a previous WIRED analysis found that in the more than six and a half years from the start of 2016 to mid-August 2022, ICE agents only sent out around 170,000 of a type of administrative subpoena called a 1509 customs summons.

The number of administrative subpoenas was revealed as part of a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security filed by the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Aaron Mackey, deputy legal director at the nonprofit, says the EFF hopes to get more details about the 185,000 estimate. The EFF originally asked for information about how many administrative subpoenas were sent to technology companies, internet platforms, and service providers by ICE or DHS since January 20, 2025. It’s not clear if that count is just for administrative subpoenas sent to those types of companies or if it includes a much broader set.

Administrative subpoenas are a powerful but unchecked investigative tool. Unlike with a grand jury subpoena or a court order, the government doesn’t have to explain to the courts why it needs the documents or what data it’s requesting from a company.

Since the start of the Trump administration, the federal government has used DHS’s administrative subpoena power to try to unmask anonymous online critics and pursue broad customer records about protesters. This includes, for example, a list of people in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area who bought a specific green beanie from REI.

Congress originally granted the use of 1509 customs summons to the then stand-alone US Customs Service nearly a century ago, with the idea that it would let customs officers inspect business records related to importing merchandise and figure out whether they owed customs duties. In 2003, Congress transferred that agency’s powers, including the ability to issue customs summons, to the newly formed Department of Homeland Security.

In the past, DHS has maintained that customs summons could be used only for specific purposes. The DHS inspector general admonished Customs and Border Protection’s Office of Professional Responsibility in 2017 for trying to use a customs summons to unmask an anonymous Twitter poster, pointing out that its own procedures manual said that customs summons could only be used to obtain information related to customs or immigrations laws.

Title: Product showcase: What the Malwarebytes Claude connector reveals about unexpected texts
Context: You can paste a link or upload a screenshot of a message, then ask Claude to check the details against Malwarebytes’ threat database
Full Text:
The Malwarebytes connector for Claude checks suspicious links, phone numbers, and email addresses without leaving the chat. You can paste a link or upload a screenshot of a message, then ask Claude to check the details against Malwarebytes’ threat database. The connector works with free and paid Claude plans and requires no separate Malwarebytes account.

Setting permissions for each tool

The connector has six tools, including options to look up domain registration details, scan several items at once, and report suspected scams.

You can set permissions for each tool separately. Ask requires Claude to request permission before each use. Always allow lets it use the tool without prompting. Block hides the tool from Claude.

Testing a connector

I tested the connector with two screenshots and left the tools set to Ask. The first showed a text claiming to come from Croatia’s Ministry of the Interior. It said I had an unpaid speeding fine and called itself a third warning. When Claude requested permission to check the sender’s number, I chose Allow once.

Malwarebytes returned Unknown for the phone number. Claude flagged the message as a likely scam, citing the sender’s Philippine country code and the pressure to act.

The second screenshot showed two IKEA delivery updates, each with a shortened link. Both came back Unknown. The scan showed that one link redirected toward an IKEA order page and marked the other Offline. Seeing the redirect gave me a detail to verify in the IKEA app without opening the link from the text.

Conclusion

Malwarebytes and Claude helped identify signs of scam and explain why the message looked suspicious. The test showed how the integration can help you understand the risks before clicking a link or replying.

Title: Anti-Money Laundering Watchdog FATF Targets Scam Compounds
Context: Often staffed by trafficked victims, 120,000 of whom are forced to carry out online scams in Myanmar alone, these operations are also supported by crypto and instant payment...
Full Text:
A leading anti-money laundering (AML) organization has called for global action to disrupt the scam compounds responsible for a considerable volume of transnational fraud.

AML watchdog the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) warned in a new report that large physical scam compounds are a major driver of a global fraud economy estimated to be worth $500bn annually.

Often staffed by trafficked victims, 120,000 of whom are forced to carry out online scams in Myanmar alone, these operations are also supported by crypto and instant payment platforms, money mules, social media, messaging services and AI-enabled content, FATF said.

The trend is increasingly one of smaller and more mobile operations, with compounds created out of repurposed casinos, rented rooms, apartments, coffee shops and even moving vehicles, the report warned.

Read more on scam compounds: Scam Centers Expand Global Footprint with Trafficked Victims

The FATF report noted that countries are generally better at tackling scam compounds through downstream action such as asset tracing and targeting victim payments.

But it called on FATF member nations to combine these efforts with upstream disruption targeting things like fraudulent advertising, recruitment activity, malicious domains and suspicious phone numbers and telecom indicators,

“With criminals weaponizing AI and other technologies to intensify their scam operations, we need to urgently modernize and accelerate our response,” argued FATF president, Giles Thomson. “This means focusing on dismantling the criminal networks behind scam compounds, working proactively with technology, social media and communications sectors to prevent and disrupt more scams before they happen, and quicker intervention to freeze and seize the proceeds of scams once they’ve happened.”

Six Principles to Combat Illicit Money Flows

With this in mind, the FATF report promoted six pillars to its approach:

Shift the focus from physical compounds to criminal leaders, recruiters and traffickers, and other supporting players

Disrupt the infrastructure and services, including stopping, tracing, freezing and recovering victim payments

Share information between financial institutions, technology companies, telcos and authorities

Act at speed across borders, as the first 24-72 hours after a scam are critical for freezing funds and recovering assets

Ensure investigations put the protection of trafficked and scam victims front and center

Continuously update approaches as scam operations decentralize and adapt

Jonathan Frost, director of global advisory at BioCatch, welcomed the focus on compounds and the need for action by platform providers.

“Those platforms need to act on what they can already see. But when push comes to shove, banks are often the last and sometimes the only line of defense,” he added. “Funds can leave an account in minutes, and customers are often groomed into trusting the scammer over their bank. Banks must detect the manipulation itself, not just the transaction, and intervene before the money moves.”

A CybSafe report published last month found that over a fifth (22%) of Brits have received a scam call impersonating a familiar person’s voice or appearance. Over a third (36%) of these reports have led to their employer losing money or data.

Title: Taiwan-Based Hacker Used BOSSAI AI Agents to Steal Taipei Emergency Dispatch Records
Context: A single attacker using AI agents pulled emergency dispatch records covering seven Taipei districts, researchers at Acronis's Threat Research Unit said last week
Full Text:
A single attacker using AI agents pulled emergency dispatch records covering seven Taipei districts, researchers at Acronis's Threat Research Unit said last week.

The agents also found a Taipei fire department platform exposing patient data from 2018, including ECG readings and ambulance video footage, without a login.

The researchers are highly confident that the attacker is a single person based in Hualien City, Taiwan. He aimed the agents at hundreds of organizations in at least 11 countries, including emergency services, banks, universities and military systems. The agents collected data or accessed systems at about 10 of them in Taiwan, Mexico and Thailand.

The evidence comes from the attacker's own server, which initially appeared to be a misconfigured development system. It turned out to be his operational attack platform, containing more than 90,000 files, including the agents' conversations, his command history, hacking tools, credentials, and victims' data.

The agents did not communicate with each other, so the attacker manually pasted one agent's output into another. Commercial AI models mostly refused to help him attack. The attacking agents therefore ran almost entirely on "abliterated" models, meaning AI models run locally with their safety training removed.

What the Agents Reached

Taiwan was targeted far more heavily than any other country, according to the researchers' technical analysis. The most serious confirmed harm there involved emergency-services data.

The dispatch records came from a city's system for 119, Taiwan's emergency number for fire and ambulance services. The agents pulled them from the system's API, and they include incident times, response types, case status, and street-level locations. They are case records, not live ambulance tracking.

The researchers' summary says breaches at emergency services and universities led to the theft of medical and personal data. Their detailed account of the Taipei patient platform, however, says only that the records were exposed.

The agents also went after five other targets tied to Taiwan's emergency services:

Target

What the agents did

Result

Fire-dispatch technology vendor

Logged into its database admin panel with default root credentials. A web shell attempt through a known CVE failed.

Access to 18 or more database tables

Emergency management information system

Found a hardcoded AES-256 key in the site's front-end JavaScript that exposed session-cookie contents, including an administrator's identity

No confirmed compromise

National disaster-response center

A scanning tool reported a critical Apache remote code execution flaw

The flaw did not exist

National fire agency single sign-on portal

Tried to guess logins (brute force)

No confirmed access

Fire-department systems in five cities

Scanned them to identify the software they run

No confirmed compromise

The report does not say whether the affected organizations or Taiwan's authorities were told, or whether the exposed data can still be reached.

Outside emergency services, the agents pulled data from an account table at a Taiwanese lending firm through SQL injection. In Thailand, they collected data from three universities in the same way, after selecting 489 potential targets across 45 institutions.

In Mexico, they collected about 206,800 home phone records containing names and addresses, using government statistics, postal code lists, and telecom authority data.

About 15 more organizations were attacked without a confirmed break-in. In at least eight other countries, targets were only scanned or lined up for attacks that had not run by the time the researchers looked.

The researchers watched the operation for 12 days. One recorded exchange shows the attacker at work on July 25.

How the AI Was Used and Where It Failed

The setup, called BOSSAI, had 12 AI agents, with 9 in use. Some built and maintained the attacker's servers and tools, while others scanned targets and carried out attacks.

Commercial cloud models did most of the building, with Grok as the main builder. When the attacker directly asked them to attack, Grok and MiniMax M3 refused and requested written proof that the work was authorized. The researchers say it is unclear whether a fake authorization letter would have changed that.

Grok made one exception, repairing a broken proof-of-concept script that the attacker then handed to an attack agent. The attacker also redirected the coding agents Claude Code and Codex to an abliterated model, though they mostly did infrastructure work. Cursor, another coding agent, attacked a Taiwanese emergency-services site while running such a model.

The abliterated models were versions of DeepSeek, GLM, and Qwen.

The agents also got things wrong. One scanning tool invented CVEs, and more than half of its high and critical findings were false positives or wrongly classified. The main attack agent also reported results that had not happened.

Who Ran It

Acronis's attribution rests on mistakes the attacker made while hiding his identity, combined with publicly available information. He reused a single identity across his legitimate businesses and his attack servers, including a GitHub profile, a logo, an SSH key name, and an email address.

His home IP address appeared during an SSH session in one of his Grok conversations.

Why he did it is less clear. Some attacks on government, emergency, and military targets looked like the work of state-backed hacking groups, while others looked like ordinary cybercrime. The researchers think he probably wanted to make money, and it is unclear whether he works for anyone.

What Stopped the Agents

What the agents found was mostly data that was already poorly protected, according to the researchers: a medical data port left open since 2018, dispatch records on a public-facing API, a lender with 16 SQL injection points, and universities running unpatched Oracle databases.

The agents failed where logins were enforced, where paywalls required a valid session, and where endpoints were properly filtered. The AI made it cheap to find and reach many targets at once, but it did not get past defenses that held.

Nine IP addresses and nine domains from the attacker's setup appear in the indicator list at the end of the analysis. None is marked as active or inactive, and most come without a note on what they were used for.

Title: The code and the court: Why your email security thinks like Napoleon
Context: A codified system is only as current as its code
Full Text:
In 1804, Napoleon gave France a code that much of the world still runs on. The Code civil replaced a tangle of local customs with a single written statute: orderly and knowable. In that tradition, the judge’s job, in Montesquieu’s phrase, is to be the mouth of the law, nothing more. Certainty was the point.

Certainty has a cost. A codified system is only as current as its code. When the world produces something the code did not anticipate — a new technology, a new fraud — there is no statute to apply, and everyone waits for someone to write one.

Your email security works exactly this way. That is the problem.

Security by statute

A signature is a statute. Someone observes an attack, writes a rule that describes it, and from that moment you are protected against that attack and its close relatives. It is fast, certain, and blind to anything the code has not been written to see.

Signatures alone were never enough, so the industry made the code bigger. Anomaly detection and behavioral models are a thicker statute book, trained on what already happened and scoring how far a message deviates from it. More sophisticated than a signature, but not a different philosophy. A zero-day is a crime with no statute.

The strongest evidence against codified defense is not the attack that fails a check. It is the attack that passes every one. When a supplier’s mailbox is compromised, the message arrives from a real domain, with valid credentials and earned reputation. Every check comes back clean because the infrastructure is genuine. Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that breaches involving a third party now account for 48% of the total, up 60% in a single year. Authentication did exactly what it measures: it confirmed the letter came from who it said, and had no rule for whether it should be believed. The code was consulted. The code said valid. The message was a theft in progress.

Attackers understand this. A codified defense is cheap to walk around. You do not break the code; you do something it was never written to cover. The FBI’s 2025 Internet Crime Report put business email compromise losses above $3 billion in a single year, much of it carried by messages that broke no rule because no rule described them.

The other tradition

The English-speaking world chose a different system. Common law does not always wait for the legislature. A judge facing a situation no statute anticipated can reason from principle and precedent to a verdict. It adapts case by case. It is not simply a code that has to be rewritten. It is a court that knows how to weigh a new set of facts.

That is the difference between detecting and reasoning. The fair objection is that a reasoning system also learns from the past. True. But there is a difference between matching a case to a stored pattern and applying a principle to a case you have never seen. A judge who has never encountered your particular dispute still knows how to weigh evidence.

None of this means throwing out the code. Most mail is open and shut and should be settled that way in milliseconds. You keep the fast rule for the easy calls and save a full hearing for the contested ones.

A court can also answer a question a code struggles with: why. A codified system can say “this matched” or “this deviated.” A verdict can cite its evidence: what the sender actually is, whether the relationship supports the request, what the message is asking for. You do not have to trust the reasoning. You check the evidence, because a ruling stands or falls on whether its facts hold up, not on the private thoughts of the judge. It is the opposite of a black box: a decision you can read, challenge, and overturn.

None of this retreats from zero trust. Zero trust governs access, who gets in and what they can touch, and assumes nothing. This is about the verdict, whether a message is what it claims to be, and there the posture is not to presume guilt or innocence but to let the evidence decide.

The court of last resort

For the highest stakes matters, a mature legal system does not let the machinery decide alone. In security, some decisions belong with the person whose money is about to move.

When a message asks for a wire, a change to vendor banking details or a payroll redirect, the right design does not render a silent verdict and hope. It escalates and asks the owner to approve the action itself. Reasoning handles the general docket. The human is the court of last resort, reserved for the decisions that deserve one. Match the process to the stakes.

No analogy is perfect. Real judges in both traditions do more than this, and civil-law systems evolve through their own doctrine.

The question worth ending on

For most of this industry’s history, there was no choice, because machines could apply a code but could not weigh evidence and reason for a judgment. That is no longer true.

There is a simple way to find out which system you are running. Ask your team how many attacks that reached a user came from infrastructure you already trust: a compromised vendor, a real account, a genuine DocuSign or Microsoft notification bent to a purpose it was never meant for. If that number is high, your defenses are not failing to enforce the code. They are enforcing it perfectly; against threats the code was never written to describe.

So, the question is not whether your defenses are up to date. A code is always, by definition, up to date with yesterday. The question is whether your security is a code or a court, and whether it can rule on the case it has never seen, because that is the only case that was ever going to hurt you.

Title: Google DeepMind’s AI Agents Make 1024-Bit RSA Keys Cheaper to Attack
Context: Google DeepMind says AI agents working under human supervision have found two ways to reduce the cost of attacking 1024-bit RSA cryptosystems
Full Text:
Google DeepMind says AI agents working under human supervision have found two ways to reduce the cost of attacking 1024-bit RSA cryptosystems.

The research, conducted with cryptographers from UC San Diego and Inria, indicates that attacks on legacy RSA-1024 require less computation than previously assumed.

“In practice, these results only affect obsolete 1024-bit RSA systems, and modern encryption protocols, which almost universally use 2048-bit or larger keys, remain secure,” said Pushmeet Kohli, VP at Google DeepMind and chief scientist at Google Cloud.

The first finding involves digital signatures and padding, the preset data that many signature standards add to a message to bring it to a fixed block size. Padding was known to make forgery harder, but its value against an attacker who can choose what gets signed was unclear.

DeepMind determined that it depends on the share of the signed block the attacker controls. “Once they control roughly half of the block or more, padding adds no protection at all,” Kohli explained.

According to the accompanying paper, this applies to the PKCS#1 v1.5 format used by the PKCS#11 signing interface of cryptographic devices such as hardware security modules (HSMs).

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

In a sandboxed test, the agents re-ran an earlier academic forgery attack on the same 1024-bit key, cutting CPU time 3.5-fold. The first forgery took 391 CPU core-years, versus 1,380 in the original study.

Two AI agents designed, ran and debugged the forgery computation in under four days, with approximately 20 messages from the human researcher, mostly approvals. The key was not factored; that would take an estimated 500,000 to 1 million core-years.

Forgery is harder when the attacker controls less of the block, such as a 32-byte hash. Even then, DeepMind found an algorithm that by its theoretical estimates is roughly 1,600 times better than the previous best method against 1024-bit keys.

The second finding concerns factoring many RSA keys of the same size, where an attacker can share the cost of one large upfront computation across all of them.

DeepMind’s agents came up with an algorithm that makes factoring each additional 1024-bit key roughly 30 times cheaper on average than the best previous approach. However, this theoretical estimate assumes an initial computation as costly as factoring one key, and the method has not been implemented.

The researchers noted that the signature attack does not recover the private key. It requires roughly 4 billion signing queries made in advance, and does not work against devices that hash messages internally.

“Together, these results show that in a new era of AI-enabled mathematics and computation, we cannot treat cryptographic hardness as a fixed assumption. Using AI to rigorously test our previously held assumptions will ensure that modern encryption stays secure,” Kohli said.
