Title: 7 tips for achieving defensive agility
Context: McGlasson points to the recent “Citrix meltdown,” a severe, ongoing security crisis affecting Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances, creating a mass wave of...
Full Text:
Defensive security agility reflects an organization’s potential to rapidly detect, adapt, and respond to evolving cyber threats and vulnerabilities without disrupting core operations. By abandoning static, rigid defense architectures, an agile defense plan emphasizes continuous iteration, automation, and cross-functional flexibility.

Defensive agility allows cybersecurity teams to rapidly adapt and respond to evolving threats while minimizing business disruption, says Anant Adya, an executive vice president at business and technology consulting firm Infosys. “As attack surfaces expand, organizations must prioritize risk quantification and identify vulnerabilities to strengthen their security posture and improve their ability to recover from attacks that are inevitable.”

Is your organization taking the steps needed to achieve a high degree of defensive agility? Read on to find out.

1. Establish a zero-trust baseline

Achieving defensive agility should begin with a zero-trust approach that continuously verifies access across users, devices, and applications, Adya advises. “An effective zero-trust strategy must be embedded into an organization’s technology framework and business lifecycle in order to build resilience and foster an organization-wide security mindset.”

As enterprises adopt AI, modernize applications, and operate across highly distributed environments, security must evolve from a protective afterthought into a business accelerant, Adya says. “By integrating zero trust into day-to-day operations and AI workflows, organizations can strengthen their ability to adapt to evolving threats while innovating faster, integrating acquisitions more securely, and scaling globally without accumulating architectural or operational debt.”

2. Modernize (and rationalize) your existing security infrastructure

Many large organizations are struggling to keep pace with emerging challenges because their systems are incredibly complex or filled with old software, custom code, and a mixture of disconnected security tools that can hinder containment speed, says Sharon Chand, cyber defense and resilience leader at Deloitte.

Chand advises CISOs to evaluate their existing infrastructure and technologies to consider how they’re currently responding to threats. Meanwhile, it’s important to streamline operations into a more integrated system. “Security organizations must also have access to AI-driven systems to detect and automate response to machine-speed attacks at the pace of adversaries,” she states.

3. Enlist AI where confidence is high and actions are reversible

Randy Gross, CISO at training and certification organization CompTIA, recommends deciding in advance which defensive actions are safe enough to happen without placing a human in the middle. “Locking an account, killing a session, or isolating a device should already be automated when confidence is high and the action is easy to reverse,” he says.

Review your strategy at least quarterly, but never equate a strategy review with operational governance, Gross warns. “In a medium-to-large enterprise, agents’ permissions and integrations may change frequently, so the guardrails around them must be continuous and automated,” he advises. “The CISO and team should also revisit their strategy when enough changes have been made to the point where risk has changed materially.”

Gross adds: “The strategy shouldn’t be just to put more AI in the SOC; it should be to reduce the latency between finding a threat and doing something useful about it.”

4. Forego higher walls in favor of dynamic, structural resilience

Defensive agility requires an enterprise system with the architectural capacity to absorb, isolate, and adapt to anomalous behavior without relying on human intervention, says Jatin Chopra, a senior software engineer at Microsoft. “It marks the transition from static perimeter defense — where you build higher walls — to dynamic, structural resilience where the environment itself constantly shifts to restrict threat propagation.”

Using an approach with sufficient capacity also detaches security from manual bottlenecking, Chopra says. “When defensive protocols are codified into the architecture rather than enforced by a review board, engineering teams can maintain high developer velocity while inherently restricting the attack surface.” It transforms security from a workflow tax into an automated platform capability, he states.

5. Beware bureaucracy that does not lead to decisive action

Stop treating your security strategy as an annual document process and begin viewing it as a loop that runs continuously utilizing data you trust, says Bob Maley, CISO at security-as-a-service provider Black Kite. Feed decisions to someone who actually has the authority to make rapid critical choices, he recommends.

Attackers are already highly vigilant, Maley warns. “When a new vulnerability opportunity lands on a Friday afternoon, nobody on a ransomware crew is waiting for a quarterly review to approve going after it,” he explains. “If your defense team needs a steering committee before it can react, the gap between their tempo and yours is where the breach lives.”

6. Embrace automation to free up human judgment

Most security teams I’ve worked with build static defenses, observes Timur Rakhmatullin, senior software engineer at Softline Solutions, a consulting and social media marketing services provider. “They set up rules, configure alerts, and write runbooks, but then something happens that doesn’t match the runbook and everyone freezes.”

Rakhmatullin believes that automation is essential. He runs automated security scans across 30-plus repositories using in-house tools. “The scans catch vulnerabilities, license issues, and other gaps,” Rakhmatullin explains. “But the key part is that any engineer can override a scan result, escalate it, or reclassify a finding in minutes.”

Still, automation does all the heavy lifting, Rakhmatullin says. “Humans make the judgment calls.”

7. Conduct regular ‘fire drills’

Rehearse ugly scenarios before they happen, suggests Chris McGlasson, founder of ClearStack Advisory, a fractional executive technology and AI strategy firm.

Know who patches, who tests, who talks to the business, and who has the authority to take something offline at 2 a.m., McGlasson says. “Write it down and run it twice a year,” he recommends. “The teams that do so treat incident response like a fire drill.” McGlasson adds that many CISOs risk disaster because they treat security like a research project instead of a fundamental initiative.

McGlasson points to the recent “Citrix meltdown,” a severe, ongoing security crisis affecting Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances, creating a mass wave of critical zero-day exploits. Citrix immediately warned IT administrators to patch their systems at once to address the issue.

As a result, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, gave federal agencies a three-day patch window, while other organizations were left to create their own timeline, McGlasson says. He notes that the shops that handled this challenging event well weren’t always the ones with the best tools. “They were the ones that already knew who patches, who tests, and who calls the shots before the advisory ever dropped.”

Agility is a muscle, McGlasson observes. “You build it through repetition.”

Title: Fake GitHub Security Tools Infect Over 2,000 PCs With Malware
Context: Cybersecurity firm Doctor Web has found malware hidden in GitHub projects that look like security tools
Full Text:
Fake GitHub security tools are spreading malware that disables defenses, steals sensitive data and infects over 2,000 PCs.

Cybersecurity firm Doctor Web has found malware hidden in GitHub projects that look like security tools. The campaign targets blockchain game fans and, more recently, information security professionals. The researchers discovered that more than 2,000 PCs were infected.

“The attackers behind these compromised development projects target blockchain game enthusiasts and (most intriguingly) …information security professionals.” reads the report. “At the time of Doctor Web’s research into this matter, more than 2,000 PCs were infected.”

The campaign started two years ago with Visual Studio projects related to blockchain games, game bots and cheats. The attackers targeted people who used crypto wallets. They hid malicious code in project files, including commands that ran before a project was built and PowerShell commands stored in configuration files. They even provided instructions on how to install Visual Studio and download the projects from GitHub, making it easy for people with limited technical knowledge to use them.

Now the attackers are targeting cybersecurity professionals. Their new GitHub projects claim to offer tools for automated scanning, security testing and log analysis. Doctor Web found one that pretends to analyze and clean results from the Fscan security scanner.

The attackers also hide malicious code in Python and Go files, using large blocks of blank spaces to make it harder to spot. Some of these fake security tools even remove the antivirus software installed on the victim’s computer.

Once a victim opens the project, a PowerShell script runs and contacts the attackers’ servers and legitimate platforms, including YouTube, Telegram, Google Docs, GitCode and Pastebin. An encrypted string it retrieves holds a link to an archive, which unpacks into a folder disguised as a Windows Photos component. Its main program is Microsoft.exe, a modular app built with the Electron framework.

It does most of the damage. The loader collects system information and sends it to a Telegram bot, keeps itself running, raises its privileges, and turns off Windows Defender, UAC, System Restore and shadow copies. It also adds its own Defender exclusions, injects code into legitimate processes, and removes McAfee, ESET and Malwarebytes antivirus products.

Its default mode, called Mode3, stacks several evasion tricks. It fakes its parent process, disables Smart App Control, removes security software hooks from ntdll.dll, makes direct system calls, and patches event tracing and antivirus script scanning in memory. If that fails, Mode2 takes over, adding Defender exclusions and injecting through PowerShell.

Three payloads follow. AsyncRAT, a remote access backdoor, runs as two identical copies on different ports, which probably lets two operators control one device. A clipper swaps crypto wallet addresses in the clipboard while taking screenshots, and a stealer takes browser data, FileZilla, MobaXterm and Total Commander configs, VPN settings, messenger files, game accounts and Discord tokens. Everything is zipped and sent through Telegram, and the malware edits the hosts file to block antivirus vendors’ domains.

The attackers are still developing the malware. Doctor Web found an unfinished component that could install itself as a system service, download Microsoft.exe again if someone deletes it, manage startup and install updates.

“Attackers are constantly updating the Trojans to introduce new features. For example, Doctor Web’s researchers discovered certain unused routines that facilitate downloading and decompressing yet another archive—Lodge.7z.” concludes the report. “It contains an Electron project that hasn’t been completed yet. The executable file’s name is WUDFHost.exe. Its code offers us a glimpse of some of the trojan’s future features.”

Doctor Web advises users to keep their antivirus software up to date and scan every file they download. The researchers warn that attackers are constantly improving the Trojans and adding new features.

Title: Former OpenAI Engineer Pleads Not Guilty to Planting Covert Device in Executive Meeting Room
Context: The OpenAI engineer who was arrested and charged last month for planting a covert audio recording device in the company's office has pleaded not guilty
Full Text:
The OpenAI engineer who was arrested and charged last month for planting a covert audio recording device in the company's office has pleaded not guilty.

According to reports from Bloomberg and CNBC, Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan made an appearance in San Francisco federal court on Friday, where he entered the plea. His next hearing is scheduled for November 17, 2026.

If proven guilty, the 35-year-old faces a maximum of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by three years of supervised release. He has been held without bail since his arrest on October 9, 2026.

Late last month, a grand jury indicted Alfozan on a single count of interception of oral communications.

Prosecutors allege that the former OpenAI employee placed a "sophisticated recording device" in an executive OpenAI conference room in what has been described as an attempt to unlawfully record sensitive conversations.

He was arrested three days before he, along with his wife and son, were scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way ticket.

"His wife and son, however, immediately left the United States without him," U.S. prosecutors said. "Rather than wait until the October 12 flight as booked, they initially planned to fly to Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, on October 11 on a one-way ticket booked and paid for by the Saudi government."

"That flight was canceled, however, when a member of the Saudi military booked and paid for yet another one-way ticket for the defendant's wife and son, this one business class to Doha, Qatar, on October 10, 2026. They did make that flight, departing San Francisco about 36 hours after the defendant was arrested."

In a subsequent court filing, it was alleged that Alfozan was in frequent contact with a member of the Saudi Royal Family via WhatsApp. He was also deemed a flight risk, with court documents claiming that the defendant took great pains to create bespoke, encrypted recording devices to record sensitive meetings involving senior OpenAI personnel and executives.

Title: The BBC has a plan for a Black Sky event, and it runs on FM radio
Context: ” The government’s Be Ready campaign warns that severe weather and cyberattacks could disrupt essential services, although it says there is no specific threat to the electricity...
Full Text:
The BBC plans to use emergency FM radio to keep the UK informed during prolonged blackouts, with a self-sufficient studio ready for 72 hours.

If electricity fails across the UK for days, the BBC says it has a plan to keep people informed. David Sillito, the BBC’s media and arts correspondent, explained the strategy in a BBC News report, starting with the 2015 Lancaster floods and ending with a simple lesson: when digital infrastructure fails, FM radio may be the most reliable way to reach the public.

On December 5, 2015, the River Lune flooded Lancaster, cutting electricity to 61,500 people. Roger Kemp, an engineering professor at Lancaster University specializing in safety and electrical systems, was watching television when the power went out. The following day, he described the scene to the BBC as almost resembling a zombie movie, with residents searching for phone reception and queuing at the only working telephone box.

Homes lost heating and lighting, while some water supplies stopped because their pumps depended on electricity. Railway stations, petrol stations and shops closed, cash machines stopped working, and traffic lights failed. Only two communication systems remained operational: copper landlines and FM radio. Local station The Bay continued broadcasting using an emergency generator and a single landline. Kemp’s subsequent report highlighted the irony: a society increasingly dependent on digital infrastructure had relied on technologies dating back decades to receive essential information.

The incident illustrated the risk of a wider catastrophe known as a Black Sky event, in which electricity, water, shops and communications fail simultaneously. At a recent UK resilience summit, discussions focused on maintaining essential services for at least 72 hours. One expression often heard in civil contingency circles, “nine meals from anarchy”, captures the concern that three days without food could turn an emergency into widespread disorder.

“We are nine meals from anarchy” is a phrase often heard in the civil contingency world. A brutal reminder of the fear that three days without food would be enough to turn a crisis into chaos. If a Black Sky event takes out electricity, water, shops and communications, there is a good reason the government wants us to have our own supplies.” BBC states.

“In a major emergency, we are being told to hunker down and turn on an FM radio, as thousands did in Lancaster. This is why the BBC has its own Black Sky plan.”

The government’s Be Ready campaign warns that severe weather and cyberattacks could disrupt essential services, although it says there is no specific threat to the electricity grid. According to government advice reported by the Express, households should maintain at least three days of food and drinking water and keep a battery-powered FM radio. Sillito also recommends a hand-cranked radio that can generate its own power.

The BBC’s contingency plan revolves around precisely this technology. Around 100 people would operate a dedicated emergency radio studio, equipped with secure communications independent of the internet, alongside enough fuel, water and food to survive at least three days without resupply. Reports published by French outlet Telesatellite and Open magazine on November 7 describe a self-contained studio, generators powering transmission facilities and FM radio as the fallback communication channel.

Only a small number of BBC staff know the complete details. The studio would broadcast pre-prepared government announcements, with scripts already published online. These include practical instructions on daily water consumption and disposing of toilet waste when flushing is impossible.

Additional reporting would come from satellite vehicles and journalists stationed at emergency centres across the UK. Transmission towers, disconnected from the internet, would use diesel generators and storage tanks ranging from 5 to 40,000 litres, providing approximately three days of power. Satellite phones would support communications between teams, with agreed meeting points and procedures if those systems also failed. FM radio remains central because it can reach almost everywhere, even during a major blackout or disruptive cyberattack.

The BBC’s planning assumptions have evolved. An insider told Sillito that the original scenario considered outages lasting five to seven days, while the latest advice from the National Energy System Operator suggests electricity could return within two to three days. The corporation’s contingency arrangements have surfaced before. In October 2022, media reports described leaked draft scripts for a national blackout, including half-hourly Radio 4 updates from an emergency broadcasting centre at an undisclosed rural location.

There is, however, a discrepancy in the Express report, which claims that only around 100 people worldwide know the full details. The BBC says approximately 100 people would operate the emergency studio, while only a small number have access to the complete plan.

Concerns about grid resilience are not new, but the massive blackout affecting Spain, Portugal and south-western France in April 2025 renewed attention to the issue. Lord Harris, chair of the National Preparedness Commission, argues that the consequences extend well beyond losing electricity. Water supplies could stop because pumping stations need power, while sewage systems could become blocked when water can no longer circulate. Governments across Europe increasingly advise citizens to maintain emergency supplies, and Harris believes the UK has been slow to prepare its population.

Some initiatives are already underway. ARIA, the government’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency, is investing £70 million in high-altitude aircraft designed to provide at least a week of emergency mobile and internet connectivity over the UK. Programme director Rico Chandra has warned that satellites alone have limitations when terrestrial networks fail.

Harris argues that decades of efficiency-driven decisions have gradually removed essential redundancies. One example is the migration of emergency services from dedicated radio systems to mobile network technology, potentially exposing their communications to the same outages affecting the public. The government maintains that the transition to 4G and 5G provides reliable and resilient communications.

“The UK has one of the most resilient electricity systems in the world, and there has never been a complete outage in the grid’s 75-year history.” The Cabinet Office states describing the UK electricity system.

Government efforts to improve resilience predate the current debate. In May 2024, then deputy prime minister Oliver Dowden launched the previous Conservative government’s disaster preparedness initiative.

During his investigation, Sillito also reconsidered the BBC’s isolated transmission infrastructure. What initially appeared outdated became a strength: independence from the internet could help keep broadcasting alive when digital networks collapse.

Yet the UK is preparing to switch off its copper landline network on January 31, 2027, while the future of FM radio is also under review. The government’s position is that copper landlines, although useful during power cuts, have become unreliable and increasingly difficult to maintain.

Kemp is less convinced that the country is moving in the right direction. Asked whether his report had improved national preparedness for a Black Sky event, he argued that the planned landline shutdown showed little consideration for how people would communicate during a prolonged power failure.

Sillito experienced a smaller reminder while preparing his report: a power cut in his own street, leaking torch batteries, missing candles and an emergency radio he could not find. His conclus: “If anything, we’ve gone backwards,” he said. “Switching off the public switch telephone network, I think shows that there has been really no thought at all about how you communicate when you’ve no longer got power.”

Context: Without Docker, shell commands are unavailable and the other features keep working
Full Text:
Wirken is an open-source gateway that sits between messaging apps and AI agents. It assumes any agent can be turned against its owner and limits what a compromised one can reach.

Take an agent that reads your chats and email, holds the keys to your accounts and can run commands. One hidden instruction in a message or a shared document could talk it into leaking a secret or rewriting files. Wirken connects Signal, WhatsApp, Telegram, Matrix, Discord, Slack, Teams, Google Chat and iMessage, plus a web chat, and runs each channel as a separate process that holds only its credentials.

Locked vault, caged shell, signed log

Credentials sit in an encrypted vault and are supplied at the edge, so neither the agent nor the model handles them. Shell commands run in an ephemeral container with no network access, and if the sandbox is unavailable, execution is refused. Reads run freely. Actions that change something ask for approval the first time and remember the answer, while deleting, installing or touching credentials asks every time.

Every action is written to a signed, hash-chained log before it runs, attributed to the person who triggered it. Verification works offline. Sample output shows 1234 rows across 7 sessions and 24 verified chain-head signatures, which demonstrates the check running and says nothing about any deployment. An altered entry fails verification.

What still gets through

Outbound traffic is only partly contained: MCP server child processes and the LLM client make their own outbound connections. Injection detection flags suspicious input and lets it through. Agents share the gateway’s address space, and only the channel adapters run as separate processes.

If you run Wirken in a shared channel, one person’s Tier 2 approval covers every sender until it expires. The tamper check depends on a key kept off the machine, and an attacker running as the same user who rewrites both the log and the key can evade it. Removing the data directory destroys the audit log, so the project recommends exporting it first.

Docker is required for the sandbox, which is on by default. Without Docker, shell commands are unavailable and the other features keep working. Setting the sandbox mode to off lets commands run with no container, and the gateway warns at startup. The installer is a shell script for Linux and macOS with a published hash to check before piping it to a shell, while Windows 11 has a separate path and a different feature set.

Wirken is available for free on GitHub.

Title: Companies seeking an MSP doubt their ability to spot cyberattacks
Context: They report less confidence in their ability to detect threats, investigate incidents, and recover when an attack occurs
Full Text:
Businesses looking to outsource cybersecurity want providers that can help them recover from attacks, manage AI risks, and explain what security problems mean for their operations, according to Barracuda What MSP Customers Need Next report.

What MSP customers need next (Source: Barracuda Networks)

66% of surveyed organizations already outsource security services to a managed service provider (MSP), while another 29% are considering or evaluating providers.

Recovery remains a weak spot

Organizations considering an MSP are not reporting more security incidents than existing MSP customers. They report less confidence in their ability to detect threats, investigate incidents, and recover when an attack occurs.

“Organizations considering an MSP are not dealing with significantly more security incidents than existing MSP customers or organizations that manage security internally. The real difference is confidence,” Michelle Hodges, Senior Vice President, Global Channel and Alliances, Barracuda, explained.

Only 29% of prospective MSP customers said they could secure compromised accounts and restore operations within hours. Another 9% needed more than a week or could not do so consistently.

Of the organizations considering an MSP, 41% described their companywide security programs and policies as being at an early stage or only partially established. That figure reached 46% for maintaining a complete inventory of third parties with access to sensitive data.

AI adds to existing security concerns

AI-related threats worried 59% of organizations considering an MSP. Their concerns included phishing messages and social engineering generated with AI, unauthorized employee use of AI tools, and AI-enabled insider threats.

Customers also need help managing their own adoption of AI. That includes setting rules for its use and maintaining control of sensitive information handled through AI tools and workflows, Hodges wrote in an accompanying blog post.

Hiring more people was not the leading answer for prospective MSP customers. Only 23% said additional staff would have the greatest impact on security. Respondents placed greater emphasis on specialist expertise, better visibility into threats, AI-assisted investigation, and more time for prevention.

Plain language matters when choosing a provider

Some 95% of existing MSP customers said technical excellence mattered, while 40% identified plain-language explanations of risks, incidents, and next steps as a factor in choosing a provider.

Customers want providers who understand their industry and everyday operating pressures, and can explain security issues to business leaders who do not have a technical background.

Title: An average of 8 minutes is all hackers need to log in with stolen credentials
Context: Attackers used stolen credentials to log in an average of eight minutes after infection across 27 confirmed infostealer cases, according to a report from Elastic Security Threat...
Full Text:
Attackers used stolen credentials to log in an average of eight minutes after infection across 27 confirmed infostealer cases, according to a report from Elastic Security Threat Command. Researchers also documented misuse of AI applications to execute commands and digitally signed remote monitoring tools to maintain access.

“An agent that holds credentials and can reach the internet is a new attack surface, whether it’s misconfigured or abused. When an attacker is behind it, its activity looks exactly like the employee who installed it. So the question for defenders isn’t whether a tool is approved; it’s what that tool is actually doing,” said Mike Nichols, General Manage, Security at Elastic.

Attackers run commands through AI applications

Coding assistants such as Claude Code and Cursor can execute system commands. Their ability to work with files, credentials, and other applications gives attackers ways to act through software installed for everyday work.

Researchers documented intrusions involving Claude Code on Windows and the ChatGPT desktop application on macOS.

In the Windows case, an attacker connected remotely to a computer and used Claude Code through its Visual Studio Code extension to prepare tools and reach an outside server through a concealed connection.

On macOS, commands run through the ChatGPT desktop application read an internal infrastructure document and then accessed the user’s saved password store.

These cases involved misuse after attackers obtained access. They do not establish that the applications contained a vulnerability or that their providers were compromised.

Stolen credentials used within minutes

Infostealers collect information such as saved passwords, browser session data, and payment details.

Confirmed infostealer findings by initial access route and platform (Source: Elastic)

Across 27 confirmed cases on customer computers, investigators observed theft operating through applications the user or operating system already trusted. These included a signed remote monitoring agent, a browser updater, a vendor installer, and Apple’s scripting utilities.

ClickFix-style verification pages were the most common entry point, appearing in 12 cases. These pages persuade people to copy and run a malicious command, often presented as a verification step or troubleshooting instruction.

The approach can bypass defenses focused on scanning email attachments because the user executes the command themselves.

In one healthcare case, delivery of a malicious installer and execution through DLL sideloading occurred about 16 seconds after the user followed the lure. DLL sideloading causes an application to load malicious code.

Captured session data can also allow attackers to use an account without entering its password again.

Remote IT tools provide continued access

Remote monitoring and management software lets IT staff connect to computers, transfer files, and run commands. Attackers can use those capabilities to control a device and deliver additional tools or malware.

Researchers confirmed 23 cases involving abuse of these applications. Phishing pages and archives containing malicious scripts led to installations, with ScreenConnect named most often.

One campaign began with a fake digital invitation and led to a hidden installation of ScreenConnect. The application connected to an attacker-controlled server and ran as a Windows service.

Another case involved an attacker uploading remote access software to a compromised server after attempts to create user accounts failed.

Phishing exploits trusted sign-in services

Attackers used trusted authentication services and preapproved applications to access cloud accounts.

Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing kits place a relay between the victim and the real login page. When the victim enters credentials and completes multifactor authentication, the attacker can capture the resulting authenticated session.

Tycoon 2FA was one of the kits discussed and remained in active use during the reporting period.

Investigators observed attackers submitting stolen usernames and passwords through an older authentication method that allowed access without a second factor in those cases.

A separate device-code phishing case persuaded a user to enter a code on Microsoft’s sign-in page. The approval granted access to a session initiated by the attacker. Subsequent activity included registering a virtual device to support continued access.

“When attackers operate inside trusted software or on behalf of trusted users, the defensive answer is rarely just deploying a new signature. Detecting and neutralizing these threats requires user and entity behavior analytics (UEBA) to baseline normal activity, alongside cross-domain visibility and active correlation across your security environment,” the authors explained.

Title: Linus Torvalds sees signs AI-prompted patch flood has peaked
Context: That’s many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI
Full Text: The worst of the patchpocalypse may be behind us, according to Linus Torvalds. Writing in his weekly kernel update post, the Linux kernel dev leader delivered Linux 7.4 rc2 – the second rough cut of the next kernel – which he rated as a big release for two reasons. One is that he left some code out of rc1, because he was busy and because it was already the largest such release in the history of the kernel. The other is what Torvalds described as “various AI fixes.” Such fixes are necessary because ever since Anthropic launched its Mythos bug-finding model in April, developers have been able to find more software flaws than was previously possible. Microsoft, for example, addressed a record 974 flaws in September – its third record fixing spree this year after it whacked 622 flaws in July and 206 in June. Oracle addressed 1,449 flaws in a single month. That’s many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI. Torvalds’ post suggests that, perhaps, the worst of this is behind us. “This time around Alexei claims that on the bpf side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true,” he wrote. That’s a reference to Alexei Starovoitov, co-creator and lead dev on the Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), the project that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs within the Linux kernel. “I think most other areas haven't reached that point yet, but it's at least a sign that we _may_ be starting to see the tide starting to turn,” he added. “Don't hold your breath, but maybe cross your fingers we'll be getting there in the not entirely distant future.” If Torvalds is correct, that’s welcome news. The Linux kernel’s 40-million-plus lines of code makes it one of the world’s bigger software projects. If AI soon stops finding flaws in other parts of the kernel beyond eBPF, perhaps the deluge of fixes developers and users alike will need to handle has peaked. ®

Full Text: Hello and welcome to the Monday, November 9, 2026 edition of the SANS Inline Storm Center's Stormcast. My name is Johannes Ullrich, recording today from Washington, D.C. And this episode is brought to you by the SANS.edu Graduate Certificate Program in Cloud Security. Today I spent a little bit time looking at our honeypot data to see if we are detecting any evidence of the sshole vulnerability being exploited. And yes, indeed, it is being exploited. Now, this investigation had a couple of hiccups. First of all, in order to exploit sshole, you must use a password that's larger than 256 characters. Well, we only record passwords up to 256 characters because, well, that's usually for brute forcing and so all that matters. On the other hand, there are sometimes passwords that are longer than 256 characters that are being recorded by our honeypots that are not related to sshole. What usually happens here is that simple scripts that are doing brute forcing are actually not checking if the login succeeded or not. So what they're doing then is they end up entering whatever bash command they would like to execute in the password field of the login. Sometimes also the username, that's where we also see them often showing up. But here, of course, the password field was what matters. And if you're looking at the data that I published as part of the diary, we saw a number of long passwords like this on November 1st. So what I'm calling here is the actual sort of exploitation of passwords that I would associate with sshole started on November 5th in our honeypots. Now, what I'm calling here an sshole password is one that basically is just letters, no recognizable bash commands or anything like this, and fills the entire 255 bytes that we are recording. The only ones that I've seen so far being used is either all uppercase letter A or all lowercase letter A. Of course, the actual content of the password shouldn't really matter when it comes to exploiting this vulnerability. I hope to follow this up maybe later this week with a look at what commands are being executed by these attacks after they're logged in. These attacks should actually work as far as our honeypot is concerned. They should sort of randomly allow some of these login attempts to log in. And on Friday, SonicWall released patches for seven vulnerabilities in SonicOS. This is significant because one of these vulnerabilities is already being exploited. The already exploited vulnerability does allow attackers to bypass multi -factor authentication for SSL VPN logins. Apparently, the problem here is if you have multiple authentication methods defined, and one of these authentication methods does not require multi-factor authentication, then an attacker essentially can use that to bypass the multi -factor authentication requirements that you may have set up for SSL VPN access. So this should be patched now. And again, it's already being exploited, which should tell you to please expedite release rolling out this particular update. In particular, of course, with SSL VPNs, we often had issues where people didn't use multi-factor authentication because, well, we all know passwords don't work. And Microsoft this weekend patched an authorization bypass vulnerability in Entra. This vulnerability would allow a user to essentially gain elevated privileges. The attacker in this case doesn't even have to be authorized. Now nothing you have to do. Microsoft already took care of it for you since this is an Entra vulnerability. So it really only affected Microsoft's cloud services and they released the advisory as they state to be more transparent about these vulnerabilities. They also say there was no exploitation happening at the time when they patched this vulnerability. Now they say exploitation is less likely, so more complex vulnerability. And hopefully now after the patch supplied, exploitation should be impossible. And a agentic coding security company, Apiiro, found that Anthropic's Claude Code under certain circumstances will add secrets to a hidden file in GitHub. The way this works is if you're requesting Claude Code to connect to an API or such, it may need credentials. And there is an option when you provide credentials to Claude Code where it basically asks, well, do you want me to ask you again about these credentials, about accessing this API? If you say no, then of course it has to remember those credentials somewhere. And the way it does so is by saving them to a .claude folder and inside there a file settings.local.json. We've actually seen in our web honeypots this weekend an increase in actually for the first time requests for this .claude directory. So attackers are definitely looking for it and Apiiro as part of their blog states that they found sort of around 1500 or so of these credential files on GitHub. There's still work in progress into how to exactly fix this. Essentially what they're proposing is to check automatically for secrets before anything is being sent to GitHub. But of course that may still keep those credentials in any other Git repositories. So not quite clear how this will be fixed. Definitely be aware of this and check with Anthropic and as a Claude Code user with any updates that you may be receiving that will fix this problem for you. Well, and that's it for today. Title: Don’t Hand Propaganda a Gift: Reading the Brenner Base Tunnel SE Breach Calmly
Context: It only helps the attackers and anyone trying to exploit the incident for an influence campaign
Full Text:
Brenner Base Tunnel SE confirms a breach and Everest claims 812 GB. What we know, what we don’t, and why overblown alarm helps propaganda more than the attackers.

Brenner Base Tunnel (BBT) SE, the company building the Brenner Base Tunnel between Italy and Austria, has confirmed that unauthorized people accessed some of its data. The extortion group Everest claims it took 812 GB of files. Nobody has verified that, and a criminal bragging about file sizes isn’t an audited source.

The timeline is thin. The intrusion reportedly dates to mid-October, Everest’s claim to 17 October, and the Austrian press broke the story on 6 November. On 7 November BBT SE told ANSA that operations are unaffected, the systems involved are isolated, and outside forensic experts and the authorities are on the case.

If real and current, drawings, surveys and site procedures would save an attacker a lot of reconnaissance. Together they could show how the infrastructure fits together, and fraudsters could borrow project names to fool contractors. Those are scenarios, not sightings.

Dates matter too. The tunnel won’t open before 2034, at a projected cost of about €11.7 billion, so older drawings may describe a design that has since changed.

Knowing how a tunnel is built does not mean being able to control it. Sabotage requires access to operational systems and weaknesses that attackers can exploit. So far, there is no evidence that attackers accessed industrial systems or tampered with the tunnel’s control functions. BBT SE has not confirmed any encryption of its systems either. Claims that ransomware could stop the tunnel therefore have no factual support.

Everest is a Russian-speaking cybercriminal group. ZeroFox has also noted that the group tends to exaggerate the amount of data it steals. Speaking Russian and operating within a Russian-speaking cybercrime environment does not prove that the group is directed by the Russian state. In July, the same group demanded CHF 10 million from Stadler Rail after using stolen credentials to access a supplier’s data platform. Production continued despite the incident.

The response should focus on practical security measures. Organizations need to identify which information was exposed, revoke potentially compromised credentials, keep document management systems separate from industrial control networks, and warn suppliers about fraudulent requests. Whether NIS2 applies to a project company that is still under construction depends on its activities and the relevant national legislation.

There is no benefit in creating unnecessary alarm. It only helps the attackers and anyone trying to exploit the incident for an influence campaign. Blaming Moscow without evidence would play directly into propaganda efforts. There are three key questions that need clear answers: which files were actually stolen, how recent and relevant they are, and who might still be able to use them.

Full Text:
Security operations startup Brava Security has emerged from stealth mode with $15 million in a seed funding round led by F2 Venture Capital and Pitango VC, with support from several angel investors.

Tel Aviv-based Brava was founded in 2024 by Israeli intelligence alumni Idan Basre, who serves as CEO, and Itay Gabbay, the company’s CTO.

Brava has built an AI-powered platform that focuses on modeling attacker behavior, simulating attacks to analyze generated telemetry for security gaps.

Using business context, the solution shows how an attack would manifest in customers’ environments, reveals what defenses could miss, and rewrites SIEM detections, while allowing security teams to investigate further.

“The hard part of security was never writing detections. It’s knowing exactly what an attack will look like in a specific environment, across all of its log sources, before it ever happens. That’s the problem our models were built to solve,” said Gabbay.

Brava says this approach closes an important gap in modern security defenses, since AI agents typically cannot investigate attacks their systems haven’t detected.

“You can’t automate a decision based on evidence no one ever proved. We’re solving the problem that comes before AI can make the right decision: making sure the security infrastructure actually sees the threats it’s supposed to detect,” Basre said.

According to Brava, its platform can provide initial insights within 10-15 minutes of onboarding. The solution integrates with more than 70 sources and destinations and does not require changes to existing security infrastructure.

The startup will use the fresh funding to accelerate product development and market expansion. It currently has an R&D team in Israel and a commercial team in the US.

Title: Inside ARTEX: AI Hacking Tools, Exposed Servers and South Korean Bank Breaches
Context: A malware-name search in AttackCapture gave 280 results with open directories
Full Text:
Hunt.io traced ARTEX servers and AI-powered hacking tools used in breaches affecting seven South Korean financial institutions.

Between late September and early October 2026, seven South Korean financial institutions had data breached through internet-facing systems. About 66,000 to 67,000 people and around 2,200 corporations were affected, and personal, employment, income and loan data was exposed. Hunt.io dug into the infrastructure behind the campaign, and its findings add a lot to what CrowdStrike and Genians already published.

CrowdStrike reported on October 7 and Genians Security Center on October 12, and both pointed to ARTEX, an open-source autonomous penetration testing framework developed in China and licensed under AGPL-3.0. CrowdStrike assessed with moderate confidence that a single Chinese-speaking individual motivated by money ran it, and not an established threat group. DeepSeek v4.1 Flash was the main model, with GLM 5.3 and Grok 4.6 as backups, reached partly through a reseller domain, xcai[.]pro.

The public indicators were a server at 38.244.50[.]120, which hosted the ARTEX console, plus a Hong Kong address and nine proxies. Genians said the ARTEX GitHub repository and Docker image were removed on October 11, though forks and mirrors remain.

“CrowdStrike assessed with moderate confidence that the operator was a single Chinese-speaking individual motivated by financial gain rather than an established threat group.” reads the report published by Hunt.io. “The infrastructure reportedly accessed these services in part through the reseller domain xcai[.]pro. Both reports described a two-server configuration, consisting of a Hong Kong-based IP address used as primary infrastructure and 38.244.50[.]120, which hosted the ARTEX console.”

Hunt.io notified the relevant national CERT before publishing, and says the report holds no personal records or credentials.

The company’s own scanning showed 38.244.50[.]120 sits on Cogent’s network in Los Angeles, with 15 open ports. The ARTEX login page, with a Chinese title meaning “autonomous penetration testing console”, appears on ports 443 and 8090. Other services include a Gemini2API admin console and a Tinyproxy server.

Searching its AttackCapture platform for that address, Hunt.io found another open directory at 23.248.226[.]250, a jump server in Hong Kong on AS138415. It held 42 files in 2 subdirectories, 105 MB in all, and the platform had logged warnings on September 5, September 26 and October 5. A file in it names 38.244.50[.]120 as the jump host, and its own comment tells the operator never to paste the credentials into a session. It sat in an open directory.

Three scripts back up the link. They keep reverse SSH tunnels alive, run a local relay, and copy files to the jump host, one tunnel is named grok2api, and the credentials file also holds keys for Zhipu AI’s GLM models, an OpenAI-compatible relay and a proxy service. That explains how several language models ran in one campaign.

The AI setup is the most striking part. A state file shows the harness is Claude Code itself, version 2.1.221, started 510 times since August 4, but it isn’t talking to Anthropic. A small proxy, ds-models-shim.py, fixes a compatibility problem by faking a model list and sending requests to DeepSeek, and another, xcai-effort-shim.py, adds a reasoning setting because the DeepSeek backend otherwise skips its reasoning step. The route runs from Claude Code through Claude Code Router, an open-source project, to xcai and then to DeepSeek.

“A small local proxy, ds-models-shim.py, addresses a compatibility issue: the official /v1/models endpoint returns a 404 response when queried against a non-Anthropic backend, preventing Claude Code from discovering the available models. The shim intercepts that specific request and returns a locally defined model list containing deepseek-v4-pro and deepseek-flash. All other requests are forwarded to api.deepseek.com/anthropic.” states the report.

The same file counts 19 custom skills, reusable instruction sets for the agent, with 147 recorded uses. They cover code audit, reconnaissance, web injection, WAF bypass testing, authentication testing, Telegram Mini Apps, APK download and decompiling, cloud phone control and payment logic testing. Next to the payment skill sat three self-registered test accounts with tokens for a cash-in deposit API, dated September 12, and a comment calls them an authorized, self-built test. The setup fits testing for insecure direct object reference flaws, a technique CrowdStrike and Genians described against Korean loan and inquiry services.

The directory also held supporting tools. A script queried FOFA, a Chinese asset search engine like Shodan, through a third-party API, and a comment says the primary membership had expired and a backup key was in use. Proxy scripts enumerated a rotating proxy service at 154.201.79[.]246:443, where 79 unique exit IPs showed up among the first 100 identities tested.

A separate directory at 23.248.226[.]250:8001 held a small staged setup for JNDI and LDAP exploitation, retrieved on October 5 at 03:42 UTC. It confirms command execution through a DNS callback, and one script lets web and LDAP traffic share a single port. Hunt.io’s analysis describes the tooling without publishing steps to reproduce it.

Other recovered files include tools aimed at a cryptocurrency exchange’s admin session and withdrawals, Linux privilege escalation exploits, iOS probe source code and Android kernel and firmware utilities. Hunt.io says their connection to the Korean breaches isn’t confirmed.

Hunt.io then showed how to hunt ARTEX servers. Searching for an ARTEX certificate issuer returned 19 IP addresses, and searching its malware classification returned 1,303 addresses across 30 countries, led by the United States, China and Hong Kong. Those figures show where addresses are registered, not where the operator sits.

“The result returned 19 distinct IP addresses, including 38.244.50[.]120. This method is precise but limited to hosts that expose a matching certificate. Systems using a different certificate will not appear in these results.” continues the report.

Matching the console’s page title returned about 1,300 IPs, and a looser search found 21 title strings, 19 of them likely ARTEX consoles, in English, Chinese, Korean, Japanese, Russian, Portuguese and Vietnamese.

A malware-name search in AttackCapture gave 280 results with open directories. One at 130.94.31[.]86:18888 in Seoul held two small scripts, and another at 156.251.11[.]39 held an SMB reconnaissance toolkit whose test script writes a file named artex_probe_11876.txt.

More hosts held exploitation kits for DedeCMS and FangCMS, a CAPTCHA bypass suite, a RuoYi and Spring administrative console exploit and CAPTCHA-based login automation. Together they show the framework attracting many operators.

For defenders, the advice is plain. Remove public access and put administration behind VPNs or allowlists, and reset SSH passwords and rotate API keys, proxy credentials and tokens that exposed files may have revealed. Patch internet-facing services, watch for unexpected LDAP and JNDI activity, DNS callbacks and remote script downloads, and store secrets in a managed vault with least-privilege permissions. Also restrict access to model gateways, watch their requests, and enforce compliance rules on managed phones. Hunt.io’s lesson is that an investigation shouldn’t stop at the first list of indicators, because

The company also published indicators of compromise in its analysis.

“The findings highlight risks associated with exposed administrative services, reusable credentials, remote access tunnels, proxy infrastructure, and exploitation tooling.” concludes the report.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

Title: CTM360 Exposes Fake Gift Card Scams Exploiting Trusted Brands
Context: Threat actors exploit consumer familiarity with established brands, frequently impersonating major retailers and consumer platforms such as PlayStation, Sephora, SHEIN, Walmart,...
Full Text:
Fraudulent reward portals and fake gift card giveaways are surging globally, tricking users into deceptive verification loops and paid subscriptions.

These scams lure victims with a simple pitch: click an ad featuring a celebrity endorsement, claim a free gift card from a well-known brand, and complete a quick "human verification" step to unlock the reward.

Read the full report here: https://www.ctm360.com/reports/gift-card-scams

Behind the polished branding, fake progress bars, and convincing promotional messages, however, no actual gift cards are provided.

Instead, these campaigns operate as large-scale affiliate monetization schemes designed to collect personal information, generate application installs, and enroll unsuspecting users in recurring mobile subscriptions.

1,000+ Incidents Exploiting Trusted Brands

Based on activity observed by CTM360, analysts identified more than 1,000 incidents linked to this recurring campaign.

Threat actors exploit consumer familiarity with established brands, frequently impersonating major retailers and consumer platforms such as PlayStation, Sephora, SHEIN, Walmart, and Amazon.

To increase credibility and attract potential victims, the campaigns rely heavily on social media distribution through:

Sponsored social media ads

Viral posts promoting "giveaways"

Fabricated endorsements from high-profile celebrities and influencers (such as MrBeast or Alix Earle)

Because the underlying infrastructure is highly modular, threat actors can swap out the impersonated brand, celebrity lure, and domain name without rebuilding the core scam engine.

How the Campaign Works: The Fake Generation Trap

CTM360 maps this activity using a structured fraud lifecycle, highlighting how victims are systematically pushed through a psychological progression of curiosity, trust, and urgency.

Once a user clicks a malicious ad, they are redirected to a fraudulent reward portal.

To appear credible, these websites display:

Cloned brand logos and colors

Fake participant numbers and live countdown timers

Fabricated testimonials from "recent winners"

After a victim selects a gift card value, the site runs a scripted, visual progress animation simulating the generation of the card on the back end.

The portal then displays a partially masked code (e.g., XXXX-XXXX-7F3A-XXXX) to convince the user that the reward is real and ready to claim.

Before the full code is revealed, the victim is presented with a deceptive "Security Check" or "Human Verification" gate.

Download Now

The Endless Verification Loop and Monetization

The "human verification" step is a deceptive pivot into what CTM360 identifies as "Trap 10." Rather than performing a legitimate security check, the verification process redirects victims to third-party activities designed to generate revenue for the operators.

Victims are pushed into an endless loop of:

Completing surveys, quizzes, and promotional offers.

Installing unwanted third-party applications or browser extensions.

Subscribing to paid mobile services through localized carrier-billing mechanisms

If a user completes a task, they are not given the gift card. The site simply reports the step as "incomplete" and pushes the victim to another offer. In all flows tested by CTM360, no reward was ever delivered.

Technical Observations: Affiliate Hand-Offs

Unlike traditional phishing that steals user credentials, this campaign operates on a volume-and-conversion model.

CTM360 observed that lure pages redirect victims through affiliate tracking URLs (e.g., passing parameters like offer_id and aff_id). This tracking token links the victim's registration directly to the threat actor's affiliate network account.

When a victim completes a mobile number submission and PIN/OTP verification for a subscription, the threat actor earns a commission.

Risks to Users and Organizations

For the victim, the fallout goes beyond wasted time. Consequences include personal information exposure, unexpected mobile billing charges, and an influx of spam.

For organizations, this represents a severe abuse of brand reputation. The campaign highlights a broader trend: attackers are operating at scale, weaponizing brand trust as a mechanism to drive lucrative affiliate conversions.

Title: The Fridge-Hacking Spree Is an Internet-of-Things Wake-Up Call
Context: Amid an onslaught of AI vulnerability discovery and AI-assisted hacking, some of the most consequential critical infrastructure attacks this year may have little to do with the...
Full Text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

Amid an onslaught of AI vulnerability discovery and AI-assisted hacking, some of the most consequential critical infrastructure attacks this year may have little to do with the technology at all—instead providing a stark reminder that cybersecurity fundamentals are still key to digital defense.

Three sites in France that handle blood and plasma bags were briefly impacted this week by widespread attacks on vulnerable internet-connected refrigerators. On Wednesday, the Établissement Français du Sang (EFS) confirmed that cold rooms storing blood were “raised to very high temperatures” on November 2. The blood samples, thankfully, weren’t altered or damaged, the EFS said, because the organization’s alarm facilities and staff quickly detected the changes and implemented fail-safe measures.

The incident, however, comes amid a wave of cyberattacks in recent days affecting supermarket chains in at least 11 European countries that also drastically increased the temperatures of their refrigerators. Pictures from across the continent show huge volumes of food being trashed following the spikes. Similar fridge attacks in October affected hundreds of French stores that were forced to throw away food. And in August, roughly six commissaries and grocery stores on United States military bases suffered similar incidents resulting in spoiled food. The Pentagon is investigating the incidents and is collaborating with French law enforcement, Reuters reported last week.

“It's been true for more than a decade now that our dependence on connected technology is growing faster than our collective will to protect it, which has exposed us to accidents, adversaries, and now potentially agents,” says longtime critical infrastructure researcher Josh Corman, who is currently the executive in residence for public safety and resilience at the nonprofit Institute for Security and Technology. “These fragile cold-chain systems are too critical to fail, but we keep experiencing hard lessons.”

It is still unclear who is behind the incidents and whether the attacks are all connected or being carried out by multiple actors. The first recent wave of attacks against French supermarkets last month appears to have been caused by attackers exploiting unpatched refrigeration controllers exposed to the internet—including software versions that allegedly used weak passwords formulated based on the date.

Many of the hacks stem from attackers exploiting vulnerabilities in temperature controllers made by the Danish firm Danfoss, and researchers say the attacks would not have been particularly difficult to pull off. Danfoss did not return WIRED’s request for comment.

Title: NHS breach helpline left staff carrying a 'significant emotional burden'
Context: NHS staff drafted into a helpline after colleagues' health data was exposed online faced distressed callers, safeguarding concerns, and a "serious emotional impact," a review...
Full Text: NHS staff drafted into a helpline after colleagues' health data was exposed online faced distressed callers, safeguarding concerns, and a "serious emotional impact," a review has found. The report [PDF] comes almost exactly a year after the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust disclosed a data breach affecting 8,003 people, including current and former trust staff and non-trust workers. A member of the public discovered the exposure in November 2025. An Excel workbook published in response to a Freedom of Information request in February 2023 retained underlying sickness absence records that users could reveal through its pivot tables. Staff assigned to the helpline described difficult calls involving shouting, anger, and distress. Particularly difficult calls involved people distressed by the sensitivity of the disclosures or potentially in danger from domestic abuse. Call handlers said they had to make safeguarding assessments without training or an established process. "Such occurrences of anger or distress were not infrequent, and this reflected the heightened emotions and distress experienced by callers to varying degrees due to the breach," the review noted. "This placed significant emotional burden on individuals working in the contact center, who were not prepared or provided support on how to deal with those." Members of the trust's clinical governance team were told just a day beforehand that they would staff the helpline. Despite their experience dealing with patient trauma, they received little preparation for the calls that followed. "The staff working in the call centers had a short training session and then the calls started coming in within minutes of the team being set up," the review noted. "Some staff had not finished reading the pre-prepared script which had arrived only 30 minutes before the center went live." Most call handlers only learned that their own data had been exposed while already working on the helpline, sometimes minutes before supporting others affected. Call handlers also said they had little choice about taking on the work and were expected to maintain their usual duties alongside it. The review stated that some staff members gave up weekends and worked long past their scheduled hours to meet the demands of both roles. "It's typical NHS, it runs on goodwill," one staffer told the team that compiled the report. The call center was only supposed to run for two weeks in December 2025, but due to the volume of calls, it was eventually stood down after 11 weeks, in February 2026. According to officials speaking at a trust board meeting on Thursday, the review and its findings have since been circulated among staff, and published online. How the spreadsheet slipped through Responding to a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request thought to be from a journalist researching a story about stress in the NHS, the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust uploaded a spreadsheet to its public FOI Disclosure log in February 2023. This contained personal data and inadvertently exposed sickness absence information and sensitive health data related to 7,715 staff, 288 non-trust workers, as well as a small number of unidentified records. Crucially, this spreadsheet was uploaded in a format that allowed users to access the pivot table from which some data was derived. The data in these pivot tables would normally have been too sensitive to be included in FOIA responses. The first failure was that the request was handled by the trust's e-Rostering team instead of the People Information Unit, which had the expertise in responding to FOIA requests with complex datasets. The e-Rostering team compiled the response using the team's own data, but incorrectly believed they had stripped the spreadsheet of the sensitive data that would later be exposed. Standard procedures instructed request handlers to follow several steps to ensure sensitive data was stripped before documents are published, some of which were skipped. For starters, one FOI officer assigned to the response either failed to run the spreadsheet through Excel's Document Inspector, which formed part of the usual procedures, or failed to act upon its recommendations. This feature can flag pivot tables and potentially hidden cached data, but cannot determine whether that data is sensitive or automatically remove the cache. Staff also failed to follow instructions to convert the spreadsheet to PDF. Investigators found that doing so prevented users clicking through to the underlying records, although they could not guarantee that no hidden data remained technically accessible. At the time, internal guidance did not require conversion to CSV, which would have removed the workbook's pivot-table functionality and embedded cache. The trust's sign-off process also focused on answering the request's questions and meeting their public relations duties, and falsely assumed that the data had been adequately sanitized before the final review. The spreadsheet was made available for 33 months, although the trust is not sure how many times it was viewed during that time. Its logs only covered the 12 months before a member of the public alerted it to the pivot table issue. These indicated that it had been accessed 340 times, although the review noted there was no way of knowing how many of these, if any, led to pivot tables being accessed, or even if it was viewed by a human, with web crawlers adding to the total view count. The trust has since implemented a number of changes to prevent a recurrence of the breach, including the mandatory password-protecting of any Excel workbook as part of FOIA responses. A senior information governance officer must now approve spreadsheet responses before executive sign-off. Revised guidance circulated in November 2025 also called for conversion to CSV, although investigators found that this requirement had not been incorporated into the formal operating procedure and recommended updating it. The review says the Information Commissioner's Office closed its case after the trust implemented its recommendations. A spokesperson for the Royal Cornwall Hospitals said: "We are deeply sorry for the accidental sharing of sickness absence data which we reported in November 2025, and for the distress and concern it caused those colleagues whose data was involved. "An independent investigation has now been completed, and the report has been published in full on our website in the interests of transparency and accountability. "The investigation has helped us understand what happened and identify areas where improvements were needed. We have already implemented a number of measures to strengthen our processes, particularly around the management of Freedom of Information requests and responses. "The protection of personal information is of the utmost importance to us, and we remain committed to learning from this incident and preventing a similar event from happening again. "We continue to provide support to colleagues who have been affected." ®

Title: SonicWall Patches Exploited SonicOS Vulnerability That Weakens VPN Logins
Context: SonicWall has patched a SonicOS vulnerability that can be used to bypass SAML authentication, warning customers that it may have been exploited in attacks
Full Text:
SonicWall has patched a SonicOS vulnerability that can be used to bypass SAML authentication, warning customers that it may have been exploited in attacks.

Tracked as CVE-2026-19868, the flaw affects the SSL VPN component of SonicOS, the operating system that runs on SonicWall firewalls. It’s one of seven vulnerabilities described in an advisory published on November 6.

“An authentication enforcement vulnerability in SonicOS SSLVPN service may allow a user with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method to bypass SAML authentication controls. Successful exploitation may also bypass SAML-enforced multi-factor authentication (MFA),” reads SonicWall’s description of CVE-2026-19868.

According to the vendor, an SSL VPN is exposed only if SAML-based login is enabled. CVE-2026-19868 has a CVSS score of 7.1, which puts it in the high-severity range. The flaw was reported by Ryan Harris of The Electronic Office.

SonicWall said its product security team “has investigated a report indicating potential exploitation of this vulnerability.”

CISA added CVE-2026-19868 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on the same day. Under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, federal agencies must address it by November 20.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Neither the vendor nor CISA has shared any details about the suspected attacks. It’s also unclear whether the flaw was exploited as a zero-day, before a patch became available.

Impacted devices include Gen7 TZ, NSa, NSsp and NSv firewalls with SonicOS 7.3.3-7015 or older. Gen8 TZ, NSa and NSv firewalls with SonicOS 8.2.2-8015 or older are also affected.

SonicOS versions 7.3.4-7013 and 8.2.3-8015 resolve the issue, and there are no workarounds. “Customers are strongly urged to upgrade to the latest release as soon as possible to mitigate the associated risks,” SonicWall said.

SonicWall’s advisory doesn’t mark any of the other six flaws as exploited. Two of them, each with a CVSS score of 8.8, affect the SonicOS management interface. One is a permissive cross-domain policy issue and the other is a session validation bug.

Under certain circumstances, a remote attacker could abuse either one without logging in to take unauthorized actions.

Three of the remaining flaws are pre-authentication buffer overflows in the SSL VPN service and the TACACS+ authentication client. Attackers could use them to launch DoS attacks at the application level.

The last one is a weak password hashing issue in virtual appliances. An attacker who already has high-privileged local access could exploit it to obtain a platform credential, which gives access to some of the platform’s settings.

Threat actors often exploit SonicWall product vulnerabilities. CISA’s KEV catalog currently includes 20 security holes, but the agency has yet to add CVE-2026-102255, which hackers started targeting last month, just days after its disclosure.

Title: Stealing more than the spotlight. [Research Saturday]
Context: " Threat actors are exploiting the hype surrounding the upcoming release of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA6) by distributing fake leaked game downloads designed to infect unsuspecting...
Full Text:
This week, we are joined by Matt Poto, Associate Triage Analyst at Huntress, discussing their work on "Grand Theft Auto VI Hype Leads to Malware." Threat actors are exploiting the hype surrounding the upcoming release of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA6) by distributing fake leaked game downloads designed to infect unsuspecting gamers.

Huntress identified malicious ISOs promoted through search engine poisoning, gaming forums, torrent sites, and social media that contain multiple types of malware, including remote access trojans (RATs), an infostealer, and ransomware. The malware can steal credentials and personal information, give attackers control of compromised systems, and encrypt or destroy files, with evidence suggesting the campaign may be targeting Russian-speaking gamers.
