Title: Composer 2.11 Adds Dependency Cooldowns
Context: The release arrives nearly a year after developers first requested the feature, bringing Composer into line with package managers that have already adopted minimum release age...
Full Text:
Composer 2.11 has introduced dependency cooldowns, giving PHP developers a native way to delay newly published package versions before they become eligible for installation. The release arrives nearly a year after developers first requested the feature, bringing Composer into line with package managers that have already adopted minimum release age policies to reduce exposure to supply chain attacks.

The new config.policy.cooldown setting allows developers to specify a waiting period in hours, days, or weeks. It is disabled by default and applies during dependency resolution, including composer update and composer require. Existing lockfile installations remain unaffected.

The feature also supports organization-wide configuration through Private Packagist, which can enforce cooldowns regardless of the Composer version developers and CI systems are running.

Preventing Cooldown Bypasses #

The original GitHub issue opened in November 2025 and gained urgency following a series of high-profile supply chain compromises. An initial implementation was submitted in December, but the feature missed Composer 2.10 as the maintainers worked through how to enforce cooldowns reliably.

In May, after additional attacks affected Packagist, developers pressed the maintainers for an update. Composer co-founder Nils Adermann explained that the feature was being held up by changes needed to make release metadata trustworthy.

The existing time field in Composer package metadata could be derived from a Git commit date or supplied through composer.json. Both are under the publisher's control, allowing an attacker to backdate a malicious release and bypass a cooldown.

Packagist introduced a new published-time field in June, recording when a version first became available through the registry. Composer 2.11 now uses that timestamp rather than trusting dates supplied by package publishers. Repositories without the required metadata cause dependency resolution to fail unless an explicit fallback is configured.

The cooldown feature is part of a broader security effort by Composer and Packagist. In a May security update, maintainers specifically cited the April compromise of intercom/intercom-php, and the May attack on Laravel Lang among recent incidents affecting the PHP ecosystem. The update outlined several security initiatives, including malware detection, version immutability, and the planned cooldown policy.

Cooldowns Are Now Standard Across Package Ecosystems #

For years, dependency management favored staying on the latest compatible releases. That assumption is changing. With compromised packages appearing on a regular basis, living on the bleeding edge has become considerably less appealing. Cooldowns are increasingly treated as standard supply chain security practice, and some package managers have already made them the default.

Composer is joining a movement already well underway across JavaScript, Ruby, Python, and Rust tooling.

pnpm introduced minimum release ages in September 2025 and made a 24-hour delay the default in version 11. Yarn has also enabled a release-age gate by default, while npm and Bun offer configurable delays. GitHub introduced a three-day default cooldown for Dependabot version updates in July.

In Ruby, Bundler added cooldown support in June, and gem.coop began testing registry-level delays earlier this year. Cargo is next, with minimum publish age support scheduled to become stable in Rust 1.100 on November 12.

Unlike pnpm and Yarn, Composer is leaving the feature opt-in, a decision its maintainers debated during development over concerns about disrupting existing workflows.

Composer also deliberately avoids automatically exempting security fixes. The maintainers rejected that approach because an attacker with publishing access could potentially create an advisory or exploit an existing one to get a malicious release through the cooldown. Developers can use --no-cooldown to install an urgent fix immediately without disabling other security policies. Composer also supports permanent exemptions for specific packages through the cooldown policy's ignore setting.

Security fixes still demand quick updates, especially as AI-assisted vulnerability disclosures accelerate, but for routine dependency updates, cooldowns are becoming best practice. Composer's implementation arrives later than many of its peers, but its adoption adds another major ecosystem to the shift toward giving new dependencies time to be examined before installation.

Title: Max-severity bug in widely used OT programming tool exploited to deliver Linux malware
Context: Unknown criminals are exploiting a maximum-severity vulnerability in Node-RED, a flow-based programming tool that is widely used in critical infrastructure, to deploy a flow...
Full Text: Unknown criminals are exploiting a maximum-severity vulnerability in Node-RED, a flow-based programming tool that is widely used in critical infrastructure, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot. Node-RED is commonly used for workflow automation in industrial control systems (ICS) and operational technology (OT) environments. It’s built on top of Node.js and is used in commercial products including Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050. In August, Siemens assigned the vulnerability identifier – CVE-2026-58115 – to describe the bug and explain its perfect 10-out-of-10 CVSS rating. Affected Siemens devices do not enforce authentication on the Node-RED HTTP interface, allowing unauthenticated access to programming nodes that can execute system commands on the device. This means unauthenticated remote attackers can create malicious flows, which is what VulnCheck researchers began documenting last Friday. “On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115,” VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity warned in a Monday advisory, adding that two Node-RED built-in nodes make this vulnerability “trivial to weaponize.” One is an inject node, which fires a message either on a schedule or once at startup. The second, an exec node, can run shell commands. “Wire one to the other and the flow executes a command as soon as it is deployed, with no further interaction,” Garrity said. Plus, these exploits come as criminals increasingly look to target internet-exposed OT and ICS devices, allowing their cyberattacks to impact the physical world and produce real-life harm. Case in point: the ongoing refrigeration controller hacks across Europe and the attacks on water systems across at least 12 US states over the summer. The activity observed by VulnCheck came from a single IP address, 4.201.105[.]116, which sits in Microsoft’s AS8075 network and geolocates to Brazil. “It didn't just scan us. It sent the complete exploit, flow and dropper, in a single POST /flows,” Garrity wrote. While there’s a lot that the researchers don’t yet know about the attacks - they didn’t retrieve a binary or staged scripts to analyze - the filename, bot-linux-amd64, indicates that the malware targets Linux running on AMD64 processors. It also suggests the malware operator may have other builds. “We did not fetch the binary, so we can't say what it does once running,” Garrity noted. Between October 30 and November 1, the researchers saw this IP address target the same Node-RED vulnerability 16 times, and log 125 hits against eight different CVEs across their wider canary network. Among the targets of the attack were a seven-year-old Apache Solr flaw tracked as CVE-2019-17558 – affecting Camunda, Gitea, MLflow, Traefik, and Joomla, alongside Node-RED. All this suggests “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” according to the researcher. One of these hits delivered a different payload pointing to a separate server (85.215.73[.]250), which VulnCheck now tracks - but doesn’t have any telemetry other than the URL. “Because the download host is a different machine from the one that sent the exploit, the likely setup is a scan-and-infect arrangement: the hosts that find and exploit vulnerable instances pull the implant from a separate, dedicated server,” Garrity wrote. The mix of old and new bugs across unrelated products indicates “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” Garrity wrote. “If you run Node-RED anywhere, including inside OT environments, check today whether it’s reachable from outside your network, apply updates where available and implement detections to reduce the risk of exploitation,” he added in a LinkedIn post. While the bug has been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, it hasn’t appeared (as of press time) in the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s KEV.®

Title: One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

Modules: AI Security; Endpoint Security; Mobile Security; Threat Intelligence
Title: A TraderTraitor's guide to getting away with billions.
Context: Hackers targeted air raid alert systems in both Ukraine and Russia over the weekend, sending false warnings of nuclear attacks and other threats. Cursor has released detection tools and indicators of compromise.
Full Text:
The FBI blames North Korea for a record-breaking crypto heist. Hackers hijack air raid alerts in Ukraine and Russia. European supermarket freezers come under attack again. Aur0ra ransomware operators put AI agents to work. Android’s SMS of Death gets a proof-of-concept exploit. Malicious Claude Code extensions infiltrate Cursor’s marketplace. Google offers a quarter-million-dollar bug bounty. ChatGPT faces a wrongful death lawsuit. Monday business briefing. Our guest is Cynthia Kaiser, SVP of Halcyon’s Ransomware Research Center and former Deputy Director of the FBI’s Cyber Division, sharing how the AI cybercrime economy is open for business and booming. The secure USB drive that wasn’t.

Today is Monday November 2nd 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

The FBI attributes last week’s record crypto heist to North Korea.

The FBI has attributed last week’s theft of more than six billion dollars from cryptocurrency exchange Binance to North Korea’s TraderTraitor hacking group. Investigators say the attackers are converting stolen assets into Ethereum and laundering funds through decentralized finance platforms and instant swap services.

Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic reports that roughly 2.9 billion dollars has been frozen or seized, leaving approximately 3.3 billion beyond issuers’ reach, spread across hundreds of cryptocurrency wallets.

Binance says it will cover the losses, protecting customer funds. The company continues investigating what it calls a complex attack involving multiple perpetrators and a self-destruct mechanism designed to erase forensic evidence.

TraderTraitor has been linked to several major cryptocurrency thefts, including the previous record-breaking 1.5-billion-dollar Bybit heist.

Hackers target air raid alert systems in both Ukraine and Russia.

Hackers targeted air raid alert systems in both Ukraine and Russia over the weekend, sending false warnings of nuclear attacks and other threats.

Ukraine’s official Air Alert app was compromised late Saturday, pushing messages in Russian warning of incoming nuclear strikes, chemical threats, and street fighting. Sirens also sounded across the country. Authorities temporarily disabled notifications, warned residents against clicking suspicious links, and restored normal operations within hours.

Early Sunday, Russia reported a similar attack on its emergency alert app. Users received bogus warnings that nuclear warheads had been launched across Russia, along with instructions to stockpile food and shelter in basements.

The Russian incident may have been retaliation for the earlier attack on Ukraine, although responsibility remains unconfirmed. Both countries acknowledged their systems had been compromised.

Supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe were once-again targeted.

Supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe were once-again targeted, remotely raising freezer temperatures and spoiling food.

Monday’s attacks affected more than 50 stores in Belgium, along with retailers in Sweden, Ireland, Estonia, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg. Some freezers were reportedly set to 50 degrees Celsius, or 122 Fahrenheit.

The incident follows a similar attack three weeks earlier that affected roughly 700 supermarkets in France. Authorities haven’t identified the perpetrators or established whether the attacks are connected.

Some affected systems rely on discontinued refrigeration controllers that no longer receive security updates. Technicians say certain equipment requires physical modifications rather than software patches.

The incidents highlight the risks posed by internet-connected industrial equipment, particularly when aging devices remain accessible remotely. For supermarkets, the consequences are immediate: spoiled inventory and costly repairs.

The Aur0ra ransomware group is extensively using AI agents to automate intrusions.

Sophos researchers say the cybercriminal group behind Aur0ra ransomware is extensively using AI agents to automate intrusions and evade security defenses.

The group, tracked as GOLD OGRE, reportedly used the AI coding tool Cursor to test endpoint security products and help conduct attacks. Human operators supplied credentials, network access, and objectives, then let AI agents handle reconnaissance, credential attacks, privilege escalation, and lateral movement with limited supervision.

Researchers observed agents adapting their techniques when initial attempts failed, sometimes gaining domain administrator access. Three organizations investigated were subsequently named on Aur0ra’s leak site.

The attackers also reportedly bypassed AI safety restrictions by describing their activities as authorized security testing.

Sophos warns that agentic AI could accelerate ransomware operations and lower the technical expertise required to carry them out.

The Android SMS of Death gets a proof of concept.

A security researcher has published a proof-of-concept exploit for an Android vulnerability dubbed “SMS of Death.” Tracked as CVE-2026-58882, the zero-click flaw allows attackers to crash phones or disrupt cellular service, including emergency calls, using specially crafted text messages.

Victims receive no visible warning, and repeated messages can trigger reboot loops requiring a factory reset.

Google reportedly patched the vulnerability in October for Android 14 through 17, although the fix wasn’t listed in its security bulletin. Older Android 12 and 13 devices remain vulnerable.

Malicious versions of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension were distributed through Cursor’s marketplace.

Attackers distributed malicious versions of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension through Cursor’s marketplace in a supply chain attack on October 29th.

Two compromised versions remained available for approximately eleven hours, potentially reaching 5,000 developer systems running Windows or macOS.

The malicious code collected system information and attempted to establish persistent remote access through reverse SSH tunnels. Cursor says those attempts generally failed because the extension lacked administrative privileges.

Anthropic confirmed its official distributions were unaffected.

Cursor removed the malicious extensions, temporarily suspended its marketplace, rotated security keys, and took steps to shut down the attacker’s infrastructure.

Affected users are urged to investigate their systems, since uninstalling the extension may leave malicious persistence mechanisms behind. Cursor has released detection tools and indicators of compromise.

Google offers a quarter million dollar bug bounty.

Google is offering security researchers up to $250,000 for vulnerabilities that could enable complete administrative takeover of Google Cloud environments.

The expanded bug bounty program rewards exploits that grant unrestricted control over cloud projects or organizations without requiring stolen credentials, existing access, or social engineering.

Remote code execution in Google’s underlying production infrastructure may also qualify.

Google has established strict testing rules to protect customer systems, including a cryptographic method for demonstrating unauthorized access without compromising real accounts.

The company says AI-assisted research is helping uncover increasingly sophisticated vulnerabilities.

ChatGPT faces a wrongful death lawsuit.

The parents of a 31-year-old Seattle software engineer are suing OpenAI, alleging that dangerous medical advice from ChatGPT contributed to their daughter’s death.

According to the lawsuit, Bowen Wan consulted the chatbot after losing her job, concerned that her epilepsy medication was affecting her English-speaking abilities during interviews.

The complaint alleges ChatGPT provided instructions for discontinuing her medication, discouraged consulting doctors, and reassured her when she began experiencing seizures.

Wan died from a seizure in February.

Her parents claim OpenAI failed to implement adequate safeguards, particularly for Chinese-language conversations.

OpenAI called the case heartbreaking, noting that Wan used an older version of ChatGPT. The company says newer models are better at recognizing medical emergencies, while emphasizing that ChatGPT cannot replace professional medical care.

Monday business briefing.

Cybersecurity investors are opening their wallets, with cloud and AI security companies leading the latest funding rounds.

San Francisco’s Upwind Security tops the list with a $400 million Series C, followed by Estonian DDoS protection provider Blackwall, which raised $100 million.

Agentic AI security startup Infisical secured $40 million, while Israeli security operations company Mave emerged from stealth with $34 million.

Mobile security provider iVerify and confidential cloud startup Modelyo each raised $17 million. Ultra Security secured $10 million, industrial cybersecurity firm Indurex raised $7.8 million, and Northstar Security landed $7 million. QuestorAI and Cygrid each raised $3 million.

On the acquisition front, healthcare technology provider Tegria purchased cybersecurity and cloud hosting firm CloudWave. Forte Technologies acquired managed security provider Business Cyber Security Solutions.

And Belgian developer security company Aikido Security launched a new workforce security business called Noon, combining its acquisitions of Poland’s Cyberly and Belgium’s Outkept.

The secure USB drive that wasn’t.

Security researcher Xusheng Li discovered that a Lenovo fingerprint-protected USB drive, advertised as offering AES-256 encryption, was essentially an ordinary SD card in an expensive disguise.

The fingerprint reader controlled access to the USB connection, but the data itself wasn’t encrypted. Anyone with physical access could simply extract the card.

Further investigation uncovered similar problems across multiple manufacturers, including hardcoded encryption keys, exposed passwords, and hidden accounts with simple credentials.

Using AI-assisted reverse engineering, Li cracked several supposedly secure products in minutes.

Lenovo has issued fixes for affected devices, although some require owners to ship their drives back or arrange firmware upgrades.

The research is a reminder that security claims aren’t always what they seem, particularly when manufacturers rely on proprietary technology nobody bothers to examine. As it turns out, some of these supposedly encrypted drives were keeping secrets from everyone except the people trying to steal them.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

And that’s the CyberWire Daily, brought to you by N2K CyberWire.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

Title: Warning: Scammers Are Targeting Voters Ahead of Election Day
Context: midterm elections, Malwarebytes reports
Full Text:
Scammers continue to target voters ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, Malwarebytes reports. The scams arrive via text message, email, or phone call, offering to help users register to vote, asking them to take a survey, or soliciting donations. The scams are designed to steal money, personal information, or credentials.

Malwarebytes observed one campaign targeting users in Minnesota, offering to add them to an absentee voter list. The link in the message takes the user to a website that asks for their personal information, which can be used to launch additional scams.

“The message is a scam, though it borrows the language of a real Minnesota voting service,” the researchers write. “Minnesota does have a permanent absentee voter list, but the link in this text is fraudulent. To check or sign up, go directly to your election authority’s official website. Other messages take the opposite approach: instead of offering convenience, they warn that you could lose your chance to vote. A message might say you are not registered to vote, your details are incomplete, or your registration is about to be cancelled. Then it offers a link to sort everything out.”

Other scams take a more threatening approach, warning users that they must pay a fine or click on a link to report for election duty.

Malwarebytes outlines the following advice to help users avoid falling for these scams:

“Go directly to official election websites to check registration, voting requirements, deadlines, and alleged penalties.

Verify donation requests independently. Find the campaign or organization yourself and confirm where your money will go.

Keep payment details out of unsolicited surveys. A political poll that turns into a request to pay for a prize is a red flag.

Check sellers before buying political merchandise. A candidate’s name or logo does not authenticate the shop.

Don’t mistake personal details for proof. A message can contain accurate information about you and still be a scam.

Keep political choices separate from requests for money or personal information. You can support a cause without responding to an unexpected message.”

Malwarebytes has the story: https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/scams/2026/10/five-election-scams-to-watch-out-for

Title: Your Artifactory is fine. Your Linux kernel hosting it might not be.
Context: In this scenario, a lost race only kills that one connection, so the attacker just tries again
Full Text:
Summary As we’ve written, AI is shrinking the time between “a fix is public” and “someone has a working exploit” to near-zero. JFrog products are not affected by Linux kernel CVE-2026-98432. Artifactory, Xray, and the rest of the JFrog Platform do not contain this flaw, as it lives in the Linux kernel itself. We are advising every self-managed JFrog customer to check their Linux hosts and update their kernels now to protect their environments, which may include hosted versions of JFrog products. Once your OS is updated, JFrog products are not at risk.

Our goal is always to protect your systems, and in some cases that may include advice on the protection of the environments your JFrog products operate in. JFrog Cloud customers are not affected by the Linux vulnerability, but if you self-manage JFrog, read on.

Your Linux kernel may be exposed, requiring you to patch it to protect your environment.

What happened

On October 15, the Linux kernel CVE team published CVE-2026-98432. It’s a use-after-free in the code that sets up new IPv4 TCP connections, caused by a race condition. The bug dates back to Linux 4.4. Upstream fixed it on October 5 following main line patching on September 17; upstream was fixed a full ten days before the CVE went public.

The kernel team scores this vulnerability a 9.8. Red Hat, Oracle, SUSE and Amazon score it lower, between 5.9 and 8.1.

Then, Anthropic published research on October 27 saying its Claude model wrote a working exploit. A remote attacker with no credentials gets a root shell on servers with a multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener. In Anthropic’s test, leaking a kernel address took 48 minutes. Getting command execution took only five more. In this scenario, a lost race only kills that one connection, so the attacker just tries again.

Importantly, Anthropic did not publish the exploit code. As of November 2, there have been no reports of attacks in the wild. MPTCP is less exotic than it sounds: since Go 1.24, Go programs request it by default on the sockets they listen on. The Go Security Team also says the underlying bug isn’t specific to MPTCP. (Tip: JFrog deployments include several Go services within versions later than 1.24.)

As a JFrog customer…

In a self-managed deployment, you own the operating system that JFrog operates in. We are responsible for the security of our products, and you for the platform underneath (host, kernel, patching) in a shared responsibility model. A vulnerable kernel under a healthy JFrog install still puts that host, and everything on it, at risk.

As of October 30, neither Ubuntu nor RHEL had released a fixed kernel. Ubuntu 22.04 through 26.10 are marked work in progress, and older releases are plain vulnerable. RHEL 8, 9 and 10 are listed as affected, with no date. Debian, Oracle Linux, SUSE and Amazon Linux have shipped fixes for at least some kernels. Check your exact release, because coverage varies within each distro.

What we’re advising you to do as soon as possible

Find out what you’re running. Version numbers lie, because distros backport fixes without bumping them. Check the changelog instead.

On Debian or Ubuntu:

apt changelog linux-image-$(uname -r) | grep CVE-2026-98432

On RHEL and its derivatives:

rpm -q --changelog kernel-$(uname -r) | grep CVE-2026-98432

If the command prints nothing, your running kernel doesn’t have the fix.

Patch where a fix exists, then reboot. A kernel update does nothing until the machine boots into it. If you build your own kernel, the fix is in 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10 and 7.3. The kernel team recommends moving to the latest stable release rather than cherry-picking the one commit.

Where there’s no fix yet, be proactive about it. Red Hat says no available mitigation meets its bar. Switching off MPTCP program by program is fragile, and the Go team says so directly: one forgotten listener and you’re exposed again. Narrow who can reach those hosts at the network layer, watch your vendor’s advisory for CVE-2026-98432, and patch the day the package is available. Another mitigation option could be using an L7 load balancer or reverse proxy with TCP termination to reduce direct exposure of vulnerable hosts. Reducing exposure doesn’t repair the bug, but it does reduce the number of people who can try to exploit it.

Make the next one simpler. If you proxy your Debian or RPM repos through Artifactory, the fixed kernel arrives in the repo your hosts already pull from. Stage it, promote it, roll it out in waves, with the same process you use for everything else. A kernel package is an artifact like any other, and it should have a system of record.

JFrog Xray scans your supply chain artifacts and images. It won’t tell you what kernel your host is running, because the kernel isn’t in either one; step one is a command you must run yourself.

The window is big, but shrinking

In an approaching-zero window from fix to exploit, rapid patching is required. The fix for this vulnerability was made public on October 5. A working exploit story hit on October 27. On October 30, two of the most widely run enterprise distros still had no update.

Our advice to protect your systems is simple:

Run the changelog check on every host that runs JFrog today. Update and reboot where a fixed kernel exists. Where it doesn’t, restrict access and subscribe to your distro’s advisory for CVE-2026-98432 so the fix doesn’t sit in a queue that could get forgotten.

Title: Beyond DKIM key rotation: understanding email replay attacks
Context: How Amazon SES helps you detect and respond Your first response is detection, not DNS changes
Full Text:
As the email administrator for your organization’s domain, you receive a Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) aggregate report showing email passing DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) verification as though it came from your domain, sent from IP addresses you don’t recognize to recipients you didn’t contact. To clear the issue, you rotate your DKIM key, confirm the new selector is live, and verify that your DMARC policy is already set to p=reject. Days later, you see that the same unfamiliar traffic is still authenticating as you.

In this post, you learn why rotation alone can’t stop a DKIM replay attack, how to confirm that you’re looking at a replay rather than a legitimate relay or ordinary spoofing, and the DNS cleanup step that most rotation guidance leaves out. You also learn how you can use Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) to detect and respond to this activity faster.

How DKIM replay works

DKIM verifies one thing: that specific parts of a message didn’t change between the signer and the receiver. The signer signs the message with a private key, and receivers fetch the matching public key from your domain’s DNS to check the signature. A valid signature continues to validate wherever the message travels afterward. Mailing lists, .forward rules, and third-party relays all preserve it, which is the protocol working as designed.

A replay attack takes advantage of that durability. The attack works as follows:

Your ecommerce platform sends a customer a legitimate response email, signed with your DKIM key.

An attacker obtains one copy of that message. They might subscribe to your mailing list, compromise a mailbox, retrieve it from a list archive, or capture it through a forwarding rule.

The attacker resends that message, unchanged, from their own servers to thousands of new recipients.

Each receiving server fetches your public key from DNS and checks the signature. The signature passes, because the body wasn’t modified. Sender Policy Framework (SPF) fails, because the sending IP isn’t yours, but DMARC requires only one of SPF or DKIM to pass with alignment. Because DKIM passes, DMARC passes, and the message is delivered as authenticated email from your domain.

Understanding what an attacker can and can’t do matters, because the limits define the problem. An attacker can’t modify your message, add new content, or read your email. The signature is only valid while the message remains byte-for-byte identical.

What an attacker gains is your domain’s reputation, which they use to deliver your genuine message to an audience you didn’t intend. A receipt or invoice becomes a lure, and email that would normally be filtered is delivered because receivers trust your domain. This is abuse of reputation and reach, not content forgery, and the distinction matters when you explain the incident to your security team.

This also explains why an enforcing DMARC policy doesn’t stop an attack. DMARC passes when SPF or DKIM passes with alignment. During a replay, DKIM passes, so DMARC passes, and p=reject does not apply. A p=reject policy is designed to stop spoofing, where a forger has no valid signature and DKIM fails. It does nothing against a message that you signed. Determining which of the two was used is what tells you how to respond.

Is it replay, spoofing, or a legitimate relay?

Email from an unfamiliar IP address that passes DKIM has three common explanations, and each requires a different response. Confirm which you’re dealing with before you make any changes.

DMARC aggregate (rua) reports provide the source IP address, message volume, and SPF and DKIM results. This is enough to identify an anomaly, but not to prove a replay. A report row might read as follows:

source IP: 203.0.113.45 | count: 4,200 | SPF: fail | DKIM: pass (d=yourdomain.com)

You need to evaluate that row against the three possibilities:

The first possibility is a legitimate relay that you haven’t inventoried, such as a mailing list, a forwarder, or an email security gateway such as an inline cloud access security broker (CASB) that you route through. The signature validly survives the relay, and this is normal email flow. In the report, the source IP address usually resolves to a known provider, and the volume tracks your actual sending.

The second possibility is replay abuse, in which an attacker redistributes a message that you legitimately signed. In this case, the DKIM-passing volume comes from an IP address that has no business relationship with you, often well above the usual number of recipients that you send to, and frequently to recipient domains that you haven’t worked with.

The third possibility is ordinary spoofing, which is a forgery with no valid signature. That row shows DKIM: fail. DKIM that passes from an unknown IP address is therefore usually not ordinary spoofing.

Aggregate counts can’t prove a replay on their own. To confirm a replay, you need message-level evidence: a specific message that you sent matched to one that reached recipients you didn’t address. If you can’t make that match, treat the activity as an unconfirmed anomaly, and begin with the enforcement and monitoring steps that follow rather than removing keys.

Set up an enforcing DMARC policy first

Before you take any other action, confirm that you’re enforcing DMARC. Many domains that encounter this problem are still at p=none, which is monitoring only. This situation is common. Every DMARC deployment begins at p=none, and many organizations do not advance beyond it because nothing appears to be broken. At p=none, receivers take no action on failures, so no change you make affects delivery, and you can’t determine what enforcement would have caught.

The first step is therefore not key removal; it’s completing your sender inventory and reaching enforcement:

Inventory every legitimate sender and relay for your domain, including your email service providers, mailing lists, and any security gateways that send on your behalf.

Bring each sender into SPF and DKIM alignment so that legitimate email authenticates.

Advance the policy one stage at a time, from p=none to p=quarantine to p=reject. Review your rua reports at each stage before you advance, typically for a week or two per stage, and longer if you have many senders to work through. The pct tag lets you ramp up gradually, for example by quarantining 25% of failing email before you increase the percentage.

After you’re enforcing DMARC, receivers that honor DMARC drop unauthenticated spoofing on your behalf. Only after this baseline is in place, and only after you have confirmed a replay of genuinely signed email, does the next step apply.

Remove the old key from DNS: routine hygiene after rotation

Most rotation guidance omits this step. Rotating a key and removing the old key are two separate actions.

Rotation means that your provider begins signing new email with a new key and selector. Removal means deleting the old public key from DNS, so that previously signed messages, including the copies that an attacker captured, can no longer be verified. If you rotate but leave the old public key published, every message ever signed with that key remains replayable for as long as the record exists. Removing the old key is what closes that window and is the step that’s commonly overlooked.

Removal affects only messages that are still in transit and were signed with the old key. After email is delivered, the receiver no longer needs your key, so we recommend that you leave the old key published long enough for in-flight email to arrive and then remove it. How much of this process you manage yourself depends on your DKIM method, which the following section describes. During a confirmed active replay, closing this window is essential.

How you manage keys depends on the DKIM method that you use with Amazon SES. With Bring Your Own DKIM (BYODKIM), you generate the key pair and publish the public key as a TXT record that you control. You can rotate and remove keys whenever you want, including removing an old key on demand during an incident. As the BYODKIM documentation states, “you can rotate the DKIM keys for your domains as often as you want.”

With Easy DKIM, a feature where Amazon SES generates and manages the keys for you, you publish CNAME records that point to AWS-hosted keys. Because your DNS points to AWS-hosted keys through those CNAME records, Amazon SES manages the underlying key material for you, so you don’t publish or remove individual keys yourself. Unlike BYODKIM, Easy DKIM doesn’t provide an on-demand option to delete a specific key immediately.

If you’re an Easy DKIM sender during a confirmed replay, your defenses are early detection (described in the following section), the duplicate-message throttling that receivers already apply, and, over the longer term, the emerging DKIM2 effort, an IETF initiative to update the DKIM specification with built-in replay resistance, which is being designed to give receivers better signals to identify and act on replayed messages at the protocol level.

How Amazon SES helps you detect and respond

Your first response is detection, not DNS changes. The goal is to identify anomalous DKIM-passing volume early, while you build the message-level evidence that distinguishes a replay from a legitimate relay.

Begin by enabling logging. Create an Amazon SES configuration set with an event destination (see Monitor email sending using Amazon SES event publishing) that streams per-message events (Send, Delivery, Bounce, and Complaint) to Amazon Data Firehose or Amazon EventBridge (see Add an event destination), tagged with the From domain.

Separately, confirm that you’re receiving rua reports for your domain. You enable these reports by adding a rua= address to your domain’s DMARC TXT record, for example rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@yourdomain.com. For the record syntax and a phased p=none to p=quarantine to p=reject rollout, see Complying with DMARC authentication protocol in Amazon SES. Reports arrive as daily XML digests, and most teams process them with a DMARC analyzer rather than reading the raw XML.

With both sources in place, you can correlate them. Compare the email that your account emitted—based on your Amazon SES delivery events—against what DMARC reports show that receivers accepted as your domain. When DMARC shows DKIM-passing volume from IP addresses outside your SPF record that exceeds the delivery events that Amazon SES recorded for that From domain in the same window, that gap is your signal. It’s also how you build the message-level case that distinguishes a replay from a legitimate relay.

We recommend three additional controls. Amazon SES sending authorization restricts which AWS principals can send using your verified identity. It doesn’t stop an external replay, but it addresses the insider and third-party vector that SPF, DKIM, and DMARC don’t cover on their own, so use identity-level policies to limit sending to specific AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principals.

Use Amazon Route 53 to set short DNS time-to-live values (TTLs) (for example, 300 seconds) on your DKIM records so that changes propagate quickly; and enable DNS query logging with an Amazon CloudWatch Logs metric filter that watches for queries to a selector that you’ve rotated away from.

A spike in lookups for an old selector is a useful early indicator of a replay attempt using a retired selector. For a BYODKIM domain during a confirmed replay, Route 53 is also where you remove the old selector’s TXT record. You can automate that removal by using an Amazon CloudWatch alarm that starts an AWS Lambda function to call the Route 53 API and retire an old selector’s record.

Scope the function’s IAM role to only the specific Route 53 hosted zone and record that it needs to change, so that it follows least privilege. Because an incorrect DNS change can have a wide effect, gate any automation behind confirmed-replay criteria and test it against a non-production domain first. For most teams, alarm-to-human is safer than alarm-to-automatic-removal.

When your domain is the one being abused

Most guidance assumes that you’re either the provider preventing abuse or the receiver detecting it. In a replay, your domain is the one whose reputation is being consumed, and you aren’t on the recipient list. As a result, you don’t have the message that everyone asks for when you report the issue.

When you file an abuse report with the provider that hosts the source IP address, they ask for full message headers. The email went to people you didn’t contact, so you don’t have the message headers. You then provide DMARC aggregate reports that show the source IP address and volume, and the provider asks for headers again. At this point, you’re unable to proceed.

To break this cycle, go to the recipients. Review your rua reports for the top recipient domains—which are often .gov and .edu domains—contact those recipients directly and request a sample message with full headers. In addition to providing the headers, that sample lets you confirm a replay rather than a legitimate relay. Build your abuse report around the IP address and the DMARC evidence rather than the message content. If the source IP address belongs to Amazon Web Services (AWS), report it through the AWS abuse process and include your DMARC reports and SPF record as evidence.

Incident response: ordered actions

If your reports show suspicious DKIM-passing email from unfamiliar IP addresses, complete the following procedure.

To respond to a suspected DKIM replay

Confirm that it’s a replay. Match a message that you sent to one that reached recipients you didn’t address and rule out legitimate relays and gateways. Aggregate data alone isn’t proof.

Reach an enforcing DMARC policy. Inventory your legitimate senders, align them, and advance from p=none to p=quarantine to p=reject. This stops spoofing.

Harden SPF to -all rather than ~all, but only after your sender inventory is complete, since -all hard-fails any legitimate source you haven’t listed.

Check the DKIM-Signature header of a fresh message to confirm that your provider signs only with the current selector.

Report the source IP address to the hosting provider and include your DMARC evidence.

Investigate the capture point, such as a compromised mailbox, a mailing list, a forwarding rule, or a newsletter subscription.

Remove the old DKIM public key after in-flight email has cleared. For BYODKIM, delete the old selector’s TXT record. For Easy DKIM, rely on the managed Amazon SES rotation together with the monitoring and receiver-side defenses described earlier.

Title: Anti-Oligarchy Activists Plan to Dox Elon Musk and Hundreds of Billionaire-Linked Homes
Context: Two of its members, interviewed by WIRED on the condition of anonymity, say they spent the past year constructing dossiers on billionaires—and one trillionaire—and the people...
Full Text:
An underground activist group says it plans to start openly doxing billionaires as part of a phased campaign against what it calls the American oligarchy—beginning this month with a release that maps the homes of Elon Musk, his brother Kimbal, and Tesla’s board, alongside investors and suppliers that keep the corporation afloat.

Two of its members, interviewed by WIRED on the condition of anonymity, say they spent the past year constructing dossiers on billionaires—and one trillionaire—and the people they consider their top lieutenants, using nearly every method available to a private investigator, and some that are not.

The pair say the group is international and includes grassroots activists, researchers, journalists, and artists, including some who received top honors in print, television, and digital media in their former careers. For security, many work in “silos” and do not know each other’s names. Through its connections, the group says it has raised more than $1.2 million from “a heartening number of wealthy class traitors” who share in the view that concentrations of extreme wealth and political power pose an “existential threat.”

In a press release Monday, the group says it intends to publish in coming releases more than 150 home addresses, most of them previously unreported. It also promises more than 3,500 records on people with a combined wealth of about $1.4 trillion, plus reporting on what the group alleges are “criminal exploits and security lapses.”

Members of the organization call themselves Capytistas, a play on Zapatistas, the Indigenous insurgents of southern Mexico.

The capybara, a placid rodent famous for getting along with almost any other animal, became the group’s avatar during the early days of Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency, as a secret rival to the Shiba Inu—the Doge meme Musk used to brand the agency. (The meme has since been reclaimed by pro-Ukranian activists who post as cartoon dogs to mock Russian propaganda and raise money for the war.)

Americans have long used the term “oligarch” to refer almost exclusively to Russian tycoons who carved up state industries after the Soviet collapse. But it entered mainstream American politics decisively in January 2025, when President Joe Biden used his farewell address to warn that an “oligarchy is taking shape in America.” No one typifies the “extreme wealth, power, and influence” Biden described more than the trillionaire Musk, who held an unpaid job as a special government employee for much of 2025 and has thrown more than $700 million into federal elections since 2023; the equivalent of roughly 15 million typical donations online.

Doxing—the Capytistas’ chosen tactic—has meanwhile become a favored weapon of political guerrillas and self-appointed state informants: In March 2025, as protesters gathered outside Tesla dealerships, an anonymous site called DOGEQuest posted what it claims were the addresses of Tesla owners and DOGE staff. Months later, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement official testified that his unit drew more than three-quarters of its deportation referrals from Canary Mission—a site with similarly nebulous funding but radically different goals: building dossiers on pro-Palestinian students and professors.

Title: Thieves pilfer environment variables from Trigger AI workflow tool
Context: Trigger offered little explanation in its Sunday security incident report, noting that its investigation had identified “exposure across a subset of organizations” and that an...
Full Text: If you're a customer of cloud-hosted AI workflow platform Trigger.dev, take heed, because your environment variables may have been exposed in a security incident disclosed on Sunday. Trigger offered little explanation in its Sunday security incident report, noting that its investigation had identified “exposure across a subset of organizations” and that an attacker had gained unauthorized access to environment variables belonging to those organizations. Whatever exploit was used to gain access has been blocked, the company added, and affected customers have been notified of steps they need to take to prevent further security problems. We likely don't have to tell The Reg readers how important environment variables are in SaaS and cloud services like Trigger. If compromised environment variables contain sensitive credentials, an attacker could basically end up with the keys to the kingdom, potentially gaining access to connected services and digital infrastructure. For those unfamiliar with Trigger.dev, it’s a platform for building AI agents and workflows in TypeScript, but here’s the kicker: Trigger advertises itself as a durable execution platform that handles pesky things like retries, scaling, and keeping long-running tasks going through crashes and redeployments, while providing tools to monitor what those tasks are doing. Trigger, the company’s site notes, can be used to “build durable AI agents that survive refreshes, redeploys, and crashes,” and is ideal for “long-running tasks with retries, queues, AI observability and elastic scaling.” In short, companies running their AI on Trigger probably want it to keep running, which makes stolen environment variables all the more dangerous. Elastic scaling, automated retries, and, as Trigger notes, the ability to run lots of concurrent operations without timeouts could compound the consequences of compromised API keys, depending on what those credentials allow an attacker to access. An attacker with stolen credentials could potentially interfere with a customer's connected services or workflows. Additionally, Trigger recently added webhooks to its offering, supporting services like Stripe, Supabase, and Slack, potentially expanding the range of integrations that could be affected if their credentials were exposed. This could be pretty bad for anyone affected. Trigger has some fairly high-profile customers, with companies like fashion brand Emporio Armani, Pentagon-supporting AI acquisitions platform GovSignals, SaaS calendar platform Cal.com, and others all listed on the company’s site. Trigger has not publicly identified which organizations were affected by the intrusion. We reached out to Trigger, which declined to provide any additional information on the incident. A company spokesperson instead told us to wait for a full incident report to learn more. Luckily for Trigger customers and those concerned about SaaS security now that AI is regularly coming up with new vulnerabilities in commonly used platforms, Trigger is open source and can be self-hosted, which might be a better alternative in this day and age than relying on a hosted service. ®

Title: Token thieves costing companies $100K+ per day in illicit LLM charges
Context: “Locking down these resources will not only protect organizations from runaway costs, but also protect the broader community from a deluge of cheap, autonomous attacks
Full Text: Victim organizations are losing millions of dollars in token charges as criminals hijack their corporate LLM access to steal expensive computing resources and AI services. These fraudulent charges from resource consumption can exceed $100,000 a day, according to a Monday report by Google's Mandiant incident responders, who saw cumulative charges at some organizations hit $1 million before the victim companies revoked intruders' access. "Whenever possible, threat actors want to use this technology to gain a scale advantage over defenders. They achieve that with agentic tools and by stealing tokens from unwitting third parties,” John Hultquist, chief analyst at Google Threat Intelligence Group, told The Register. “Locking down these resources will not only protect organizations from runaway costs, but also protect the broader community from a deluge of cheap, autonomous attacks.” This tactic of hijacking access to LLMs is called LLMJacking, and it’s been increasing steadily over the past two years. In one extreme case, documented in an August report from CrowdStrike, a token thief sent about 200,000 API requests in just two minutes. In one case detailed in the report, a group Google tracks as UNC6993 illicitly gained access to LLM API keys, then generated additional keys and enabled services within the victim’s cloud projects, racking up $100,000 in charges. The threat intel biz also documented a different token thief subscribing victim accounts to Pay-As-You-Go agreements to access advanced models on the victim company’s dime. The crook selected premium foundation models, launched high-volume inference streams, and used a “burn and rotate strategy” to bypass rate limits by creating and deleting short-lived service accounts while auditing the billing interface to monitor financial impact. In yet another incident, an intruder executed more than 500,000 LLM API calls in less than eight hours using stolen third-party API keys to power a token routing service called Jet Night, according to a Monday report from Google. “Given Jet Night’s per-token costs to users are so far below typical market rates GTIG believes the service relies on stolen keys to operate profitably,” the report says. “For example, Jet Night offers an unlimited token plan for approximately $60 USD per month with alleged access to frontier models, a consumer service level that would typically run between $100 and $250 per month.” Jet Night has also admitted to multiple outages on its public Telegram channel, which the Google threat hunters note is “likely due to stolen keys being revoked as victims discover their respective compromises.” Specialized LLMjacking roles As more criminals join the LLMJacking ecosystem, Google says it has documented a division of labor between the criminals that establish initial access to compromised cloud and AI services, and those that manage downstream monetization infrastructure, called “LLM Mixers.” In one case that Mandiant responded to in mid-2026, UNC6993 compromised a cloud instance through a misconfigured Service Account key and used this access to grant further access to a model API. The crooks also spun up a session hijacking page purporting to be an application portal to join a group of LLM users. “This page tricks users into navigating to the legitimate LLM service website, and pasting their raw JSON payload containing an active access token, which was then posted to the backend API to bypass password and multifactor authentication (MFA) controls,” the report says. Google predicts miscreants will “increasingly prioritize LLMJacking” compared to other types of resource theft like cryptojacking. And to prevent cloud LLM service abuse, the security firm says defenders should prioritize identity and access management plus supply chain security, and use a centralized secrets management platform to rotate keys and secrets. Also apply least-access privileges to users and service accounts, ensuring that they only have permissions necessary to complete their roles and tasks. And automate secrets scanning within codebases to identify and then remove any API keys and secrets added to source code. ®

Title: Mutipath TCP: Use and Detection, (Mon, Nov 2nd)
Context: The only widely used implementation I have observed is iOS/iPadOS
Full Text:
Last week, an often-ignored TCP option, introduced in 2020, made the news due to a new vulnerability in Linux's implementation (RFC 8684, CVE-2026-98432)

Instead of looking at the vulnerability, I am using this diary to talk a bit about multipath TCP (MPTCP) and how you may see it used in your network.

What is MPTCP?

Traditionally, TCP is a connection-oriented protocol. Connections are established between a client and server, and host IP addresses are not expected to change for a specific connection. This restriction to a specific path does not always match modern system architecture. For example, mobile devices may switch from a local WIFI network to a cellular network at any time. Having to re-establish TCP connections may break applications. At the same time, servers often have a hard time "filling" high-bandwidth links using a single TCP connection due to limits on Window Size and the sequence number range [RFC 6182]. MPTCP is supposed to solve these problems by allowing connections to be split and handed over between different IP addresses.

The only widely used implementation I have observed is iOS/iPadOS. In this case, IPv4 connections to Apple (17.0.0.0/8) often utilize MPTCP [Apple]. MPTCP was initially used for Siri, and later for other services like Apple Music.

Two versions of MPTCP are currently defined and used: v0 and v1. At first,

MPTCP Options

The MPTCP Option (0x1e, 30) is followed by a byte containing 4 bits indicating the subtype and 4 bits indicating the version (0 or 1).

+----------------+--------------+----------------+----------------+ | TCP Option | Option Length|Subtype| Version| Flags | +----------------+--------------+----------------+----------------+ | 30 | variable | | 0 or 1 | | +----------------+--------------+----------------+----------------+

MP_CAPABLE (subtype 0): Indicates MPTCP support. Both sides must include it in the TCP handshake for MPTCP support to be enabled. Each MP_CAPABLE option also carries an 8-byte key that will later be used to identify and authenticate the different sub-sessions.

MP_JOIN (subtype 1): A second TCP connection may join an initial connection using the MP_JOIN option. This connection will typically be initiated by the client, but may originate from a different IP address. The RFC does specifically allow the server to initiate the second (or additional) connection. The RFC states: "It is permissible for either host in a connection to initiate the creation of a new subflow, but it is expected that this will normally be the original connection initiator." Ports should be the same, but do not have to be. Of course, this also accounts for common firewall rules. The web server will likely listen only on port 443, and the client's firewall will reject inbound SYN packets.

DSS (Data Sequence Signal, subtype 2): Each TCP connection which is part of MPTCP maintains its own sequence numbers, and acts just like any other "normal" TCP connection. To stitch the content of multiple connections together, the DSS option is used. It maps the respective's TCP sequence numbers to the sequence numbers of the combined connection.

ADD_ADDR/REMOVE_ADDR (subtypes 3, 4): these options are somewhat similar to MP_JOIN, but instead of actually setting up an additional connection, they advertise (or remove) additional addresses or ports that can be used.

MPTCP Detection

The best way to detect MPTCP is to look for TCP Option 30. Here are a few ways to do so:

Wireshark/tshark: Wireshark has a "mptcp" display filter keyword. As so often, Wireshark does make it easy.

tcpdump: There is no great way to match TCP options in tcpdump. But MPTCP packets, particularly SYN packets, tend to have large TCP headers, so a quick match on TCP header length can help. For example: 'tcp[12]>0xd0'

Suricata: Use the "tcp.hdr" keyword to inspect TCP options. The tricky part is that the option length isn't always the same. But there should be at least one MP_CAPABLE message that includes both the sender and receiver key, making this option 20 bytes long. The first three bytes are |1e 14 00| for version 0 or |1e 14 01| for version 1.

Snort: Snort does not have a keyword to inspect TCP options, and as far as I know, no way to filter for multipath TCP. The snort_decoder "experimental TCP option" alert only triggers on specific option types reserved for experimental use.

Zeek: By default, zeek does not log options, but it does offer the tcp_option and tcp_options events that can easily be used to log MPTCP. For example:

event tcp_option(c: connection, is_orig: bool, opt: count, optlen: count) { if ( opt == 30 ) { print(fmt("MPTCP between %s and %s", c$id$orig_h, c$id$resp_h)); } }

Title: Armadin Tests Find 88% of Severe Flaws Outside Vendor Advisories
Context: Some 88% of the critical and high-severity weaknesses found in live attack tests on enterprise environments this year would not have been identified through vendor advisories or...
Full Text:
Some 88% of the critical and high-severity weaknesses found in live attack tests on enterprise environments this year would not have been identified through vendor advisories or other outside sources, new data has suggested.

The figure comes from a report published on November 2 by Armadin, the offensive security startup launched by Mandiant founder Kevin Mandia, based on AI-driven attacks against its clients' live systems.

The clients span nearly a dozen industries, but Armadin did not disclose how many organizations or findings the data covers.

Read more on exposure management: AI Threats and Alert Fatigue Challenge Cybersecurity Teams

Most Severe Findings Sat Beyond Advisories and Logins

Defects in software the clients had written themselves made up 67% of the critical findings and 78% of the high findings that advisories could not cover. Vendor products deployed in ways no advisory describes, such as administrative consoles exposed to the internet, accounted for 24% and 22%.

The remaining 9% of critical findings, and under 1% of high ones, were zero-days Armadin found itself, including one in an identity governance platform whose vendor took almost four months to issue an advisory.

Nearly 70% of critical and high findings sat on the unauthenticated attack surface. Of the documented attack chains, 82% began without credentials, and 56% of those went on without a password or key ever being presented.

In more than 70% of client environments, Armadin said it reached a critical outcome in three steps or fewer without valid credentials.

Exposed Service Accounts Created Further Attack Paths

Just under half of the chains that started without authentication relied on an exposed credential, 71% of which belonged to applications or service accounts rather than people. Nearly 90% were reachable without extraction, often in repositories, configuration files, backups, logs or cloud settings.

In one engagement, Armadin started from an unprivileged domain account and used a flaw in backup software to read the credentials it held. That led to a hypervisor management server and, via a domain controller backup, to domain administrator hashes.

Fixing the severe findings meant shipping application code in 51% of cases, changing a setting, permission or policy in 43% and rotating an exposed credential in 32%, with many needing more than one step.

Armadin's recommendations included policies for provisioning, storing and rotating service account credentials, and checks of pipelines and code repositories for exposed secrets.

By its count, 93% of severe findings needed no third party to act, leaving the fix in each organization's own hands.

Title: Nuclear threats and street brawls: Russia, Ukraine report attacks on their emergency alert apps
Context: According to the messages sent to devices after the compromise of Ukraine's alert app, the fake warnings pertained to various threats, such as street fights in Kyiv, chemical...
Full Text: Cyberattacks on both Russia’s and Ukraine’s emergency alert apps resulted in fake messages about missile and nuclear strikes broadcast to the public. Officials from both countries confirmed the attacks, which occurred at similar times, on Sunday evening. According to public statements and messages sent via social media, Ukraine’s alert app was hit first, with the country’s Air Force quick to dispel nuclear fears. "The Air Alert app has likely been compromised," it said via Telegram at around 2100 UTC. "There is no radiation threat! Stay calm, follow our messages on our channel!" At around 0030 UTC on Monday, Russia's Ministry of Emergency Situations confirmed the country’s app had also been abused, with fake messages sent to citizens' devices. "Attention! The Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations' mobile app has been subjected to a massive cyberattack, allowing attackers to send fake information to the public," it said, also via Telegram. "Work is currently underway to patch the vulnerability and restore normal operation." The ministry issued an update around 90 minutes later, saying the app was once again functioning normally, and pointing out that an attack on the app was not the same as a compromise of the state’s national alert system. "Citizens are alerted through primary channels: regional and municipal alert systems (sirens, loudspeakers), communication networks (SMS messaging), and television and radio broadcasts. The mobile app is merely an additional, supporting information service," it stated. Ukraine's Ministry of Digital Affairs also issued a public announcement reminding citizens about how to receive emergency warnings while its “Alarm!” app was down. These include enabling iOS and Android emergency alerts, state-controlled sirens, and other official sources, such as the official social media accounts of Ukraine's government. According to the messages sent to devices after the compromise of Ukraine's alert app, the fake warnings pertained to various threats, such as street fights in Kyiv, chemical attacks, and radiation hazards. Alerts about the threat of nuclear fallout from official government warning systems would normally lead to panic, however, one of the earliest messages sent to citizens was written in Russian and referenced the "Oreshnik" missile, which was an immediate signal that the message may not be genuine. Equivalent alerts sent to Russian citizens also warned of impending nuclear strikes "at all regions of Russia," referencing "P1-Sun," the name of a Ukrainian attack drone. Oleksander Merezhko, who chairs the Ukrainian parliament's foreign affairs committee and noted the suspicious Russian-language alert, told the BBC the attack was almost certainly part of Russia's cyber war. "It's a very unpleasant fact but it is part of cyber war and people in Ukraine understand that," he said. "It is possible and we are quite prepared for such possibilities." Russia has not explicitly blamed Ukraine for the attack on its app, and official sources say the app is running as normal. Ukraine's announcement of the alert app cyberattack came almost simultaneously with the official conclusion of a six-day ceasefire in Kherson. Russia agreed to the rare temporary suspension of conflict to allow hundreds of Ukrainians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Olehsky. Russia did not agree to a proposed extension of the ceasefire, which officially ended at around 2100 UTC – around the same time Ukrainians began receiving fake warning messages. ®

Title: 5 stars for sale: Inside the underground fake review trade
Context: 5 stars as a service In the first example, discovered on a major English-language underground forum, a seller operating under the handle “aqenova” advertises both five-star...
Full Text:
Recently, our team exposed sophisticated scam kits designed to steal sensitive data and trick consumers. But underground marketplaces are not just for malware and stolen passwords. They also offer services designed to manipulate your opinion of the products and services you buy every day.

In our latest research, we examined cybercrime forums where sellers advertise illicit “reputation management” services. For the right price, these underground operators offer to flood a product with glowing, five-star ratings or remove negative reviews. This shadowy industry works both ways—artificially boosting reputations and deliberately hiding legitimate complaints.

A major shift we are seeing in this space is the adoption of new technology. We also found that cybercriminals are using AI to automate these fake review campaigns. This could allow them to quickly generate realistic, human-sounding feedback in large volumes without much manual effort.

5 stars as a service

In the first example, discovered on a major English-language underground forum, a seller operating under the handle “aqenova” advertises both five-star review generation and negative review removal services.

The seller’s operations span widely used platforms, including Google, Trustpilot, Yelp, and various mobile app stores. By simply asking prospective buyers, “Just tell me which platform reviews you need?” the seller presents reputation manipulation as something buyers can just order on demand.

Five-star reviews and removal services

Decoding the seller’s FAQ

Analyzing another seller’s (TrustForge) “Frequently Asked Questions” section revealed some surprising details about how these operations reportedly run behind the scenes.

First, the seller emphasizes that real people manually post these reviews, offering a guarantee for both successful delivery and “non-drop”—meaning the platform won’t flag and remove the feedback later.

Remember, a real person posting a review doesn’t mean they’re a real customer. The important question is whether they actually used the product or service and are describing an honest experience.

Second, it appears this is a well-coordinated team effort rather than a solo operation, as the seller charges an extra fee if a buyer wants the main operator to write the review text personally.

However, what caught our attention most was their confidence in beating platform checks. The seller guarantees their fake reviews will stay active, claiming they rely on a closely guarded “private method.” According to TrustForge’s own statements, this method has allowed them to post more than 10,000 fake reviews.

Reputation management FAQ

The clean-up crew: Making bad reviews disappear

A single negative review is often all it takes to create a bad first impression of a product or service. When those negative comments start to pile up, they can completely ruin a business’s reputation and bottom line.

Recognizing how desperate businesses can be to protect their image, our research team discovered underground services specifically offering to remove “fake” or “unfair” reviews from major platforms like Google and Trustpilot.

Of course, the boundary between what is genuinely fake and what a business simply considers “unfair” can be blurry. Businesses can legitimately challenge fabricated reviews, but these services raise concerns about whether genuine customer complaints could also be targeted.

If legitimate customer complaints disappear, consumers lose information that could help them decide where to spend their money.

An offer to remove “fake” or “unfair” Google reviewsAn offer to remove ”fake” or “unfair” review Google reviews

On average, having a single review removed through these underground services costs between $100 and $200. However, the pricing jumps dramatically depending on the platform.

For instance, one seller advertised Airbnb review removal for around $1,100 per review.

When you check a business’s reviews, you’re looking for patterns in other customers’ experiences. If genuine complaints disappear, you could miss repeated problems with refunds, product quality, or customer service.

$1,100 to remove a “fake” or “unfair” Airbnb review

Artificial intelligence, artificial reviews

During the last few months, our research team spotted an interesting thread on an underground forum where two users discussed using AI to mimic human E-E-A-T.

E-E-A-T stands for Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness. It is a quality evaluation framework outlined in Google’s Search Quality Rater Guidelines, which human evaluators use to assess content quality. E-E-A-T itself is not a direct ranking factor.

In the discussion we observed, one user asked the community if it was possible to use AI to effectively fake these qualities when writing product reviews and artificially boost website rankings. The answer was a resounding yes.

Another user claimed they had never experienced problems getting Google to index their completely AI-generated reviews.

AI vs. E-E-A-T

Behind the scenes: The IP addresses for fake reviews

To keep fake reviews from being flagged and deleted, scammers need to look like everyday consumers. To help do this, they can use something called “residential and mobile proxies,” which route their traffic through other internet connections to disguise where it comes from.

Think of an IP address as your computer’s caller ID. When scammers use bulk IP addresses from giant data centers, platforms may spot and block that traffic as coming from commercially hosted infrastructure. Residential proxies, on the other hand, route traffic through real, physical home internet connections—just like the Wi-Fi you use in your living room. Mobile proxies work the same way, but use real cellular networks.

Our team recently discovered a seller on an underground forum acting as a direct supplier of these residential and mobile connections. The seller explicitly advertises them as perfect for running fake review campaigns.

Residential and mobile proxies advertised for fake review campaigns

How to avoid being misled by fake reviews

The main goal of this research isn’t to make you panic or stop trusting every online review you read. We want to raise awareness about what happens behind the scenes, so you can make more informed buying decisions.

If a product or offer seems too good to be true, but is backed by a mountain of perfect five-star reviews, take a moment to pause. Scammers often use these artificially boosted ratings to make a bad deal look reassuring.

Read recent reviews and some of the middle-rated ones, rather than relying on the overall score. Look for recurring details about the things that matter to you, such as durability, delivery, or getting your money back.

Look for repeated wording or sudden bursts of glowing feedback. These signs don’t prove a review is fake, but they’re reasons to take a closer look. Check the seller’s contact details and return policy, too.
