Title: Report: Most Fraud Attacks Target Existing Customer Relationships
Context: A new report from TransUnion has found that 81% of digital fraud attacks target existing customer relationships, with more than half of U
Full Text:
A new report from TransUnion has found that 81% of digital fraud attacks target existing customer relationships, with more than half of U.S. businesses reporting increased scam and fraud activity over the past year.

“Identity-based fraud attacks often arise before organizations have sufficient information to establish trust in new customers,” the report says. “While account creation is a critical trust-establishing event, most fraud exposure occurs after the customer relationship has already been established. Different risk patterns appear across account creation, login, and financial transaction activities, especially for AI-enabled fraud. For instance, AI can help fraudsters rapidly generate or modify identities, credentials and interactions to target the weakest controls across the customer lifecycle.”

Most respondents cited synthetic identity fraud, which uses exposed consumer information and AI to craft phony personas, as their top concern over the next two years.

“Forty-three percent of U.S. business leaders said the growing scale and sophistication of fraud is placing significant or severe pressure on their organizations,” TransUnion says. “Synthetic identity fraud is a key concern, with 67% expecting it to increase over the next two years and 53% citing it as the threat they are least prepared to address. In the U.S., 51% of business leaders reported increased scam and authorized fraud activity over the past year. U.S. lenders face an estimated $2.4 billion in exposure tied to synthetic identities as of June 30, 2026.”

The increase is partly due to adversarial use of AI tools, which allow attackers to drastically improve the scale and sophistication of social engineering attacks.

“AI has fundamentally changed the economics of fraud by automating activities that once required significant human effort, including creating identities, generating content, and targeting victims,” TransUnion says. “This allows fraudsters to accelerate and scale their attacks faster than organizations can adapt their detection capabilities and mitigation strategies.

TransUnion has the story: https://newsroom.transunion.com/81-of-suspected-digital-fraud-attacks-target-existing-customer-relationships-transunion-finds/

Title: Frozen part II: Hackers remotely defrost produce in Euro supermarkets ... again
Context: The cyberattacks on commercial refrigerators and freezers in Europe continue, as a slew of grocery stores in Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden report widespread food...
Full Text: The cyberattacks on commercial refrigerators and freezers in Europe continue, as a slew of grocery stores in Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden report widespread food wastage as a result of miscreants raising the temperatures to highs of 50ºC (122°F). In Belgium, around 40 Delhaize stores were affected after the attackers reportedly switched fridges and freezers into defrost mode overnight, between Sunday and Monday, resulting in stock issues. Diego Louwers, a Proxy Delhaize store manager in Overijse, near Brussels, told RTL Info that the consequences of the cyberattacks were "catastrophic," forcing the store to throw out the entirety of its fresh and frozen products. "We can't have anything worse in our line of work," he said. "We have to throw away all of our merchandise, and it's both heartbreaking and very complicated operationally." A Delhaize spokesperson said it took steps to ensure stores remain stocked, although fresh and frozen products are "temporarily somewhat limited." "On Monday, 2 November, we identified an IT incident affecting the refrigeration systems in several dozen of our stores," they said. "We immediately took the necessary measures to keep our stores operational and ensure that our customers can continue to do their shopping as usual. "In the affected stores, the range of fresh and frozen products is temporarily somewhat limited. Our distribution centres are operating normally, and there has been no disruption to deliveries to our stores. "We are, of course, continuing to ensure that our products are stored and presented under optimal conditions, so that we can provide our customers with the quality and freshness they have come to expect from us." Around 15 Carrefour stores are also reportedly affected, as are sites operated by Intermarché, Spar, and Shop & Go stores located at Q8 service stations. Belgium’s De Laet & Van Haver chain of butcher shops reported temperature rises in its appliances too, but followed up with a statement on Monday saying there was no impact on its produce, and all stores remain open. Simultaneously, similar issues have affected Swedish grocery chain ICA, which confirmed attacks on a "small number of stores." "We can confirm that we have been informed of an incident overnight affecting a small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA’s central network," a company spokesperson said. "The incident impacted the stores’ refrigeration and freezer systems. ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation." ICA did not respond to questions about the scale of food wastage nor when normal operations are expected to continue. One store, ICA Nära in Böda on Öland, said via social media that it is open today but has no fresh or frozen produce to sell. "Unfortunately, we are one of the stores whose refrigerators and freezers have been hacked," it said. "We are open as usual, but unfortunately we have no refrigerators and freezers to sell. "We have no status on when the refrigerators and freezers are expected to be up and running again." The store manager, Mats Olsson, told SVT that he arrived to work on Monday morning and was greeted by a puddle of water and freezers set to 55 degrees C – a tale echoed by other managers across the country. Coop stores are affected by similar attacks too, with six locations in central Sweden experiencing fridge-freezer issues, according to a company spokesperson. Likewise, at least 13 SuperValue stores in Ireland are also affected, with fresh and frozen food being thrown out, according to parent company Musgrave speaking to RTE. The news comes less than a month after various grocery chains in France resorted to discarding bucketfuls of produce after their appliances were remotely defrosted by cybercrooks. Carrefour, Coopérative U, Intermarché, Monoprix, and others were hit with cyberattacks in mid-October, and hundreds of stores across the chains were reportedly impacted. At least some of the affected stores were running outdated firmware on their Danfoss refrigeration controllers, and shortly after the attacks were confirmed, CERT-FR published an alert pertaining to numerous Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controller compromises. Other retailers, such as Coopérative U, confirmed they were not Danfoss customers. It remains unclear if the latest attacks across Europe used the same methods as those used for the disruption in France last month. None of the companies that spoke to The Register on Monday responded to questions about who was behind the intrusions. ®

Title: My Journey to the Center of America’s Political Spam Text Hell
Context: On April 2, 2025, the day after Cory Booker finished his 25-hour Senate floor speech, I received the same first-person appeal from “Cory” three times in less than two hours,...
Full Text:
They’re meant for a family member who I’ll call John, for privacy reasons. John lives in California and has made small donations to Democrats. I live in New York and have made no political donations at all. We have different names, phone numbers, and bank accounts—a distinction that has apparently proven difficult for a substantial portion of the American political fundraising industry.

For years, I diligently opted out. I’ve replied “STOP” 49 times since 2021, by my phone’s count. Sometimes “Stop2End,” when that was the magic word. In November 2025, I told Jon Ossoff’s campaign some version of “stop.” It did not stop. Since then, I’ve received 13 more texts boosting his campaign, from nine different numbers.

When the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee texted to inform me that Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, and Joe Biden were calling me personally to action, I replied “eat shit.” That didn’t work either.

Exhausted, I decided this month to figure out what the hell was going on. Why did so many campaigns have my number? Why did they think it belonged to someone else? And why wouldn’t they fucking stop?

For starters, I downloaded my Messages history and pulled out the political texts I’ve received in recent years. Since March 2022, I’ve gotten 1,735, from 812 different phone numbers. By any measure, this is simply too many texts—nearly none of which were meant for me.

James Carville had written 27 times, soliciting money for at least a dozen political organizations. Ken Burns wanted help electing Jacky Rosen, then Roy Cooper, then Sherrod Brown. On April 2, 2025, the day after Cory Booker finished his 25-hour Senate floor speech, I received the same first-person appeal from “Cory” three times in less than two hours, sent by three different fundraising operations.

The thing is that John—the person these campaigns had me confused with—isn’t a particularly big donor. Federal Election Commission records show roughly 160 contributions since 2017, totaling about $1,700. The median gift was $6. This year, John donated six times, for a total of $51.

In the same period, my phone received 725 fundraising texts literally begging for his money.

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee alone sent 60 of them—22 in the first 20 days of October—from 28 different numbers. My relative had given it $5, once, in 2020. The DCCC sent another 41 messages; it had received $8. House Majority PAC, which has never received a dime from John that I could find, kept offering to multiply contributions by as much as 900 percent.

I understand the logic of these messages on some level. They are cheap, and the strategy isn’t all that different from how a lot of scams work—spray out messages and pray someone will bite. You don’t need many people to respond for it to pay off. What I couldn’t understand, though, was how I’d gotten wrapped up in all of this. I didn’t have to look far for the answer.

Almost every text contained a link that, after a few redirects, led to ActBlue, the platform Democrats use to process donations. Helpfully, many of those links carried tracking codes—strings of letters and numbers identifying the fundraising appeal, the message being sent, and sometimes where the campaign got the recipient’s contact information.

An October DCCC link, for instance, contained acq_sms.p2p_fr_2026.10.13_b1_dccc_rent_4mtch_st. Squint a little and you can make out abbreviations for acquisition (“acq”), peer-to-peer fundraising (“p2p_fr”), and a rented list (“dccc_rent”). But one word kept appearing in these strings across messages from otherwise unrelated campaigns: Sterling.

Sterling Data Company is a relatively small firm that uses AI to help Democrats find people likely to give them money. In 2022, Forbes reported that Sterling had assembled a database of roughly 30 million political donors, with hundreds of details about some of them, including what cars they drove and what they watched on Netflix. Sterling says it uses that information to predict who might donate to a particular candidate.

Sterling appears to get much of its information from other data brokers, combining details about people’s age, location, politics, and donation histories into voter profiles that campaigns can buy or rent.

Of the 725 texts I’d received this year, nearly half contained tracking codes that appeared to reference Sterling. They came from dozens of PACs and campaigns, including the DCCC, DSCC, James Talarico, and Mark Kelly.

FEC records show that a Biden joint fundraising committee paid Sterling about $1.87 million for donor lists over four months beginning in November 2023. Around the same time, a text from the committee reached my phone with a code containing strl2b.

The DSCC’s first reported payment to Sterling came on November 22, 2023—the very day I received one of its texts tagged STL2. According to FEC data, the committee has continued paying Sterling, including roughly $250,000 this summer, which preceded another wave of Sterling-tagged texts.

Those recent texts all appeared to link back to a common platform. Dozens of campaigns had their own web addresses, but I could see that they used nearly identical software and tracking codes, often ending in tier1. Sterling’s own website advertises something it calls “Tier 1 contact data intelligence,” though I couldn’t establish whether the two were connected or who ran the system. Still, the breadcrumbs were leading me to suspect that, at some point, a Sterling database mixup had lumped John together with my phone number.

“High-frequency solicitation is a necessary evil,” Martin Kurucz, Sterling’s CEO, tells me when I ask about all of this. “Few people give, so every campaign chases the same donors, and texting at scale works too well to skip.”

Kurucz declined to discuss Sterling’s proprietary data but confirmed that the company handles the texting itself and can rent the same record to multiple campaigns. Sterling limits how often individuals can be contacted, he said, though he didn’t specify what those limits are.

“No contact database is perfect,” Kurucz says. Even matches made with moderate confidence are generally accurate enough to be worth using, he says. Wrong numbers tend to drop out of circulation because the recipients don’t engage.

Kurucz wouldn’t confirm that Sterling has caused the deluge of misdirected text messages my way, but he also didn’t deny it. Instead he offered some advice for making them stop: Don’t respond at all.

I found that there’s another way out: lawsuits. At least two people have successfully gotten a settlement out of Democratic organizations over apparently misdirected campaign texts, which presumably included never being contacted again.

That seems like a lot of work, though. Meanwhile neither of those lawsuits established how the wrong names got attached to their numbers. I still don’t know for sure how mine got mixed up with John’s. But the outcome is the same: The DSCC now texts me more often than my mother. Replying “eat shit” another hundred times won’t change that.

Title: FBI Attributes Binance Heist to North Korea’s TraderTraitor
Context: “At current prices, the attacker now controls around $3
Full Text:
North Korea was behind the theft of more than $6bn from cryptocurrency exchange Binance last week, according to the FBI.

A brief statement from the Bureau published on October 31 attributed the breach to the TraderTraitor group (aka Jade Sleet, UNC4899, Slow Pisces).

“The FBI, together with partners at the US Secret Service and the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), has observed TraderTraitor actors converting stolen assets primarily into Ethereum (ETH),” it read.

“It is expected these assets will then be further laundered by converting them using decentralized finance products (DeFi) and instant swap services as they prepare them for further laundering stages.”

Read more on TraderTraitor: US and Japan Blame North Korea for $308m Crypto Heist.

The FBI and its partners urged crypto entities including THORNode operators, RPC node operators, instant exchanges, DeFi services, blockchain analytics firms and other virtual asset service providers to “block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets.”

According to Blockchain analytics company Elliptic, around $2.9bn of the stolen funds have been frozen or seized, but that still leaves almost $3.3bn outside the reach of issuers.

“At current prices, the attacker now controls around $3.25bn of assets that cannot be frozen by an issuer, spread across more than 800 addresses. This includes around 584,000 ETH ($1.32bn), 18,327 BTC ($1.42bn) and 233 million XRP,” Elliptic explained.

“The ETH includes TRX laundered through bridges, which arrives on Ethereum and is split across hundreds of fresh wallets. Almost all of the stolen TRX has now been laundered. The XRP, SOL and NEAR, worth around $439m, have not moved at all since they were stolen.”

Binance Investigation Continues

Binance has said it will cover the costs of the incident, so customer funds are not in danger. However, it continues to investigate the actual cause of the breach.

Originally, the firm claimed that a compromised DevOps laptop may have been the source of the incident, but later added that it “uncovered additional points of breach” in what it is describing as a “complex attack.”

The attack was carried out by more than one individual, and used a “self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as it ran,” which has made forensic analysis harder, according to Elliptic.

TraderTraitor, which also has links to the Lazarus Group, APT 38 and AppleJeus, has been pegged for a string of historic crypto heists.

These include attacks on Japanese firm DMM, which cost the firm $308m, as well as Alphapo ($60m), CoinsPaid ($37m) and Atomic Wallet ($100m). TraderTraitor was also blamed for the previous record setter for biggest ever crypto breach, when it stole $1.5bn from Bybit.

Title: Hundreds of Mundane AI Apps Are Hiding Sexually Abusive Deepfake Features
Context: At first glance, the self-proclaimed “pet portrait” app Viefur appears to be just another AI slop generator
Full Text:
At first glance, the self-proclaimed “pet portrait” app Viefur appears to be just another AI slop generator. Using digital coins sold in the app—around $4 will buy 130 coins—pet photos can be turned into an “anthropomorphic portrait,” with the critter dressed in “human clothing” and inserted into bizarre scenes. Think a hamster wearing beach shorts, sunglasses, and lounging in a swimming pool or a Hawaiian shirt-wearing cat, drinking from a coconut.

All of this is cover for what appears to be the app’s true purpose: creating sexually abusive deepfake images.

A WIRED investigation found the app is part of a network of more than 400 connected domains and apps that, like Viefur, often claim to be everyday services—such as language tuition or AI workout coaches. When accessed under certain conditions, however, apps in the network stealthily load a web interface allowing the generation of explicit AI sexual images and videos using photos users upload. The apps include AI scenes such as “bedroom rape” and “threatening knife,” where a man holds a knife to a woman’s neck.

The network was discovered hiding in plain sight, by multiple researchers, after they investigated links from thousands of video ads containing explicit deepfake content that were published on Meta’s Facebook and Instagram. As WIRED has reported in recent months, hundreds of these ads contained AI generated child sexual abuse material, including images of real children and a member of a European royal family. The ads reached tens of thousands of people and have prompted investigations from regulators around the world.

In each case, the ads linked out to the deceptive apps in Apple and Google’s app stores—allowing people to generate explicit images and make payments using Apple and Google Pay. The network behind the nudify apps appears to have been publishing them for around a year, at times publishing dozens per week. This is despite Google, Apple, and Meta saying they enforce their policies that do not allow harmful deepfake content on their platforms.

The apps and domains investigated by WIRED appear to be run by Chinese developers and a Hong Kong registered entity called KeLing Technology Limited, according to a review of web domains and how the services operate. Email addresses linked to the entity, apps, and related services, did not respond to multiple requests for comment from WIRED, but after being contacted, they appeared to erase public connections between KeLing Technology Limited and the deepfake tools.

“This is an organized, commercially run operation: One operator behind hundreds of disposable apps and domains, cloaked to pass App Store review and pushed through tens of thousands of Meta ads under fake payer names,” says Paul Bouchaud, a lead researcher at the nonprofit AI Forensics, who investigated the network. “They don’t expect enforcement to catch up, and so far it hasn’t.”

Hidden Behavior

Download one of the apps in the deepfake network and you may see exactly what was advertised—such as an app to create AI pet pictures. But behind the scenes, researchers found, the apps are quietly making determinations about whether to show the benign content or load a web interface showing explicit deepfakes.

“Each time the application is downloaded, there is a call to the server with some information, such as where the user is coming from, the language, some unique identifier, and then the server replies whether or not to show the explicit or the non-explicit version of it,” explains Bouchaud, who reverse engineered the apps’ and associated websites’ code. They say there’s no clear list of reasons why one user may be shown the explicit version of an app, but one trigger appears to be downloading it after clicking an associated ad on Meta’s platforms.

A leading blockchain analytics company has revealed details of a security breach involving an AI agent.

Chainalysis said in a post on October 30 that an external actor used “offensive agentic techniques” to gain unauthorized access to undisclosed internal systems and tools.

“Some non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed, including such information relating to your organization and users,” it continued.

“We are in the process of determining the records for your organization that were accessed and will provide a detailed breakdown as soon as that analysis is complete.”

Read more on agentic attacks: AI Agent Carries Out Multi-Stage Data Theft Attack.

Chainalysis clarified that the incident is unrelated to the Binance heist last week. It also claimed to have no evidence that the threat actor was able to access investigation content like graphs, notes or cases, or transaction query results.

These sensitive pieces of data could allow an unauthorized third party to snoop on blockchain investigations carried out by Chainalysis customers. The firm has been busy this week helping the community to understand who carried out the Binance raid, for example.

The firm also said that it had no evidence that clear-text passwords, multifactor authentication (MFA) secrets or user session tokens had been accessed, meaning customer accounts should be safe.

A Warning for Customers

However, Chainalysis did warn customers about possible follow-on attacks.

“Chainalysis users should continue to be hyper-vigilant of unexpected password reset requests or authentication prompts,” it said.

“If your organization has not yet enabled two-factor authentication, we strongly recommend doing so. Your Chainalysis account manager can help you complete that process.”

The firm said it has been working “around the clock” to investigate the unauthorized activity, patch any affected vulnerabilities and harden its systems.

“We have engaged world-class third-party cybersecurity experts and are using sophisticated large language models to support a broader review of our platform’s security and strengthen our defenses,” it added.

“This work extends beyond the exploited vulnerabilities to enhance our security posture across the platform.”

Title: Inside a successful AWS European Sovereign Cloud exercise to demonstrate independent operation
Context: The AWS European Sovereign Cloud is a new, independent cloud partition for Europe that became generally available in January 2026, with its first AWS Region in Brandenburg, Germany
Full Text:
On Saturday, October 24, 2026 we conducted a successful exercise demonstrating that the AWS European Sovereign Cloud can operate without depending on any infrastructure outside the European Union (EU). This was the first public technical exercise demonstrating the independence of a sovereign cloud Region.

The AWS European Sovereign Cloud is a new, independent cloud partition for Europe that became generally available in January 2026, with its first AWS Region in Brandenburg, Germany. It is physically and logically separate from other AWS Regions, with no critical dependencies on non-EU infrastructure, and all customer content and customer-created metadata remains in the EU.

The AWS European Sovereign Cloud is managed through dedicated European legal entities established under German law and operated entirely within Europe. My fellow Managing Director, Stefan Hoechbauer, and I called for the exercise. We are EU citizens residing in the EU, responsible for its management and operations, including its infrastructure, technology, and services. Only EU residents located in the EU control its operations and support, and AWS is gradually transitioning the AWS European Sovereign Cloud to be operated exclusively by EU citizens located in the EU.

What we did

In standard operations, the AWS European Sovereign Cloud uses two global systems: the AWS Global Network backbone, and a dedicated system operated by the local EU team to manage limited, controlled transfers of operational AWS data. As we explained ahead of the exercise, neither is critical to running the AWS European Sovereign Cloud. During the exercise, the team switched off both systems, and traffic that normally travels across the AWS Global Network backbone rerouted securely over the public internet.

The AWS European Sovereign Cloud can operate independently at any time, and for several hours on October 24 the team showed exactly that, running it on only its own software and hardware resources, operated by EU-resident staff within the EU.

Workloads continued running, and customers could still access their data. The exercise did not affect service availability within the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, other AWS Regions, or private connectivity through AWS Direct Connect. When the exercise finished, traffic returned to its normal path.

Why we ran it

Transparency is at the core of our digital sovereignty commitment, so we ran the AWS European Sovereign Cloud exercise openly and reported back on the outcome. The exercise produced verifiable technical and operational evidence that the AWS European Sovereign Cloud can continue to operate independently within the EU. It turns a design claim into a verified result. Organizations in regulated industries and the public sector can take this result to regulators and their boards as evidence for their compliance and assurance documents.

What customers and partners are saying

“Digital sovereignty is ultimately about trust and safeguarding business continuity. The successful demonstration of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud’s operational independence is an important proof point for European organizations with the most stringent sovereignty requirements. Combined with Capgemini’s European heritage, presence and AWS capabilities, we can deliver a sovereign proposition in Europe, for Europe, by Europeans, enabling clients to accelerate secure and resilient cloud and AI transformation at scale whilst assuring business continuity.” – Fernando Alvarez, Chief Strategy and Development Officer and Group Executive Board Member, Capgemini

“Autonomy, resilience and operational control are foundations driving digital sovereignty concerns across the public sector and regulated industries. Achieving sovereignty requires more than a sound and consistent architecture; it demands operational evidence to build trust. The AWS European Sovereign Cloud team has provided evidence, supporting organizations on the transformation of their critical data and digital assets toward greater sovereign control. Having engaged with this team since the inception of the project, and as a Launch Partner of the AWS Digital Sovereignty Competency, Atos helps customers define their sovereignty roadmaps, adopt the appropriate graduated solutions, and confidently operate and govern their target sovereignty posture.” – Michael Kollar, Digital Sovereignty Leader and Head of Cloud & Modern Infrastructure and Digital Workplace, Atos Group

“For organizations in regulated industries, meeting strict data and operational requirements cannot come at the cost of a great customer experience. Running on the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, Genesys can help European organizations deliver exactly that, with their data and operations kept in the EU. Seeing the AWS European Sovereign Cloud operate independently under real conditions helps give our shared customers added confidence to move their most sensitive workloads to the cloud.” – Daniel Karadza, Senior Director, Partners and Alliances, EMEA Central and Benelux, Genesys

“Operational independence is a defining pillar of digital sovereignty, and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud has shown what that means in practice. It runs without reliance on any infrastructure outside the EU and is operated entirely by EU residents, which makes it a strong fit for Europe’s regulated industries and public sector. As an early collaborator with the AWS European Sovereign Cloud team before its launch, Accenture is uniquely positioned to help clients navigate sovereignty requirements and scale with greater confidence and control.” – Emanuele Baldassarre, Managing Director, Accenture

Learn more

To learn more about the design and digital sovereignty controls of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, visit aws.eu. If you have questions about this exercise or want to discuss your workloads, reach out to AWS Support or contact your AWS Account team.

Title: Spooky New Infostealer Malware Uses AI to ‘Autodox’ Victims
Context: Then the malware does a second, deeper sweep using its first-round findings
Full Text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

New research shared exclusively with Kernel Panic shows that hackers have started adding AI functionality into a new strain of infostealer malware, making it possible for the system to automatically profile victims and quickly surface the highest value targets and their information. Dubbed “Volta-Autodoxer” because of how the malware refers to itself internally, the finding by Cisco Talos researchers sheds light on the ways that commercial LLMs are being used to augment and enhance the capabilities of established types of malware.

Often hidden in counterfeit software, infostealers are designed to live up to their name, grabbing usernames, passwords, authentication tokens, cookies, credit card data, and more from infected machines. Many of the biggest data breaches in recent years—from the widespread Snowflake-linked breaches that included AT&T and Ticketmaster to the theft of a terabyte of Disney data—have resulted from hackers accessing targets using login details gathered by infostealers. Overall, the malware has been used to steal hundreds of millions of credentials in recent years.

“Volta is pretty mature as a stealer. It casts a pretty wide net for what it collects,” says Ryan Fetterman, a security researcher at Cisco Talos. “It compiles all of those things together, ultimately producing a serialized dossier that it can send to a couple LLM models. It’s asking the model to act like an intelligence analyst and produce structured citation-backed assessment of the victim. It’s like a prioritization and analysis function.”

Talos flagged the malware using its new CAIRN framework, built to identify hacking tools that incorporate AI capabilities. Fetterman notes that Talos did not track whether Volta has been used in the wild.

Volta’s traditional infostealer capabilities are powerful and seem to be geared toward targeting younger internet users with robust digital lives. It sweeps for passwords stored in browsers, Microsoft OAuth tokens, cookies, payment cards, and crypto wallet seed phrases, but also active Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions. Then the malware does a second, deeper sweep using its first-round findings. By looking through the target’s Gmail or another central account, Volta builds a fuller picture of the victim, their location, and their habits using data like receipts and order history from services including UberEats and DoorDash.

Once all of this is done, the malware feeds its findings into AI tools for analysis using OpenRouter, a service that can send prompts to multiple different AI providers. Volta defaults its requests to Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6. But apparently preparing for the possibility that the model’s guardrails could block the activity, Volta is built with fallbacks to the Chinese open weight Moonshot AI Kimi K2 and, if that fails, Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash. Building in fallbacks and relying on cost-effective, older-generation models are common techniques among attackers.

Today we are joined by ⁠⁠Subhajeet Singha⁠⁠, Senior Security Researcher at ⁠⁠Acronis⁠⁠ Threat Research Unit, discussing their work on "Red Heron exploits Gitea n-day flaw in multinational campaign, exposing new Linux rootkit." The campaign involved deploying persistent backdoors and a newly identified Linux implant called JITTERLY, which contains an undocumented rootkit, SIXZUT, capable of hiding files, processes, and network connections while protecting the malware from removal. Acronis assesses with moderate confidence that Red Heron operates within a PRC-linked context, highlighting how quickly attackers can weaponize newly disclosed vulnerabilities and turn exposed development platforms into gateways for broader network compromise.

Title: Crypto's biggest withdrawal.
Context: Attackers exploit a critical GitLab flaw. GitLab patched the flaw earlier this month and has released additional threat detections after observing exploitation attempts.
Full Text:
Binance suffers a record-breaking cryptocurrency heist. Attackers exploit a critical GitLab flaw. Russian disinformation targets U.S. elections. Treasury sanctions North Korean IT worker operations. A cyberattack halts Polymarket trading. GCHQ loses track of thousands of storage devices. An abandoned Mac app leaves security risks behind. Japan Airlines reports a third-party breach. An AI-powered command-and-control framework emerges in the wild. Our guest is Josh Devon, Co-founder & CEO of Sondera, winner of the 9th annual DataTribe Challenge. We bid farewell to the captain who inspired a generation of innovators.

Today is Friday October 30th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Binance suffers the largest cryptocurrency hack on record.

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has suffered a staggering $6.3 billion theft, reportedly the largest cryptocurrency hack on record. Researchers at TRM Labs and Chainalysis attribute the October 29 attack to North Korea’s TraderTraitor operation. Attackers moved funds across ten blockchains, with most of the theft occurring in just 20 minutes. Binance says its preliminary investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which may have provided access to systems authorized to move funds. The company found no evidence that private wallet keys were stolen. Instead, attackers apparently manipulated transaction-signing infrastructure, including an Ethereum feature that allowed them to automate withdrawals. Cryptocurrency issuers and networks have frozen billions in stolen assets, but estimates suggest attackers still control between $2.4 billion and $3.3 billion. Binance has promised to reimburse affected customers, while significant questions remain about the security controls protecting its wallets.

A maximum-severity GitLab vulnerability is under active exploitation.

Attackers are actively exploiting a maximum-severity GitLab vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated remote code execution. CISA has added the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-97229, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and ordered federal agencies to secure affected systems by Sunday. The vulnerability involves an integer overflow in GitLab’s regular expression compiler, allowing attackers to execute malicious code through specially crafted CI/CD configurations. GitLab patched the flaw earlier this month and has released additional threat detections after observing exploitation attempts. The Shadowserver Foundation reports nearly 2,800 internet-exposed GitLab Community Edition instances, though it’s unclear how many remain vulnerable. The latest discovery follows several serious GitLab security issues this year, including another recently exploited vulnerability that could expose sensitive credentials and other secrets.

A Russian disinformation group targets U.S. elections.

Researchers say a covert Russian influence operation is targeting Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico in Texas with fabricated allegations of misconduct. Analysts at Alethea and Clemson University attribute the campaign to Storm-1516, a Russian disinformation group that spread similar false accusations during the 2024 presidential election. The latest attack involved videos that researchers at Graphika believe were AI-generated. Initially attracting little attention, the videos gained traction after several influential accounts on X amplified them. One received more than 850,000 views in its first 24 hours. U.S. intelligence assessments indicate Russia has recently intensified its election interference efforts, particularly in competitive Senate races. While much of the activity targets Democrats, intelligence officials haven’t concluded that Moscow is explicitly favoring either party.

Treasury officials sanction Russian and North Koreans over fraudulent IT worker operations.

The U.S. Treasury Department has sanctioned Russian and North Korean nationals and companies accused of supporting Pyongyang’s fraudulent IT worker operations. Two Russians allegedly laundered millions in cryptocurrency earned by North Korean operatives working remotely for American companies. Treasury also targeted North Korean managers overseeing IT workers in Russia, along with a company accused of using artificial intelligence to help operatives secure U.S. jobs. The broader scheme involves North Koreans using stolen identities to obtain lucrative technology positions, then funneling earnings back to Pyongyang. Some workers have also stolen sensitive information and extorted employers. U.S. officials say the proceeds help fund North Korea’s weapons programs. The sanctions follow a Justice Department operation targeting laptop farms used to disguise workers’ overseas locations.

Polymarket suspends trading following a cyberattack.

Prediction market Polymarket temporarily suspended trading Thursday after a cyberattack involving a third-party service provider disrupted its international platform. The company says trading has resumed and promises to reimburse affected users, but hasn’t disclosed the extent of the losses or identified the attacker. Blockchain security researchers traced more than $2.1 million in suspected cryptocurrency theft to a single account. Security firm Hudson Rock identified the compromised provider as website performance company DebugBear, which separately acknowledged a security incident and urged customers to remove its embedded code. Researchers discovered malicious code apparently designed to identify cryptocurrency wallets and transfer their assets to an attacker-controlled account. Polymarket removed DebugBear’s code from its website. There’s currently no evidence that other DebugBear customers were compromised.

GCHQ laments missing storage devices.

Britain’s intelligence agency GCHQ cannot account for thousands of storage devices potentially containing sensitive information. The Investigatory Powers Commissioner says USB drives, hard disks, and memory cards remain unaccounted for years after the problem was first identified. Some devices may contain intercepted communications and other highly sensitive intelligence data. The watchdog expressed frustration over GCHQ’s slow investigation. The agency acknowledged shortcomings in its tracking system but says it has implemented corrective measures. Officials are still determining how many devices are actually lost.

An abandoned Mac app causes security headaches.

An abandoned version of the once-popular Popcorn Time streaming app left hundreds of thousands of Macs potentially vulnerable to attack. Researchers at Eye Research discovered that Time4Popcorn installed a persistent update checker that could download and execute code with elevated privileges, even years after users stopped opening the app. With the developers long gone, attackers could potentially hijack expired update domains to distribute malware. Researchers found no evidence of exploitation, but estimate 250,000 to 350,000 Macs were affected. They took control of an abandoned domain and used the update mechanism itself to disable the vulnerable checker on more than a million Macs and Windows PCs. Other vulnerabilities remain, however, and some update domains are still uncontrolled. Researchers recommend uninstalling Time4Popcorn entirely.

Japan Airlines suffers a third-party data breach.

Japan Airlines says a breach at its technology provider, Amadeus IT Group, exposed personal information belonging to 92,000 customers. Compromised data includes names, reservation codes, and flight details. For approximately 2,000 passengers, attackers also obtained passport numbers, contact information, and frequent flyer numbers. The airline says payment card information and flight operations were unaffected.

The disclosure comes amid a wave of cyber incidents in Japan, including breaches affecting millions of customers at a Sony-owned internet provider, Burger King Japan, and gaming company Capcom. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has called for emergency cybersecurity measures, warning of growing risks from stolen personal information. Japanese and American defense officials have also discussed strengthening cooperation against cyber threats as the country grapples with the recent attacks.

An AI-integrated command-and-control framework is found operating in the wild.

Cisco Talos researchers have discovered an AI-integrated command-and-control framework called NIK C2 operating in the wild. The Windows-based malware combines credential theft, keylogging, surveillance, and remote access with direct access to OpenAI’s API. Attackers can use AI to analyze stolen information during an active intrusion, potentially accelerating their operations. The malware can even use a victim’s own OpenAI API key, potentially charging them for the attacker’s AI requests. NIK C2 also includes screen-locking ransomware that demands cryptocurrency payments without encrypting files. Its capabilities extend to lateral movement, security evasion, and persistent access. Talos observed active infrastructure and multiple versions of the malware, suggesting ongoing development. Researchers warn that integrating AI directly into malware could significantly reduce defenders’ opportunities to detect and interrupt attacks.

We bid farewell to the captain who inspired a generation of innovators.

We say goodbye today to Sir Patrick Stewart, who has died at the age of 86.

His was a remarkable life. From a difficult childhood in a working-class Yorkshire home, he found his way to the Royal Shakespeare Company, where he spent decades mastering his craft. And then, approaching 50, he took a chance on a science fiction television series that he wasn’t entirely convinced would succeed.

And in doing so, he became Captain Jean-Luc Picard.

For those of us who grew up with Star Trek, it’s difficult to overstate what Patrick Stewart brought to that role. Picard was thoughtful, principled, intellectually curious, and deeply committed to the idea that humanity could become something better. He valued diplomacy over violence, reason over impulse, and the dignity of every individual. He was a leader who listened, who questioned his own assumptions, and who understood that having the authority to give an order didn’t necessarily mean it was the right order to give.

And there’s something else worth remembering. Star Trek inspired generations of scientists, engineers, programmers, and technology professionals. People who watched those shows as kids and went on to build the technologies that shape our world today. The communicators, the tablets, the voice-controlled computers, the extraordinary networks connecting people across unimaginable distances. For countless young viewers, Star Trek wasn’t just entertainment. It was an invitation to imagine what technology might make possible, and then go out and make some of it real.

Patrick Stewart helped make that future feel worth pursuing.

He also reminded us that intelligence and kindness weren’t mutually exclusive, that leadership could be compassionate, and that even in a universe filled with extraordinary technology, the most important questions were still fundamentally human ones.

Now, you might reasonably ask, “What does this have to do with cyber security?”

Well, as it happens, Captain Picard was something of an early adopter of multifactor authentication. Whenever the Enterprise’s auto-destruct sequence needed to be activated or canceled, the ship required authorization codes and confirmation from multiple senior officers.

Even in the 24th century, apparently, you couldn’t just blow up the Enterprise with a single password.

Sir Patrick Stewart gave us many wonderful performances over a long and extraordinary career. But for generations of us who looked to the stars and imagined a better future, he’ll always be our captain.

Thank you, Sir Patrick.

And that’s the CyberWire.

Title: “Are We Exposed?” What CISOs Need to Know About Their Software Risk
Context: Curl When it comes to Curl and its underlying transfer library libcurl, the threat can affect the very foundation of internet data transfer
Full Text:
Recent events have once again highlighted the need to quickly answer the question, “Are we exposed?”

We now face threats to businesses and governments from vulnerabilities and compromises in three fundamental components used in software development: Curl, PHP, and LiteLLM.

Curl

When it comes to Curl and its underlying transfer library libcurl, the threat can affect the very foundation of internet data transfer. With libcurl embedded in many enterprise environments – from backend microservices and container runtimes to automated CI/CD pipelines and shell scripts – this vulnerability carries potential systemic risk. The core threat centers on high-severity flaws disclosed in October 2026, notably a high-severity HTTP/2 use-after-free issue (such as CVE-2026-92392) where a malicious upstream server handling an upload can corrupt client-side memory and, under specific conditions, trigger remote code execution or application crashes on the machine initiating the transfer. Because libcurl negotiates HTTP/2 by default for HTTPS URLs when the server supports it and applications rarely inspect what libcurl does under the hood, development stacks and automated deployment pipelines that have not upgraded to a fixed version can remain exposed to hostile external endpoints.

LiteLLM

Regarding LiteLLM, JFrog Security Research detected the problem within 2 hours, and the errant LiteLLM package, version 1.107.0, has already been removed from PyPI. Reflecting the open-source community ecosystem’s continually improving maturation, the package maintainers have already published a report. But from 11:39 to 13:23 UTC on October 21, 2026, software developers, agentic agents, or your build systems could have downloaded that package from PyPI, and affected Docker images remained available until 14:20 UTC. The ripple effect of a compromised package or vulnerable component getting into an environment doesn’t just impact the developers or security team. It also impacts IT Ops and, down the line, auditors. Every change impacts the whole organization. Executives, the business decision makers who determine where to invest and allocate resources, need a way to understand where they sit in this maturity. Do they have complete visibility or not?

PHP

In the case of PHP, two CRITICAL-severity PHP core vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619), were disclosed and referred to publicly as PHP2Shell. The bugs can allow unauthenticated remote code execution and Heartbleed-style memory disclosure in PHP itself, independent of the application running on top of it, according to public advisories. Within days, news outlets reported on the vulnerabilities, and CISA issued an alert urging organizations to patch immediately, including CNBC and the BBC, CISA.

“Are We Exposed?”

When a CISO wrestles with the question of “Are we exposed?”, their triage process should focus on these key issues:

Is it really a threat?

Where is it being used?

What is the business impact?

Do I have a reporting or disclosure obligation under rules or standards that apply to my organization, such as those of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), PCI DSS, or, for product manufacturers, the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA)?

Did we block it?

How do we fix it?

The CISO’s ability to answer these questions with confidence depends on how well they’ve integrated their tools, people, processes, and security program to provide that visibility and respond quickly to security incidents. The ability to do this, in turn, is a reflection of the maturity of their overall security program and how well they can protect, monitor, and govern the full gamut of software development operations – whether it’s on the developer’s workstation, in agentic workflows, or implemented directly by AI coding agents.

A true assessment of your organization’s abilities to determine your strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats is critical to providing a full 360 view of your risk posture.

Hands-On Assessment Experience

As a CISO, I’ve done these assessments on a number of occasions, for both new deployments and as an ongoing protective measure to help keep the business protected as new threats and vulnerabilities evolve.

These assessments should be broadly based and take into account business objectives, employee capabilities, workflows, data usage, and the maturity of the infrastructure. Covering these bases should give you an accurate compass of where you are and where you need to improve.

This should, of course, include your tools, but should not lead to one of the classic mistakes organizations make, which is over-focusing on tools, simply because they’re the easiest thing to measure. The other areas mentioned above are easy to overlook, but extremely important to a realistic assessment, as tools without the right people and processes won’t achieve the objective of protecting your business.

JFrog’s Security Maturity Assessment

Based on JFrog’s experience working with many of the Fortune 100 customers and through the expertise of our in-house security research team, we’ve actually built our own Security Maturity Assessment. It lets organizations self-assess their software supply chain security program maturity across 11 domains, based on their answers.

I strongly recommend taking a few minutes out of your busy day to complete the questionnaire, as it assesses the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and risks in your software development operations and could help you identify where to start when it comes to ensuring you can truly answer the question: “Are we exposed?”

Takeaways

The question of “Are we exposed?” can be complicated and difficult to assess, but recent high-profile security incidents don’t give CISOs the luxury of taking days to come up with a reply. Corporate executives and board members need fast, accurate answers.

Having complete visibility into your people, processes, workflows, tools, and dependencies gives you the leverage to protect your business under the pressure of the latest attacks. Take the first step in securing your applications by evaluating your operational maturity with JFrog’s Security Maturity Assessment or speaking with one of our domain experts today.

Title: Devs Hit by Trojanized Claude Code Extension for Cursor
Context: The SolarWinds-style attack in miniature lasted only 11 hours, from 9:27 a
Full Text:
Anthropic's official Claude Code extension for the Cursor VS Code Marketplace was hijacked and swapped out for a malicious version with a persistent backdoor.

The SolarWinds-style attack in miniature lasted only 11 hours, from 9:27 a.m. GMT to 8:35 p.m. GMT, on Oct. 29, according to Cursor's disclosure. Any software developers who downloaded or updated Claude Code in their Cursor integrated development environment (IDE) during that time would have received a malicious version 2.1.313, which pilfered sensitive data from infected machines and, in a minority of cases, could have allowed attackers persistent, privileged access to users' systems.

Cursor stated that "at most 5,000 users were affected," and that they will be contacted about the incident directly.

Separately that same day, researchers described an unrelated exploit in Cursor, allowing attackers to deploy arbitrary code to developers' machines via Cursor's built-in browser.

Related:Anthropic-Themed Phishing Emails Bypass Top Security Tools

Cursor did not immediately respond to an inquiry from Dark Reading regarding both of these stories.

Cursor's Claude Code Conundrum

For some, the notion of a compromised "extension" might evoke browser extensions, which are so frequently vulnerable, suspicious, and outright malicious that cybersecurity news concerning them tends not to evoke much panic, even in extreme cases.

Extensions in coding environments are a different beast. "IDE extensions are scarier than browser extensions because, unlike browser extensions, they are designed to have the same level of permissions as their host," Gal Weizman, security researcher at Forever Security, tells Dark Reading. "They can run code, access the filesystem, fire network requests and more."

On Thursday, an attacker tried to leverage the power afforded by coding environment extensions by sneaking a 66-line loader on top of the real extension's legitimate code. According to an analysis from the community threat intelligence platform OpenSourceMalware, everything about the extension remained the same besides this lone edit to its extension.js file.

As soon as the extension loaded — without need for the user to establish a Claude conversation — the new file is revved up. It attempts to add an attacker-controlled key to victims' SSH configurations, with the goal of establishing reverse tunnels that act as a backdoor into the compromised systems.

The malicious extension also attempts to make those connections persistent by registering background processes — for macOS systems, a LaunchAgent; and for Windows, scheduled tasks running with system privileges, plus a fallback Startup script. This whole business was doomed from the start, Cursor wrote, since turning on the local SSH service requires administrative privileges, which the Claude Code extension only possesses in "highly unusual circumstances."

Related:'Gheist' Weaponizes GitHub Tokens to Steal Cloud Secrets

Victims weren't totally out of the woods, though, as the malicious code also exfiltrated system information via separate Web requests. Stolen data was limited to hostnames, usernames, operating systems (OS), OS architectures, home directory paths, environment variable names, working directories, configured Git emails, and public IP addresses.

Cursor Contains Compromise

Cursor's public disclosure suggests that the security incident was its own, not Anthropic's. The malicious version "was not developed by Anthropic," the SpaceX-owned company reported.

In response to the discovery, Cursor took a variety of steps to protect itself: rotating its keys, checking for tampering in other extensions, and taking its marketplace temporarily offline and rebuilding it. It also worked with the relevant cloud hosting provider to take down the attacker's malicious infrastructure.

Cursor did not specify how the intrusion occurred in the first place. While acknowledging that it's not yet known what happened here, Weizman explains, "Historically, the most common way extensions and plug-ins get hijacked is through theft of locally stored credentials that allow publishing new versions of these packages."

Related:10 Software Security Practices Built for the Next 250 Years

"Enabling 2FA for publishing such extensions is an excellent way to significantly mitigate such risk in the future. Relying on an access token as the only gate for pushing such critical software significantly increases the risk of this happening," he says.

More Security Concerns for Cursor, AI Assistants

On the same day of the Anthropic Cursor attack, Weizman published separate research detailing weaknesses in the browsers built into top desktop AI assistants today, which could be exploited to devastating effect. His test cases included Claude Desktop, GitHub Copilot, Codex, VS Code, and Cursor. Cursor has arguably the worst issue of the bunch.

In his experiments, Weizman's team created a clean-looking website, with a visible HTML chip concealing a malicious shell command in its attributes. Then they opened up the site in a built-in Cursor browser. "When the command hit Cursor's safety sandbox and was blocked, the agent — on its own, with nothing in the page telling it to — switched the sandbox off and tried again. The control worked. The agent talked itself out of using it," Weizman wrote in the report.

The attack didn't work universally across all models. When it did work, the browser escape allowed the researchers to deploy an arbitrary app to their test victim's computer. And just like the malicious Claude Code extension, the app ran with the victim's full permissions. Cursor did not respond to Forever Security's disclosure, but the company quietly patched the issue on Oct. 1.

“IDEs are becoming more agentic. They're being given agentic capabilities, which can introduce dangerous architecture. It can be very risky when things go wrong," Weizman says.

"Here we've had two examples of that: built-in browsers, and what happened with Claude Code, both of which impacted Cursor," he concludes. "And because of the rapid pace at which this is happening, security isn't necessarily keeping up."

Title: Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down
Context: Threat actors who exploit vulnerable populations and employ highly deceptive social engineering tactics are only improving faster with the help of artificial intelligence
Full Text:
Pushes for public-private partnerships to address escalating cyber threats have been on the industry's radar for years. Collaboration has been a focal point in cybersecurity conference panels and government initiatives. Calls for more information-sharing and analysis centers have been persistent.

As director of preemptive cyberdefense at Silent Push, Michael Sweeney had a front-row seat to this kind of partnership when his company recently took part in "Operation Blackout," a coordinated international operation to take down criminal networks operating out of West Africa. Operation Blackout coordinated efforts by the United Kingdom's National Crime Agency, the U.S. Department of Justice, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and private industry partners — including Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Silent Push — to disrupt criminal networks behind pig-butchering, romance, and cryptocurrency scams. The DoJ announced that the campaign resulted in dozens of arrests, the rescue of trafficking victims, and the removal of more than 3.7 million fake social media accounts.

Related:Why CTF Competitions May Be More Important Than Ever

As the UK's main law enforcement agency, the National Crime Agency hosted Joint Disruption Week in London in early October to bring together the DOJ and the FBI with private industry partners to share real-time intelligence. In addition to U.S. authorities and private industry partners, the Nigerian Joint Case Team on Cybercrimes, the Nigeria Police Force - National Cybercrime Center, and Ghanaian Cyber Security Authority also participated.

The Joint Disruption Week marked the first coordinated effort specifically focused on West Africa, according to the DOJ, which noted that global commitments are essential to dismantling the far-reaching scam centers.

The goal of these operations is to tackle scam activity at the global scale it has reached today, explains Sweeney. The more people who participate, the "better off we are," he affirms.

"The idea is not only to stop the current scams, but also to look across all of these different events," Sweeney tells Dark Reading. " We're [industry and government] all needed together in order to get this successfully taken down."

Why You Should Report Scams

Data taken from scams reported through the FBI's Internet Complaint Center and the UK's National Cyber Security Centre formed the initial basis for Operation Blackout. From there, law enforcement compiled information, including the domains the scammers used and the infrastructure they set up to manipulate people for money.

Related:AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes

Then the collaboration really began. Meta provided some of the data that helped drill down to specific regions — a surprising move, since social media platforms don't generally cooperate with law enforcement, despite threat actors abusing platforms to lure in victims. Several other organizations sent signals to further paint a picture of the attacker's intent and infrastructure.

Silent Push's role involved providing 35,000 domains, creating more than 70 detection rules to trigger alerts when malicious activity occurs, and fingerprinting, Sweeney says. All of those are considered the "common choke points" that help researchers and authorities map the threat actors' network patterns.

All of that was analyzed, and the data augmented each other to provide the evidence authorities needed to take down the scammers, says Sweeney.

"Once you get everyone in the room with all the data, it becomes easier to see the big picture," he says. "From that, see where the attacks are coming from, the commonalities, and who is the most important person to take down in the operation, and where you want to go to get these people."

"Let's Go Faster"

Sweeney attributed the success of Operation Blackout and other operations he's worked on over the years to how clear the mission was; everyone was on the same page about the goals and importance of data sharing, he says. Many of the legal or jurisdiction blockers that would otherwise prevent them from sharing information and hinder actual action were removed, including data-sharing agreements with users.

Related:Vulnerability Management Isn't About the Score — It's About How It Applies to You

A number of providers were also involved, including Starlink. While each platform offers different services, they united in a shared stance. That camaraderie and energy that accompanied it were palpable, says Sweeney.

"We come together [to] say, 'If you're abusing our services, we're going to do everything we can to stop you, and we're going to pull in law enforcement,'" he says.

One thing Sweeney would like to change was the pace; he would like to see these partnerships move faster and conduct more operations as scammers drain billions from the U.S. economy. Threat actors who exploit vulnerable populations and employ highly deceptive social engineering tactics are only improving faster with the help of artificial intelligence.

What draws him to this work is the people who just reported a scam or who're too ashamed to come forward at all. They should know they aren't alone and that people are working hard to fight back, says Sweeney.

"Everyone really wants to stop it, so pacing may be the only frustration," he says. "Let's do more. Hit them while they're down so that more people don't have that moment where they're having to figure out how to report a scam.”

Modules: AI Security; Identity Security Posture Management; Vulnerability Management; Network Security
Title: Crim spent $7K+ on AI services in extortion attacks, then left evidence for all to see
Context: “We found no evidence of vulnerability exploitation in the cases examined
Full Text: A n0n ransomware operator tried to break into 23 organizations across 14 countries, but couldn't secure its own front door, leaving its server exposed with all of its methods on view. The criminals used a mix of new (AI) and old (stolen credentials) tooling during their data-theft spree, and in some cases not only stole and encrypted files, but also deleted data and backups, eliminating victims’ ability to recover their information. And despite the fear and hype around the breachpocalypse, with AI finding and developing exploits for critical vulnerabilities affecting most organizations across the globe, these crooks did not exploit a single bug to gain entry into any of their victims’ IT environments. “In every documented compromise in this investigation, access relied on weak or stolen credentials,” said Ensar Seker, chief information security officer of threat intelligence firm SOCRadar. “What stands out is the combination of AI-assisted development and very conventional entry points,” Seker told The Register. “We found no evidence of vulnerability exploitation in the cases examined.” The gang breaks into organizations at scale using widespread Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) scanning and automated FortiGate SSL-VPN credential stuffing. To access US-based IT managed services provider ChiBiTek, the crew used a 15-thread residential SOCKS5 proxy pool to test credentials (ip:port:user:password) against FortiGate portals (GET /remote/login). The operators also gained entry using exposed cloud credentials and reused hosting portal sessions. In one case linked to e-commerce site Fanatics, SOCRadar found that n0n used an exposed AWS access key with permissions to list, read, and delete objects in S3 buckets. The criminals then used this key to pull data from 40 S3 buckets, with up to 110 GB per bucket, and ultimately deleted data, including bank-transaction archives, and purged keys across 12 sensitive buckets. AI-assisted extortion While the threat hunters didn’t find any evidence of a fully autonomous attack system, the ransomware operator did use AI to assist with these intrusions, incurring more than $7,216 in AI usage costs by October 22. Specifically: the criminal or criminals used OpenCode, an open-source AI coding agent, configured with 154 model entries across seven providers. Models included Gemini, Mistral, Nemotron, Llama, Claude, GPT-5.x, Grok, Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek, MiniMax, Qwen, and many, many others, some with safety training removed and others marketed as “uncensored” models. “The operator used AI to write and debug hundreds of scripts. That shows how AI can help an attacker turn basic access into a broader, tailored operation,” Seker said. “The destructive behavior is equally significant,” he added. “The operator did more than steal and encrypt files: in some cases, it deleted data and backups, and in one case changed firewall policies to block traffic. That creates a recovery problem that a decryption key alone cannot solve.” SOCRadar’s threat hunters found the operator’s workspace - a publicly accessible Python HTTP file server hosted in Sweden at 185.157.161[.]148 on port 8877 - last month, and documented the exposed directory in snapshots on September 25 and 26. “Across those snapshots, we identified 1,719 files, including attack scripts, ransomware source code, extortion infrastructure, and an AI coding agent environment,” Seker said. “This gave us visibility into the operation behind the victim listings, including how the operator prepared attacks and handled stolen data.” Meet n0n It also provided a close look at n0n, a newcomer to the data-theft and extortion game that has claimed 108 victims since it emerged last month. On October 12, the group added 38 maritime, port and logistics organizations across 18 countries to its leak site in a single batch. Researchers have linked at least 21 of them to customers of South Korean maritime software provider CyberLogitec, although the software provider has not confirmed an intrusion. The crooks set an October 19 deadline for the maritime firms, with ransom demands ranging from $400,000 to $28 million, payable in Bitcoin. After the deadline, however, none of the 38 listings were marked “settled” and none of their payment addresses showed any transaction. All affected organizations’ stolen data was published. While a handful of the gang’s claimed victims have been marked “honored - data destroyed” on n0n’s leak site, indicating the victim orgs paid the ransom demand, SOCRadar hasn’t validated any transactions on-chain. In its profile details, the security shop rates the gang a 10 out of 10 for "aggressiveness" and a zero out of 10 for “lethality.” The group is believed to be based in Russia, although the server uncovered by SOCRadar, which it attributed to a single operator or small team, didn’t provide any definitive geographic or national attribution. Every case that the exposed server documented followed the same lifecycle, moving from initial access to establishing persistence and credential collection via hidden admin accounts disguised as services, covert proxies, credential and session-token theft, mailboxes and emailed multi-factor authentication codes. The crooks then collected sensitive data and sent everything to the operator’s central storage with the attack impact shifting between data-theft, encryption, destruction, and network disruption, depending on the targeted organization. After breaking into Transcom, a Netherlands-based financial services provider, the crims sent a secondary ransom alert directly to PayPal's security team, even though the compromised data was only on Transcom's network. Stupid mistakes and n0n security basics Finally, the crims send ransom notes, post a countdown clock on the leak site, establish negotiation rooms and emails for victims - and then leak the stolen files or destroy backups when the organizations don’t pay up. In some cases, and to apply increased pressure on victimized companies, n0n also broadcasts automated countdown warnings to businesses’ service providers, clients, and media outlets. Despite its aggressive tactics, the operator in this case - as with other stupid criminals The Register has gleefully documented in earlier stories - still struggles with basic security hygiene. “There is a striking gap between operational ambition and security discipline,” Seker said. “The operator invested thousands of dollars in AI services while leaving its own workspace exposed. The locker also contained hardcoded encryption keys, with evidence suggesting reuse across victims. An operation can have serious destructive capability while still making fundamental mistakes.”®

Title: GM cracks the petty cash box for multistate driver tracking settlement
Context: The settlement comes more than two years after a 2024 New York Times investigation found that GM had been selling the data collected from vehicle owners through its Smart Driver...
Full Text: General Motors is taking what looks like a light slap on the wrist from a coalition of 35 states and the District of Columbia after agreeing to settle allegations that it collected drivers' data without proper consent and sold it to data brokers that supplied insurance companies. The Washington state AG's office said on Thursday that GM had reached a $220 million settlement with 36 attorneys general over the automaker's collection and sharing of driving data, including precise location information, speed, seatbelt use, and other metrics. According to investigators, GM sold that data to brokers, which in turn supplied it to insurance companies that could use it to set customers' premiums, without drivers' informed consent. For reference, the $220 million settlement, which will be distributed among the participating jurisdictions, equates to less than 7 percent of GM's $3.3 billion in net income attributable to stockholders for its third quarter, which ended on September 30, 2026. Don't spend it all in one place, y'all. The settlement comes more than two years after a 2024 New York Times investigation found that GM had been selling the data collected from vehicle owners through its Smart Driver program. That program, part of GM subsidiary OnStar’s offering, collected the aforementioned data and handed it back to vehicle owners in reports designed to inform better driving habits. Unbeknownst to Smart Driver subscribers, their data was also being forked over to data brokers despite GM telling customers it wouldn't share that information with insurers without their express consent. The insurers ultimately obtained the data by purchasing it from brokers with which GM had struck deals. To make matters worse, the Washington AG's office said GM incentivized dealerships to enroll customers in Smart Driver, with employees in some cases accepting terms and conditions on customers' behalf without their knowledge or consent. GM also failed to notify many drivers that their information was being collected and shared. Its OnStar app incorrectly told more than 370,000 drivers they were not enrolled in Smart Driver, even as GM continued collecting and selling their data, according to investigators. “The data GM sold was personal, identifiable, and specific,” the AG’s office said. GM canned the Smart Driver program in April 2024, just over a month after the New York Times exposed its data-sharing practices, citing customer feedback. In addition to the monetary pittance it’s handing over to the states, GM also agreed with the 36 AGs to limit the driving data it collects, better protect customer PII, and establish a "comprehensive data privacy program.” The Washington AG’s office described its settlement as “significantly stronger than any other resolution reached with GM for this conduct.” Speaking of those other terms, GM finalized its settlement of the same allegations with the Federal Trade Commission in January 2026. The FTC order required GM to obtain drivers' express consent before collecting, using, or sharing covered driving data, subject to certain exceptions. It also required the company to offer a simple way for drivers to request a copy of their data, request its deletion, and disable precise geolocation data collection where their vehicles support it. The state of California separately reached a $12.75 million settlement with GM in the matter in May; a separate case in Texas is ongoing. “This agreement … reinforces steps we’ve taken to strengthen our privacy practices,” a GM spokesperson told The Register, though the company noted that it still stands by driver data collection as a best practice. “Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share,” the spokesperson added. ®
