General Recommendations

As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends protecting network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends configuring the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity

Additional Resources

For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories

Terms of Use

The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use.

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the exploitation risk of this vulnerability.

Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, and ensure they are not accessible from the internet.

Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolate them from business networks.

When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most recent version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as its connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

Summary

Users of Industrial Edge Devices are advised to consult the respective Security Advisories for their devices (for Siemens Industrial Edge devices see Additional Information). Industrial Edge Device Kit contains multiple path traversal vulnerabilities that could facilitate an authenticated remote attacker to access sensitive internal information. Title: Microsoft: Chinese State Actor Used AI to Compromise ConnectWise Tenants
Context: Microsoft assessed that a threat actor, tracked as Storm-0940, utilized agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to target hundreds of organizations globally across a...
Full Text:
A Chinese nation-state actor was responsible for the compromise of Microsoft365 tenants used by ConnectWise, which led to IT management software provider taking a number of its cloud services offline.

Microsoft assessed that a threat actor, tracked as Storm-0940, utilized agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to target hundreds of organizations globally across a broad range of industries, beginning in September 2026.

The China-aligned group was able to obtain privileged access to a number of organizations’ cloud infrastructure, including ConnectWise, often in less than three hours from initial targeting.

The campaign targeted industries such as aerospace and defense, automotive, chemicals, energy, financial services, government, legal, manufacturing, media, military, semiconductor, software, technology, and think tanks and non-profits.

Storm-0940 has been active since 2021 and its primary objective is data theft. It uses password spraying and exploitation of internet-facing applications for initial access, and establishes persistence in cloud environments by adding credentials to existing OAuth applications.

Attackers Target ConnectWise Customers

After gaining unauthorized access to the ConnectWise multi-tenant application, the China-aligned actor targeted the IT services firm’s downstream customers using the ARTEX platform to accelerate scanning and reconnaissance, password spraying and OAuth application abuse.

The group attempted to sign-in to more than 2250 tenants at 2900 sign-in attempts per minute. Microsoft said the pace of this supply chain attack gives defenders little time to detect and respond.

Microsoft revealed that it had identified multiple customer environments with evidence of follow-on activity, including reconnaissance, application credential modifications to establish persistence, and changes involving identities, groups and privileged roles.

“After acquiring control of the identities of multiple ConnectWise cloud applications, the AI agents operating on behalf of the threat actor continued to use the same IP range to authenticate to customer environments using the illicit access acquired through these stolen app credentials, effectively taking advantage of the already established trust by these apps within a tenant,” the tech giant explained in a blog dated October 21.

In an update published on October 21, ConnectWise acknowledged Microsoft’s findings and the extensive use of AI to compromise its Microsoft365 tenants.

“Nation-state actors are increasingly targeting the software supply chain, because one trusted connection can open the door to many organizations. AI now lets them test those connections at what Microsoft calls 'machine speed'. MSPs are in the middle of that chain. They are targets in their own right, and they are also a path into every client they serve,” the company wrote.

ConnectWise Cloud Services Remains Offline

ConnectWise first identified suspicious activity in its network on October 15, before discovering unauthorized access to application identities within its Cloud Backup environment on October 17.

The discovery resulted in several ConnectWise cloud services including Cloud Backup (previously known as SkyKick), SaaS Security and Cloud Management being taken offline while the company investigates the incident.

These services remain offline, according to the company’s status page.

However, ConnectWise said in an advisory on October 22 that it had started a phased restoration of its Cloud Backup service.

“We expect restoration to take several days and will share service-specific availability and reconnection instructions as confirmed. Keep affected connections disabled until formal instructions apply to your service,” it told customers.

The firm added that existing backup archives remain encrypted, isolated, and preserved, with no indication of compromise, while there is no evidence that other ConnectWise products and services are impacted by the incident.

Customers have also been advised to review individual Microsoft 365 tenants for unauthorized changes or persistent access.

The ARTEX Agentic AI Platform Threat

ARTEX is a multi-agent large-language model (LLM) that can use any AI model to automate a variety of offensive security workflows, including penetration test from reconnaissance through data exfiltration.

The agents then accumulate the discovered assets and vulnerabilities into a graph during the penetration test, Microsoft explained.

While the platform’s user interface and generated output default to English, the framework can be switched to Korean, Mandarin, Spanish, or Japanese.

In October 2026, CrowdStrike reported that a China-based threat actor used ARTEX to discover vulnerabilities and compromise specific services in South Korean financial organizations, a campaign that resulted in the exfiltration of data.

Title: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure
Context: Now the patches have been released, the Amazon Threat Intelligence team has publically confirmed they observed a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating October 17
Full Text:
Someone tried to exploit two critical vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language four days before the vulnerabilities were published and the flaws are now being exploited in the wild at scale, according to Amazon.

The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively known as ‘PHP2Shell,’ could allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) and server takeover on any websites relying on any PHP version released in the last decade – going back to version 5.4.

PHP is used by approximately 69.7% of websites whose server-side programming language is known, according to recent W3Techs data. These include many content management systems (CMS) like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento as well as e-commerce and web services platforms.

The bugs were discovered by security researchers at California-based security firm Calif and Google Cloud’s Wiz, with collaboration from OpenAI’s Patch the Planet project, in August. Public disclosure was scheduled for October 21, when the PHP Foundation planned to release the security patches.

However, on October 20, a pseudonymous user of the Hacker News forum leaked some information about the flaws before the patches were ready.

This led to many organizations across the world, including French public administrations, the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre and the University of Vienna taking their websites offline to prepare for and then apply the patches.

Now the patches have been released, the Amazon Threat Intelligence team has publically confirmed they observed a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating October 17. The attempt occurred in MadPot, an internal honeypot system created by Amazon Web Services (AWS) to monitor, study and disrupt global cybercrime.

Early Exploitation Attempt Likely From A “Threat Actor”

The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network. According to the Amazon researchers, this suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure.

In addition, they said they identified multiple proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits for PHP2Shell on October 21, around 12 hours before the vulnerability’s scheduled disclosure at 2pm GMT.

The earliest exploit was detected at approximately 2am GMT, with further attempts targeting the company’s MadPot sensors between 2am and 8am GMT from additional infrastructure.

According to the researchers, variations in the payloads and anonymization infrastructure suggested that multiple threat actors were involved. However, it was unclear whether the attempts would have succeeded against real-world systems.

Further PoC exploits emerged within hours of the release of the PHP2Shell patches, which were used against Amazon’s sensors almost immediately.

The researchers warned that PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.

Emerging Evidence of PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempts

Other security and threat intelligence teams have started to report active exploitation attempts of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 in the wild.

Matthew Prince, co-founder and CEO of Cloudflare, said on X his company saw “thousands of attempts to exploit” the vulnerabilities within the 10 hours that preceded the disclosure.

“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now,” he added.

Other security firms, including Beelzebub, Ellio, Recorded Future, VulnCheck, WatchTowr and Wiz have also observed evidence of exploitation attempts in the wild for both vulnerabilities.

Title: The Keys Are in the Browser: Secret Exposure Across AI-Built Websites
Context: Twelve keys in one bundle are twelve live credentials shipped at once, and five sites like this are five accounts an attacker can exploit
Full Text:
Cyble scanned 1.3M+ newly registered domains and found AI-built sites leaking live secrets to the browser: OpenAI keys, Stripe keys, and database tokens.

Spinning up a website no longer takes a developer. A prompt to an AI app-builder returns a working, styled, deployable site in minutes, and when one template works, the same operator clones it across a dozen domains before launch. That is also how secrets end up in plain sight.

Over a month, Cyble Research and Intelligence Labs (CRIL) scanned more than 1.3 million newly registered domains, identified the ones built by AI app-builders, and read their public front-end code for exposed credentials. We built our own classifiers to spot AI-generated websites as they are registered, paired with a scanner that pulls exposed keys and credentials straight from their public code. On 35 of the 22,306 AI-built sites we identified, a genuinely private secret was sitting in the browser: live OpenAI keys, Stripe secret keys, backend database tokens, and, in several cases, a single credential cloned across a whole fleet of domains.

Thirty-five is a small number, since counting every key-shaped string on an AI-built site is easy and misleading, as most are meant to be in the browser; a single reCAPTCHA key appeared on thousands of sites. We kept only the credentials that are never supposed to leave a server. Those are the findings below.

This report walks through the two leak patterns we observed, what appears exposed, what an attacker can do with these keys, and how to shut down the exposure.

AI-built Websites are leaking the keys that power them

An AI-built site generates its content with a Large Language Model (LLM), and the key to that model often ships in the page the visitor downloads. That is the plainest pattern we found, and the most on-the-nose.

Five AI-built sites carried live OpenAI API keys in their client-side code, sixteen distinct keys across them, and four of the five are confirmed AI-generated. One AI-writing site stands out on its own: it shipped twelve different OpenAI keys, one per content category, as plain values in its bundle. Figure 1 shows a single entry, with the key masked.

Figure 1 – Live OpenAI keys embedded as plain values in an AI-writing site’s JavaScript (key masked by CRIL).

A handful of sites, but each key is sensitive to exposure. An OpenAI secret key is a billing credential: anyone who reads the page can spend the owner’s balance, exhaust the rate limit, or run the bill up until someone notices and revokes it. Twelve keys in one bundle are twelve live credentials shipped at once, and five sites like this are five accounts an attacker can exploit.

Clone-and-leak: one secret across a whole fleet

An AI builder makes the hundredth site as cheap as the first, so an operator clones a working template across many domains, and whatever secret sat in the template now sits on every copy. We saw this in two shapes.

A Slack webhook shared across a 13-domain fleet. Thirteen near-identical domains, each a short word (ask, call, chat, get, hello, hey, hi, its, join, let, meet, my, see), glued to one brand, all served the same client bundle, and all embedded the same live Slack incoming-webhook URL. Figure 2 shows the URL in the shipped bundle, masked.

Figure 2 – One Slack webhook shared across a 13-domain fleet, in each site’s shipped bundle (secret and workspace IDs masked).

Anyone who can read the page can post messages to the operator’s Slack workspace via that webhook. That works for spam, for phishing aimed at the operator’s own staff, or for flooding a channel.

One Stripe secret key across four domains and two brands. A single Stripe secret key appeared on four domains under two separate brand names. The same sk_live_ value across all four points to one operator, or one shared Stripe account, behind every site. Figure 3 shows the assignment.

Figure 3 – The same live Stripe secret key reused across four domains under two brands.

A Stripe secret key provides full API access to the account, including the ability to create charges, issue refunds, and read customer and payout records. That one key exposes the operator’s whole payment account on every domain in the fleet.

The 13-domain Slack fleet runs on Bubble, a no-code and AI app builder, as confirmed by Bubble’s x-bubble-perf response header and client markers. Bubble serves each app from a dynamic.js bundle, and any value a developer places in a client-accessible field ships inside that bundle in plain text. The Stripe cluster runs on a Next.js build instead, which shows that the pattern spans builders rather than tracing to a single platform.

What else is exposed

Four AI-built sites exposed a Supabase service role JSON Web Token (JWT) on their front ends. A service-role token bypasses row-level security and grants full read and write to the project database. In terms of impact, it sits at the top of the set because it opens the entire backend rather than a single service.

Most of the remaining secret-looking strings on AI-built sites carry no/minimal exposure.

3,824 sites shipped browser-safe values: reCAPTCHA site keys, Stripe publishable keys, Supabase anon keys, builder telemetry tokens.

2,172 sites carried Google API keys, which matter only if they are unrestricted.

1,461 sites exposed a Supabase or Firebase backend address, which is a real exposure only when that backend’s rules are open.

Filtering those out is why the confirmed count is 35, not several thousand. Table 1 breaks the 35 down by type. The values stay withheld, and a few sites appear under more than one row.

What an attacker can do with these

Every credential in Table 1 is a working key to a live account. An attacker reads a public web page, copies a value, and calls an API. Here is what that buys them, key by key.

OpenAI and other LLM keys: Run inference on the victim’s account until the bill or rate limit stops them. On a metered account, that is direct financial loss; on a funded one, it is a free, anonymous model endpoint that the attacker can point at anything, billed to the victim and running under their quota and identity.

Stripe secret key; Drive the victim’s payment account through Stripe’s own API: create and refund charges, push the account toward fraud, and pull the customer list, email addresses, and payout history. One key is a money problem and a data-breach problem at once.

Supabase service-role token: Read and write the entire production database, past whatever row-level security the app configured. That means stealing every user record, altering or deleting data, and planting content the app will serve back to its own visitors.

Slack incoming webhook: Post into the operator’s own Slack as if from inside. Flooding a channel is a nuisance case; the real risk is internal phishing.

AWS access key: With the paired secret and enough permission, reach into the owner’s cloud: spin up resources (crypto-mining is the usual first move), read storage buckets, or pivot further in.

GitHub token or OAuth secret: Read or push to the owner’s source repositories or misuse their identity integration.

One exposure counts many times over. When the key sits on a cloned fleet, it is live on every domain in that fleet, so an attacker who finds it on one site has compromised all of them.

Conclusion

AI app-builders made it almost free to publish a website, and just as free to clone one, and most of what they produce is worth nothing to steal.

The exceptions are what we went looking for. A small, steady set of these sites hand over the key that runs them, and when an operator copies one site across a fleet, the leak rides along to every domain.

Against the millions of domains registered each month, the number is tiny, but every hit is a live account an attacker can reach and exploit just by opening the page.

If you build on these tools, read your own shipped code before you publish it. If you defend an organization, assume your keys may surface on sites you never built and look for them.

Cyble’s Threat Intelligence Platforms continuously monitor emerging threats, infrastructure, and activity across the dark web, deep web, and open sources. This proactive intelligence empowers organizations with early detection, impersonation, infrastructure mapping, and attribution insights. Altogether, these capabilities provide a critical head start in mitigating and responding to evolving cyber threats.

Our Recommendations

For developers and AI-builder users:

Keep every secret key (OpenAI sk-, Stripe sk_live_, a Supabase service-role token) in a server-side function or backend workflow, never in a client-accessible field.

Use only the browser-safe variants on the front end, publishable and anon keys, and enforce access with Supabase row-level security, Firebase rules, and API key restrictions.

Rotate any key that has ever sat on the client side, and treat it as already compromised.

Read your own page source before you ship, and search it for sk-, sk_live_, service_role, and hooks.slack.com. If you find them, so can anyone.

For SOCs and defenders:

Monitor public code and newly registered domains for your own keys and webhooks; don’t just paste sites.

Treat a secret found on one domain of a template fleet as exposed on all of them, and scope the response to the fleet, not the domain.

Title: Cloud Security Maturity Lags Despite Widespread Adoption, SANS Warns
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Nearly all organizations now run production workloads in the cloud, yet only 40% consider their cloud security strategy advanced or optimized, highlighting a significant maturity gap, according to SANS.

This is according to the 2026 SANS Cloud Security Survey Insights report which surveyed 400 IT and security professionals.

SANS found that 51% of respondents were running enterprise-scale (2501 to 10,000 workloads, containers, or instances) or hyperscale (more than 10,000) environments and 73% already having a dedicated cloud security team or role.

The report also noted that 93% of organizations already run production workloads in the cloud and 65% run more than one provider.

SANS noted that because so many respondents have a dedicated team for cloud security, it indicates that a maturity gap persists despite organizations being well-resourced.

Overall, 45% of respondents described their cloud security strategy as “intermediated” with partial implementation of a defined strategy.

This partial implementation is an issue, according to the report, and leads to security incidents.

Misconfiguration Make Up Nearly Half of Critical Cloud Incidents

The report found that misconfiguration is the leading cause of critical cloud incidents (45%), close to double that of the next highest factor, credential theft, which made up 22% of incidents.

What’s more, misconfigurations often remain in place for significant periods, with around half of organizations (49%) found to need more than 24 hours to close a known critical gap.

"Misconfiguration is not an exotic attack class. It is a known gap sitting in an account somebody already owns," said Serge Borso, SANS Principal Instructor. "What makes it persist is not the attacker. It is the distance between finding the gap and fixing it, across too many consoles with nobody clearly owning the result. That is why consolidation and enforcement matter more right now than implementing yet another detection tool. The industry has finished deciding to move to the cloud and is now paying for how fast it did.”

Despite the security maturity gap, cloud security budgets were found to be increasing for most, with 28% of respondents reporting significant investment to modernize or adopt new technology such as AI or Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform (CNAPP), and another 42% reporting incremental growth.

Overall, 70% of organizations are spending more on cloud security than a year ago. Only 7% reported budget cuts.

Just 21% of respondents said their organization runs a single consolidated CNAPP platform. Meanwhile, 31% still maintain separate point solutions across Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM), Cloud Workload Protection Platform (CWPP), and Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management (CIEM). Of those surveyed, 23% are actively evaluating a move to consolidate.

The SANS data points towards three priorities for security teams in the year ahead:

Strengthen cloud security by enforcing automated policy checks in infrastructure-as-code pipelines, preventing misconfigurations before deployment

Reduce security tool sprawl by consolidating posture management, workload protection and identity security tools into unified platforms

Extend zero trust beyond authentication by adopting continuous, context-based controls that limit what users and workloads can access after login

Title: ZDI-26-790: OpenSSL CMS AuthEnvelopedData Improper Validation of Integrity Check Value Vulnerability
Context: An attacker must first obtain the ability to modify CMS AuthEnvelopedData messages in order to exploit this vulnerability
Full Text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to tamper with CMS AuthEnvelopedData messages on affected installations of OpenSSL. An attacker must first obtain the ability to modify CMS AuthEnvelopedData messages in order to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of AES-GCM message authentication codes. The issue results from an improper integrity check. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to tamper with authenticated data.

Additional Details

OpenSSL has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://openssl-library.org/news/secadv/20260609.txt

2026-10-22 - Coordinated public release of advisory

Usage: python3 exploit.py --host TARGET --rce 'id>/var/www/html/proof.txt' Purpose and vulnerability mechanisms ==================================== This is a pure-HTTP, application-independent research exploit for an isolated lab. Its default endpoint is ``/index.php`` and is configurable with ``--path``. With no ``--rce`` it stops after reproducing the overlong ``Set-Cookie`` disclosure. With ``--rce [COMMAND]`` it composes two distinct PHP memory-safety mechanisms. Bare ``--rce`` runs the documented default and verifies ``/proof.txt``; a custom command is delivered without claiming that its execution was verified. 1. The A1/B1 disclosure is derived from 9bie's cross-request session-state chain. An upload-progress request reaches an OOM bailout before request state is safely reset; a later request in the *same mod_php child* consumes the stale ``PS(id)`` and encodes an attacker-forged ``zend_string`` into the session cookie. This is strongest-fit **CVE-2026-109619** behavior: request- owned session globals outlive their backing request heap. OOM is the producer, but the security boundary crossed by this stage is request lifetime. This is mechanism-based attribution, not a CNA reassignment of any individual public PoC. 2. The optional final sink is adapted from Cookiengineer's OOM RCE. Multipart amplification exhausts the stock 128 MiB heap while ``_zend_hash_str_add_or_update_i()`` has counted but not initialized its final ``HashTable`` bucket. Same-request shutdown walks the incomplete bucket into a forged object, a libphp-only ``jump_fcontext`` ROP chain, and ``zif_system``. This is the incomplete-state/cleanup mechanism of **CVE-2026-109618**. Worker discovery, chunked transfer, prefork saturation, the full-pool scrub, and the clean holder rebind are delivery/affinity techniques, not additional CVEs. The scrub exists because the validated Apache environment can retain children already marked for graceful retirement when its IPv6 listener wakeup fails; without it, a second invocation may place A1 and B1 in different processes. The post-scrub repin is concurrent so VPN latency cannot recreate an idle-surplus window. Debugger mappings were used only to calibrate and independently verify the constants below; successful end-to-end runs derive their live bases from the HTTP cookie. Validated exact environment (2026-10-23) ======================================== This profile is intentionally build-specific. Title: No time to PHP around.
Context: Critical PHP flaws threaten millions of websites. Security firm watchTowr says it has confirmed the vulnerabilities are real, while researchers at Sansec warn that widespread attacks could begin within minutes of the patches becoming available.
Full Text:
Critical PHP flaws threaten millions of websites. Weak certificates from an Indian authority spark a global security scramble. Investigators probe a U.S. consulting executive’s alleged ties to ShinyHunters. SafePay ransomware hits at least 600 critical infrastructure organizations. Researchers find troubling security biases in Chinese AI-generated code. A $10 million initiative bolsters cybersecurity for small U.S. utilities. An American pleads guilty to stealing from thousands of servicemembers and veterans. Leo Scott, Managing Director of DataTribe, is talking about their upcoming Cyber Innovation Conference and the 9th annual DataTribe Challenge. Two pallets of GPUs never make it to baggage claim.

Today is Wednesday October 21st 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

PHP vulnerabilities put millions of web sites at risk.

PHP is a widely used, open-source programming language that powers the behind-the-scenes functionality of websites. It runs on web servers, handling tasks like processing forms, managing user accounts, interacting with databases, and generating web pages. Popular platforms including WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla rely on PHP. Because it’s so widely used, a serious PHP vulnerability can potentially affect millions of websites.

Now, PHP administrators are bracing for two potentially critical vulnerabilities that could put millions of websites at risk. PHP maintainers have announced plans to release patches for two flaws, each carrying a severity score of 9.2 out of 10.

The warning follows leaked, but unverified, details of an exploit tool called PHP2Shell, reportedly capable of executing code on servers running popular platforms including WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento.

Security firm watchTowr says it has confirmed the vulnerabilities are real, while researchers at Sansec warn that widespread attacks could begin within minutes of the patches becoming available.

One researcher estimates that 1.3 million internet-connected hosts may be affected.

Administrators are being urged to inventory their PHP applications, prepare backups, and arrange emergency maintenance windows. Patches are scheduled for release at 14:00 UTC, though maintainers warn they could arrive earlier if exploitation is detected.

Given PHP’s enormous footprint, the potential consequences extend across much of the web.

An Indian cert authority unlocks a global security headache.

Security teams worldwide are scrambling to contain a potentially massive Internet security problem after researchers discovered eight digital certificates with private keys so weak that attackers could use them to impersonate virtually any website.

The certificates belong to India-based certificate authority eMudhra. They’re intermediate certificates, meaning they can be used to issue other certificates that browsers and applications automatically trust.

Normally, cracking their encryption would be practically impossible. But these keys were astonishingly weak, containing as little as three to eight bits of entropy. One researcher described the situation as “bonkers.”

Major browsers and several applications have already blocked the certificates, and there’s currently no evidence they’ve been maliciously exploited. But cleaning up the broader Internet could take years.

Cryptography expert Filippo Valsorda compares the challenge to the 2014 Heartbleed vulnerability, warning that this recovery could be even more complicated. Linux systems, embedded devices, forgotten servers, and Internet of Things equipment may require individual updates.

The immediate concern involves attackers intercepting encrypted communications, particularly VPN connections. Exploitation requires positioning oneself between communicating parties, something that’s easier for attackers controlling local networks or possessing sophisticated surveillance capabilities.

Most modern browsers have implemented protections, although Microsoft’s Edge on Windows 10 reportedly remained vulnerable in some circumstances.

The incident exposes a fundamental weakness in Internet trust: even the strongest encryption depends on the security of the organizations issuing certificates.

And when one of those organizations gets the fundamentals spectacularly wrong, the cleanup becomes everybody’s problem.

Investigators believe an executive at a major U.S. consulting firm helped operate ShinyHunters.

Federal investigators examining the ShinyHunters hacking group are scrutinizing executives at two ransomware negotiation firms over their alleged relationships with the cybercriminals.

According to KrebsOnSecurity, investigators believe an executive at a major U.S. consulting firm helped operate ShinyHunters’ extortion website, which pressured nearly 100 victims to pay ransoms.

Authorities have also arrested Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky on extortion-related charges. Investigators reportedly uncovered communications linking him and other negotiators to ShinyHunters after Dutch police arrested a suspected group member and accessed his Signal messages.

The investigation raises troubling questions about conflicts of interest in the ransomware negotiation business. Some firms reportedly collect fees based on the size of ransom payments, creating financial incentives that may favor the criminals over their victims.

The allegations remain under investigation.

SafePay ransomware has compromised at least 600 critical infrastructure organizations worldwide.

The SafePay ransomware group has compromised at least 600 critical infrastructure organizations worldwide since emerging in August 2024, according to a joint advisory from U.S., German, and British authorities.

SafePay has become one of 2026’s most active ransomware operations, targeting organizations across four continents.

The group gains access through stolen credentials, brute-force attacks, vulnerable VPNs, and exposed network devices. Once inside, attackers escalate privileges, move laterally using legitimate administrative tools, disable security software, and steal sensitive data before encrypting systems.

SafePay employs double extortion, demanding cryptocurrency payments in exchange for decryption tools and promises not to publish stolen information.

The group also reportedly calls victims directly to pressure them into paying.

Authorities are urging organizations to strengthen defenses against SafePay’s increasingly widespread operations.

New research raises questions about the security of code generated by Chinese AI models.

The United States has banned Chinese AI startup DeepSeek from federal civilian agency systems, citing national security concerns. The Department of Homeland Security says DeepSeek’s China-based infrastructure could expose sensitive American data to Chinese authorities.

Beijing condemned the restrictions and warned of possible retaliation, adding another complication to already strained U.S.-China technology relations.

Meanwhile, new research raises questions about the security of code generated by Chinese AI models.

Cybersecurity startup Hirundo tested Alibaba’s Qwen3-Coder and found it produced significantly more vulnerable applications for American defense contractors than Chinese ones. Seventy percent of applications generated for U.S. contractors were exploitable, compared with 59 percent for Chinese contractors.

Applications built for a Hong Kong democracy advocacy group were also more likely to leak secrets.

Hirundo says the discrepancies disappeared after researchers modified the model to remove what they characterize as Chinese Communist Party political alignment.

The findings suggest that AI coding assistants may introduce security risks influenced by their training and underlying model behavior.

A $10 million initiative looks to help smaller U.S. utilities defend against cyberattacks.

Accenture, Dragos, and the SANS Institute are launching a $10 million initiative to help smaller U.S. utilities defend against cyberattacks.

The new nonprofit Community Cyber Resilience Foundation will initially provide free cybersecurity technology, hardware, deployment assistance, and training to as many as 500 water, wastewater, electric, and natural gas utilities.

The announcement follows a surge in cyberattacks affecting more than 100 American water systems across over a dozen states.

Eligible utilities must have annual revenues below $100 million, a threshold covering more than 50,000 organizations nationwide.

Participants will receive access to Dragos security technology, Accenture implementation support, and SANS operational technology training.

The initiative aims to address a growing cybersecurity divide between large infrastructure operators and smaller utilities struggling with limited budgets, aging equipment, and staffing shortages.

An American pleads guilty to an identity theft scheme targeting U.S. service members.

A 45-year-old American has pleaded guilty to orchestrating an identity theft scheme that targeted thousands of U.S. servicemembers and veterans.

Robert Wayne Boling Jr. operated from the Philippines, using stolen personal information to access victims’ bank accounts and steal money and veterans’ benefits between 2014 and 2019.

Prosecutors say Boling obtained sensitive records from a former U.S. Army medical records contractor stationed in South Korea.

The operation relied on dozens of money mules in the United States who received stolen funds and transferred portions of the proceeds to the Philippines.

Boling was deported to the United States and arrested in May. Two accomplices have already been sentenced, while two others remain fugitives.

Boling faces up to 40 years in prison for conspiracy to commit wire fraud and money laundering.

Two pallets of GPUs never make it to baggage claim.

A Brazilian electronics distributor is looking for nearly half a million dollars’ worth of missing graphics cards, and it’s taking its search to Instagram.

Oderço says two pallets of high-end Nvidia RTX 5090 GPUs arrived at São Paulo’s Guarulhos International Airport, then apparently vanished.

After getting nowhere with official inquiries, the company turned to social media, saying nothing like this has happened in its 38-year history.

The missing shipment is valued at roughly $470,000, although the company hasn’t disclosed exactly how many cards disappeared, or when.

The timing is particularly unfortunate. RTX 5090s are already in short supply, with retail prices reaching thousands of dollars per card.

Whether the shipment was stolen, misplaced, or swallowed by some bureaucratic black hole remains unclear.

For now, Oderço is hoping the internet can help locate its missing hardware.

Which is perhaps fitting, considering how many people have already been searching the internet for an RTX 5090.

And that’s the CyberWire.

Title: Limits of Java Certificate Bypass: Fingerprint Blocklist Insights
Context: TL;DR Sonatype's tests found that Java's blocked
Full Text:
TL;DR

Sonatype's tests found that Java's blocked.certs rejected the listed certificate encodings but accepted re-encoded versions that still validated in the tested configurations.

We reproduced the behavior with ECDSA- and RSA-signed intermediates associated with the eMudhra incident. Each re-encoded certificate had a different SHA-256 fingerprint.

The results apply to the JDK versions and trust-store configurations tested. Follow current vendor guidance and verify the protections in the runtimes and trust stores you deploy.

A certificate blocklist can reject a known-bad certificate and still miss another encoding of it.

We saw this while examining Java's response to the eMudhra certificate incident. The mitigation uses SHA-256 fingerprints to identify compromised intermediate certificates. But a certificate’s fingerprint is calculated from its exact encoded bytes.

During an AI-assisted review, Sonatype Research Labs asked Opus 5.5 whether Java's exact-fingerprint blocking could be bypassed. The AI model flagged that exact-byte matching might leave room for equivalent certificate encodings.

We confirmed the behavior for both ECDSA and RSA certificates: re-encoded intermediates had different SHA-256 fingerprints, yet still validated in our Java trust-store tests. This points to a limit in exact-fingerprint blocking: it can identify the certificate bytes it knows about without necessarily covering every equivalent encoding.

Here, we’ll explain how the re-encoding works, what the tests show, and what teams should check before relying on a certificate blocklist as their only mitigation.

How It Started: eMudhra Certificates Compromised

Several eMudhra intermediate certificate authority keys were compromised on October 20, 2026, allowing anyone who obtained a key to create certificates that could be trusted as part of a chain to a trusted root. Browser and platform vendors responded with blocks and trust-store changes.

This also prompted a Java mitigation: add the affected intermediates to blocked.certs. Our research began with a narrower question: does that fingerprint-based block reject every valid encoding of those certificates?

How Exact-Fingerprint Blocking Works

A certificate is a structured document: it contains information such as the subject, public key, issuer, validity period, and a digital signature. In Java, blocked.certs identifies certificates by their SHA-256 fingerprints. The fingerprint is calculated from the certificate's encoded bytes, so even a small change to those bytes produces a different fingerprint.

This makes fingerprint blocking precise, but the match depends on the exact encoding in the blocklist. If a certificate can be re-encoded and still pass signature validation, the new encoding may have a different fingerprint and may not match the listed entry. To test whether an alternate encoding could still validate in practice, we examined two signature formats: ECDSA and RSA.

Changing the Encoding Changes the Result

We tested two certificate chains from the eMudhra incident advisory: one with an ECDSA-signed intermediate and one with an RSA-signed intermediate. For each, the reproduction added the original intermediate's SHA-256 fingerprint to a copy of a JDK's blocked.certs file, changed the intermediate's encoding without its private key, then checked whether the chain still validated.

The two encoding changes were:

ECDSA: The script changes the signature value from s to n − s, another valid representation of the signature.

RSA: It removes the NULL parameter from the outer signature algorithm identifier. The signature over the certificate data remains unchanged.

Both tests produced the same result:Java rejected the original chain whose intermediate fingerprint was listed, but trusted the chain with the re-encoded intermediate, whose fingerprint was different. After the relevant roots were removed from the copied JDK’s trust store, both chains were rejected.

Verify the Mitigation in Your Runtime

Teams should verify certificate mitigations in the Java runtimes and trust stores they deploy. Removing the relevant roots rejected both chains in our tests, but it can also interrupt legitimate TLS connections. Before changing a trust store, identify dependent services, test their certificate chains, and monitor for TLS failures after deployment.

Follow current vendor guidance and document any exceptions. These results cover only the JDK versions and trust-store configurations we examined, so validate the controls separately for other runtimes and TLS paths in your environment.

Full Text:
Sonatype is responding to the industry-wide eMudhra certificate authority incident, which affects certificate trust stores used by certain Sonatype products and distributions. We are updating affected components. In the meantime, apply certificate trust-store updates provided by your operating-system, runtime, and application vendors.

What Happened

On October 17, 2026, a researcher reported that the private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities (CAs) could be recovered because they were generated with insufficient randomness. Six affected intermediates were for TLS certificates and two were for code signing. Someone with an affected TLS key could create a certificate for a website or service, which could be accepted by clients that still trust the affected chain.

Browser and operating system vendors have taken steps to block the affected certificates. Other software may rely on separate or bundled certificate trust stores that need updates, so organizations should also check systems beyond browsers and operating systems.

Sonatype Impact

We are preparing updated Docker images and patch releases with current certificate trust data. The tables below list the impacted Sonatype products and their remediation status. Existing Docker images and bundled JVMs do not update automatically.

Title: Best practices for integrating IAM Roles Anywhere with your PKI
Context: This tool is compatible with the credential_process feature available across the AWS SDKs
Full Text:
Using temporary credentials is a security best practice to reduce the risk from credentials getting compromised. With AWS IAM Roles Anywhere, now your workloads outside of Amazon Web Services (AWS) will be able to access AWS resources by obtaining temporary security credentials in AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). IAM Roles Anywhere relies on public key infrastructure (PKI) to establish trust between your AWS account and certificate authorities that issues certificates to your workloads that run outside AWS. PKI involves the generation, distribution, and verification of digital certificates through public key encryption.

In this post, we show you some best practices, considerations, and solutions for integrating your PKI with IAM Roles Anywhere. In this post, we assume that you have a foundational knowledge of IAM and IAM Roles Anywhere. For more information, see the IAM and IAM Roles Anywhere documentation.

Note: As of July 2026, AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) supports exportable public certificates that can be used on workloads outside AWS (containers or on-premises). Additionally, ACM supports the ACME protocol for automated certificate issuance and renewal on external workloads. These capabilities complement IAM Roles Anywhere by providing both identity (using X.509 certificates for IAM Roles Anywhere) and encryption (using ACM public/private certificates) for hybrid environments.

X.509 certificates for workload identity

If you’re running multiple workloads in your infrastructure, you’re probably assigning unique workload identities and specific user permissions. In this environment, your workloads can use PKI tools like Active Directory Certificate Services to centrally manage and monitor the identities and permissions at scale. The same principles of segregating unrelated workloads apply to PKI and IAM Roles Anywhere. If you’re issuing certificates to your workloads today, they can probably be used with IAM Roles Anywhere without any changes.

As shown in Figure 1, the access boundary and permissions of Workload A can be very different from that of Workload B when accessing AWS resources, depending on the organization’s needs. In such scenarios, it’s recommended to establish a unique machine identity for each workload. This can be achieved by issuing a separate X.509 certificate with distinct identity attributes signed by your certificate authority (CA). To set up an effective PKI solution for machine identities, you must configure the appropriate certificate attributes and anchor the trust model around those attributes.

Figure 1: Workloads outside of AWS accessing AWS services

Temporary access credentials

Workloads with distinct CA signed X.509 certificates exchange certificates with IAM, as shown in Figure 2, to get temporary security credentials for the session. The signature validation process used by IAM Roles Anywhere verifies the certificate issuer and the subject before providing the temporary credentials. To enable this verification process, an IAM Roles Anywhere trust model should be set up by either uploading your CA’s digital certificate as a trust anchor or by referencing an existing AWS Private Certificate Authority (AWS Private CA) certificate. In this post, we focus on using a trust anchor.

To help define the appropriate scope for the temporary credentials, it’s recommended to configure distinct IAM roles for each workload to assume. Workloads must use X.509 certificates issued by your CA. These certificates are exchanged with IAM to get temporary security credentials for the session.

Figure 2: Getting temporary credentials from IAM using CA issued X.509 certificate

Setting up a trust model for IAM Roles Anywhere is a three-step process, see Extend AWS IAM Roles Anywhere to workloads outside of AWS for more information.

Create a trust anchor.

Set up IAM roles with the IAM Roles Anywhere trust policy that will be assumed by your non-AWS workload.

Configure profiles with IAM roles and attach relevant session policies. This instructs IAM Roles Anywhere to use your selected session policies whenever you request credentials for any of the attached roles.

Trust model

The trust model is centered around setting up the right trust relationship between IAM Roles Anywhere and your CA by configuring a trust anchor. The model connects the role, the IAM Roles Anywhere service principal, and identities encoded in X509 certificates that are issued by a CA.

Certificate attributes

Certificates are a binary record with encoded key/value pairs as certificate attributes. Let’s look at one of the X.509 certificates to understand different attributes of certificate that are important for IAM Roles Anywhere PKI validation.

The following is an example PEM encoded certificate file that can be decoded with tools like openssl.

-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- MIIKOzCCCSOgAwIBAgIQDlnyZvBeKjgHm1jJ++CbgDANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQsFADBE MQswC ........... -----END CERTIFICATE---- Certificate: Data: Version: 3 (0x2) Serial Number: e0:5d:b7:72:56:fa:75:e3 Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA512 Issuer: C=US, ST=CA, L=San Francisco, O=MyCompany Inc., OU=AC, CN=MyCompany CA Validity Not Before: Sep 15 00:09:17 2023 GMT Not After : Sep 18 00:09:17 2023 GMT Subject: C=US, O=MyCompany, OU=eCommerce, CN=WorkloadA Subject Public Key Info: Public Key Algorithm: id-ecPublicKey Public-Key: (384 bit) pub: 04:3b:74:e1:68:06:fa:b0:3d:fe:f7:5f:74:80:05: X509v3 extensions: X509v3 Subject Alternative Name: DNS:ecommerce.mycompany.com, DNS:*ecommerce.mycompany.com, URI:spiffe://mycompany.com/workload/ecommerce X509v3 Basic Constraints: critical CA:FALSE X509v3 Key Usage: critical Digital Signature Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA512 30:64:02:30:19:a7:a0:33:49:ce:e1:cb:76:6e:c0:f3:c5:66:

IAM Roles Anywhere extracts values from the subject Common Name (CN), issuer, and Subject Alternative Name (SAN) fields of the authenticating certificate and makes them available for policy evaluation through the sts:sourceIdentity and principal tags. When configuring your PKI, set short validity periods on the certificates issued to workloads. Short-lived certificates limit the window of exposure if a certificate is compromised and reduce the need for active revocation.

"aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/CN": "WorkloadA" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Issuer/CN": "MyCompany CA" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/DNS": "ecommerce.mycompany.com" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/URI": "spiffe://mycompany.com/workload/ecommerce" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/Name/CN": "WorkloadA"

Note: An empty Subject CN in a certificate isn’t supported by IAM Roles Anywhere.

Trust policy and effective permissions of credentials

IAM Roles Anywhere clients fetch temporary credentials for IAM Roles using the API method CreateSession. To successfully authorize this API call, the IAM role trust policy should trust the IAM Roles Anywhere service principal as shown in the following example.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "rolesanywhere.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": [ "sts:AssumeRole", "sts:TagSession", "sts:SetSourceIdentity" ], "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Issuer/CN": "MyCompany CA", "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/CN": "WorkloadA", "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/Name/CN": "WorkloadA" }, "ArnEquals": { "aws:SourceArn": [ "arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:trust-anchor/TA_ID" ] } } } ] }

As a security best practice, consider using additional condition statements to evaluate the session PrincipalTag attributes extracted from the certificate to further restrict authorization of temporary credentials. If the workloads have ephemeral certificates with a dynamic subject CN, then the issuer or SAN principal tags can be used to define condition statements in the trust policy. The trust anchor shown in the preceding trust policy helps establish the trust between IAM Roles Anywhere and the CA in your PKI.

Plan for trust anchor placement

Depending on the CA platform, you can configure one or more intermediate certificates in your PKI certificate hierarchy, as shown in Figure 3. The certificate level the trust anchor is placed at affects which end-entity certificates IAM Roles Anywhere accepts, and therefore which workloads are authorized to assume a role. To create a trust anchor, export the certificate bundle for the issuing CA certificate from your external CA platform in PEM-encoded format and upload it to the trust anchor console.

Figure 3: Certificate hierarchy in an external PKI

See the Solution deployment section to onboard a sample solution and verify your certificate bundle.

Fine-grained access control is vital for security because it allows organizations to precisely define and restrict permissions, minimizing the risk of unauthorized access and data breaches. The effective permissions of the temporary security credentials are an intersection of resource-based, identity-based, and session policies as shown in Figure 4. By setting up the trust anchor and profile configuration in IAM Roles Anywhere with session policies, you can limit the permissions for each session.

Figure 4: Effective permissions of session credentials

Credential helper

To obtain temporary security credentials from IAM Roles Anywhere, use the credential helper tool. This tool is compatible with the credential_process feature available across the AWS SDKs. The credential helper manages the process of obtaining temporary security credentials using IAM Roles Anywhere and returns them in JSON format. The private key of the workload and its CA signed certificate are the two critical parameters provided to the credential helper tool. To use this tool, you need both an end-entity certificate and a trust anchor created in IAM Roles Anywhere. As of December 2024, the credential helper (version 1.4.0 and later) supports Trusted Platform Module (TPM) 2.0.

The following is an example of how to obtain temporary security credentials:

$ ./aws_signing_helper credential-process \ --certificate /path/to/certificate \ --private-key /path/to/private-key \ --trust-anchor-arn arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:trust-anchor/TA_ID \ --profile-arn arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:profile/PROFILE_ID \ --role-arn arn:aws:iam::account:role/role-name-with-path

When credential-process is used with AWS SDKs, the temporary credentials are stored in memory and refreshed automatically. However, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) invokes credential-process on every command. Each invocation creates a new IAM Roles Anywhere session, which adds latency to every CLI call. To avoid this delay when using the AWS CLI, we recommend using the update command, which writes refreshed credentials to a file that the CLI reads on each invocation without calling credential-process again.

When you use update, credentials are written to a credential file on disk and any user or process who can read the credential file might be able to read and use those AWS credentials, so it’s recommended to use serve unless your business has a specific use case that needs to read AWS credentials from a file. The serve command can be used to vend temporary credentials through an endpoint running on the local host using the same URIs and request headers as Instance Metadata Service Version 2 (IMDSv2). When using serve, no AWS configuration files are needed because the AWS SDKs can discover the server endpoint.

Just-in-time compared to short-lived certificates as workload identities

To help mitigate the risk around the exposure of your business-critical resources to compromised certificate user sessions, it’s recommended to use certificates with just-in-time credentials or short-lived access credentials. Just-in-time certificates are issued by a CA for immediate use for authentication on a system or application. The CA uses the roles and policies defined in IAM to determine when, and under what conditions, a workload can establish a session. With just-in-time access, admins don’t have to worry about revoking access if the users’ access roles change. Because the access credentials are recreated for each access request, any role changes can be applied in real time. Just-in-time access requires support from your CA, so verify compatibility with your CA before implementing it.

It’s recommended to tailor the validity periods for short-lived certificates to align with business requirements, workload lifecycle, and your organization’s risk tolerance. AWS Private CA offers a short-lived CA mode specifically designed for certificates with validity periods under 7 days. This mode is priced at $50 per month (compared to $400 per month for general-purpose CA mode), making it cost-effective for high-volume, ephemeral workload identities such as containers and serverless functions. For more information, see AWS Private Certificate Authority and How to use AWS Private CA short-lived certificate mode. See Zero trust on AWS for information about how short-lived credentials support a zero trust architecture.

Best practices for private key storage

Safeguarding private keys is of paramount importance in any environment. A private key is created by the certificate owner when requesting certificates with a Certificate Signing Request (CSR). The CA providing your certificate doesn’t create or have your private key. In fact, it’s recommended that no one outside your administrators should ever be given access to this material. Guardrails should be implemented to make sure the keys aren’t stored in an online repository.

Using the credential helper with IAM Roles Anywhere, you can integrate with PKCS #11-compatible modules. For implementation details, see How to implement cryptographic modules to secure private keys used with IAM Roles Anywhere. With the credential helper (version 1.1.0 and later), IAM Roles Anywhere supports PKCS #11 integration, so you can use private keys stored in hardware security modules (HSMs) or software-based secure stores and avoid storing them to disk. Additionally, as of December 2024, the credential helper supports Trusted Platform Module (TPM) 2.0, enabling private keys to be generated inside the TPM and marked as non-exportable. With TPM-backed keys, the private keys can’t be extracted even if the workload host is compromised. This is the strongest private key protection available for on-premises and hybrid workloads using IAM Roles Anywhere.

If your organization doesn’t implement PKCS #11–compatible modules, IAM Roles Anywhere supports credential helper version 1.0.5 for X.509 certificates and private keys stored in macOS and Windows certificate stores. This delegates the signing operations to keys stored within those OS-specific certificate stores. In Windows, both CryptoAPI and Cryptography API: Next Generation (CNG) are supported; in macOS, Keychain is supported. In these environments, the private key will never be directly readable, and the signing operation would be delegated to the secure store instead, which will improve security posture of your environment. If you have multiple certificates, then use the --cert-selector flag of the credential helper tool to search for a specific certificate (and associated private key) through the certificate subject, issuer, and serial number. The corresponding keys are x509Subject, x509Issuer, and x509Serial, respectively. These keys can be specified either through a JSON file format or through the command line. The following is an example of both approaches:

If you want to use a JSON file, it should be similar to this:

[ { "Key": "x509Subject", "Value": "CN=Subject" }, { "Key": "x509Issuer", "Value": "CN=Issuer" }, { "Key": "x509Serial", "Value": "15D19632234BF759A32802C0DA88F9E8AFC8702D" } ]

If the preceding example is placed in a file called selector.json, it can be specified with the --cert-selector flag through file://path/to/selector.json.

The same certificate selector argument can be specified through the command line as shown in the following:

--cert-selector Key=x509Subject, Value=CN=Subject Key=x509Issuer, Value=CN=Issuer Key=x509Serial, Value=15D19632

Monitoring trust anchor certificates

Monitoring certificate expiry in PKI is crucial for maintaining secure communication, because expired certificates can lead to authentication failures, leaving systems vulnerable to unauthorized access. Compliance and regulatory requirements often mandate timely renewal of certificates, making monitoring certificate expiry essential to avoid legal penalties and maintain organizational integrity.

Using IAM Roles Anywhere, you can receive notifications for CA certificate expiry and end-entity certificate expiry. IAM Roles Anywhere can send metrics, events, and notifications through multiple notification channels as shown in the following table:

The preceding notifications thresholds are default settings, which you can customize using the steps in Customize notification settings in IAM Roles Anywhere.

Best practices for trust anchor certificate rotation

Consider rotating your certificates using blue/green deployments to seamlessly roll out new certificates without affecting service availability. Use automation to integrate certificate rotation testing in your blue/green deployment pipeline. See the sample AWS CloudFormation template in the Solution deployment section to build your automation pipeline.

As shown in Figure 5, two trust anchors have been created; one for each environment. Using this approach, you can test the certificate rotation process in a controlled staging environment before applying it to the production environment, thus reducing the risk of certificate-related outages.

Figure 5: Trust anchor certificate rotation in blue/green deployment

Solution deployment

The sample solution template is available in the IAM Roles Anywhere — External PKI Integration repository on GitHub. It contains the following main steps:

Creates a distinct IAM role with policies scoped to the resources that workload requires.

Assigns a trust relationship to a IAM Roles Anywhere principal.

Creates a trust anchor using a certificate bundle from an external CA.

Creates a profile with the required IAM Roles.

Important: The SessionDurationSeconds value must not exceed the IAM role’s MaxSessionDuration setting, which defaults to 3600 seconds (1 hour). If you request a longer session than the role allows, the CreateSession API returns an error. The companion template keeps both values in sync by setting the role’s MaxSessionDuration to the same parameter value. If you configure the role separately, update its MaxSessionDuration to match your desired session length. For more information, see IAM Roles Anywhere CreateSession API.

If the workload’s subject CN (WorkloadSubjectCN) doesn’t match the x509Subject CN of the authenticating certificate, the CreateSession call is denied. The same conditional verification applies to WorkloadIssuerCN and WorkloadSANCN.

The template enforces three certificate attribute conditions in the IAM trust policy: issuer CN, subject CN, and SAN CN must all match the values configured as parameters. Additionally, the trust policy scopes role assumption to the specific trust anchor Amazon Resource Name (ARN), preventing other trust anchors in the same account from assuming that role.

Conclusion

In this post, we discussed how AWS IAM Roles Anywhere, empowered by X.509 certificates, introduces a dynamic and secure way to manage workload identities and issue temporary access credentials. By understanding the trust model, using certificate attributes, and implementing fine-grained authorization, organizations can gain granular control over the effective permissions of these credentials.

The choice between just-in-time and short-lived certificates as workload identities depends on your specific requirements.

Adhering to best practices for private key storage is essential to maintain the integrity of your security infrastructure. Regularly rotating trust anchor certificates helps ensure the long-term trustworthiness of your system.

As you embark on your journey to implement IAM Roles Anywhere and integrate it with your PKI, remember that a well-architected approach to certificate management is a cornerstone of robust and resilient cloud security.

For additional deployment guidance, see Planning for your IAM Roles Anywhere deployment, which covers end-to-end deployment planning including network architecture, monitoring, and operational considerations.

Title: PHP2Shell Makes PHP Inventory and Patch Ownership Urgent
Context: As Turunen warns: "The age of AI has also sped up exploitation where it's likely we are going to see scaled up attacks imminently across the internet
Full Text:
Updated October 23, 2026: PHP disclosed a related follow-on issue, CVE-2026-115560, involving an unlikely remote code execution (RCE) vector under unusual session settings. PHP recommends disabling session.upload_progress.enabled until the next regular bugfix release. See our research and recommendation in Sonatype Guide for more details.

TL;DR

PHP2Shell is the name being used for two critical PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Both can allow unauthenticated remote code execution.

PHP says all PHP installations serving web requests are at risk, with the highest risk in Apache configurations using mod_php. Fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

Organizations should inventory PHP across their environments, prioritize internet-facing systems, monitor for suspicious activity, and apply the update through PHP or the relevant distribution or product vendor. If a system cannot be remediated promptly, consider taking it offline until it is fully mitigated.

On October 23, 2026, PHP disclosed CVE-2026-115560, a separate follow-on RCE issue. Temporarily disable session.upload_progress.enabled as PHP recommends, then apply the complete PHP fix when available.

PHP2Shell Is Two Critical Flaws in the PHP Runtime

PHP2Shell refers to two vulnerabilities in PHP's internal request handling. Because PHP is used in websites, applications, and products, affected installations may be managed by different teams or supplied through different vendors.The urgent work is to find those systems, establish who owns each one, and verify that the fix reaches every deployment.

Sonatype's PHP2Shell Security Event tracks current guidance and response recommendations.

CVE-2026-109618 involves out-of-memory handling: PHP may interrupt a request while internal data is only partly initialized, then handle that data incorrectly during cleanup.

CVE-2026-109619 involves a stale global state that can persist after its underlying memory has been freed.

PHP says CVE-2026-115560 can occur when an application configures session.serialize_handler as php_binary or php_serialize, switches it to php at runtime before calling session_start(), and leaves session upload progress enabled. PHP had already listed disabling upload progress as a mitigation for CVE-2026-109619. This setting does not cover every affected path, and that a PHP release containing the complete state-reset patch is the reliable remediation.

Under affected conditions, the flaws can allow a remote attacker to execute code without authentication.

Ilkka Turunen, Sonatype's Field CTO, puts the operational priority plainly: "The immediate priority is clear accountability: know where PHP is used across your services and products, who owns remediation, and how quickly fixes can be deployed."

The Hard Part Is Finding Every PHP Installation

Organizations may know that their public websites use PHP but have less visibility into internal portals, older services, appliances, or software that bundles its own runtime. Different teams may also install and maintain PHP through separate operating system distributions, hosting providers, or third-party vendors.

Turunen expects remediation to extend beyond visible websites and services. PHP is bundled into other products and remains in older environments, creating what he calls "a long tail of environments needing to apply this patch."

A complete response starts with an inventory that connects each runtime to an owner and a patch path. Teams should identify:

Which internet-facing and internal systems run PHP.

The PHP version and how it is supplied or maintained.

Which applications, containers, images, appliances, and products include a PHP runtime.

The business or service owner responsible for remediation.

Whether a fixed package is available from PHP, the operating system distributor, hosting provider, or another vendor.

Include systems that are easy to overlook: older applications with little traffic, test environments that remain reachable, and deployments maintained outside the central platform team. An incomplete inventory can make an organization believe remediation is finished while vulnerable installations remain online.

PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project. PHP says some distributions and long-term support vendors provide backported fixes, and it has also published source backports for selected older branches. Organizations using these versions should confirm the status with their distribution or vendor, or plan an upgrade to a supported release. Do not assume an upstream version number alone tells you whether a vendor-maintained package includes the fix.

Patch, Verify, and Monitor Across the Estate

PHP says updating to a fixed release is the only complete solution. Temporary controls can reduce exposure to specific attack paths, and a web application firewall can add protection for traffic routed through it. Cloudflare reported deploying protections and seeing attack traffic aimed at its customers, while urging users to patch.

If a system cannot be remediated promptly, the UK National Cyber Security Centre advises organizations to consider taking it offline until it is fully mitigated. If it must remain available, assign an owner and document interim protections and a reassessment date.

The discovery and response also highlight the role AI is playing in vulnerability research. The Wall Street Journal reported that Calif and Wiz researchers used AI tools during a PHP source-code audit, and that developers, researchers, and distributors coordinated on fixes after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure.

As Turunen warns: "The age of AI has also sped up exploitation where it's likely we are going to see scaled up attacks imminently across the internet."

What Organizations Should Do Now

PHP2Shell is a test of whether organizations can find, own, and update the software running across their environments. PHP has published fixes, but a release only reduces risk when the update reaches every affected runtime, including those inside products and services maintained by other vendors.

Organizations should:

Inventory systems running PHP, prioritizing internet-facing systems.

Monitor internet-facing PHP systems for suspicious activity.

Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, or apply the relevant vendor backport. Include products and services that bundle PHP.

Check PHP, distribution, and third-party vendor advisories for updates, especially when running PHP 8.1 or older.

If a system cannot be remediated promptly, consider taking it offline until it is fully mitigated.

For ongoing details and links to current advisories, see the official PHP security advisory.

Title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
Context: Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server
Full Text:
Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

Image: Shutterstock.com, Sashkin.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.
